If the Steelers had worn black pants with the bumblebee uniforms, I probably wouldn't have ranked them on this list, but they decided to wear a mustard-gold color that hurts your eyes just to look at.
It's been 12 years since the Packers have worn this throwback, and that's probably for the best. The Packers wore this throwback for the first time in 2010, and they wore it multiple times through the 2014 season. However, they did make one big change during that five-season span. In their first game with the throwback, they wore a brown helmet.
Green Bay packers 1929 throwback. pic.twitter.com/LgfV0AJzqK
When they wore the uniform for the final time in 2014, they wore a gold helmet (The NFL implemented a one-helmet rule from 2013-2021, so the Packers were only allowed to wear one helmet color in that span and that was their gold one. The one-helmet rule was rescinded in 2022 ).
. @packers throwback uniform is from 1929- year of first NFL title. Rodgers grateful it doesn't include leather helmet pic.twitter.com/chYdMdUiZb
I don't love either combo, but the version with the brown helmet is the one that we're officially putting at No. 5 on this list.
For the 100th anniversary of their franchise, the Giants went full Frankenstein in 2024, creating a throwback jersey that ended up combining a bunch of things they probably shouldn't have. They used a 1938 helmet design, a 1933…
author: John Breech

title: Ranking all 32 NFL edge rusher groups: Myles Garrett puts Rams at No. 1
summary: Edge rushers have never been more valuable, and several contenders enter 2026 with elite tandems capable of wrecking games
full_text:
The rich became richer when the Los Angeles Rams acquired Myles Garrett in the biggest trade of the 2026 NFL offseason. The chances of anyone containing this beastly defense and preventing the Rams from winning a second Super Bowl in six years became significantly slimmer when the transaction went through. But did the move automatically give Los Angeles the best edge rusher group in the league? There is stiff competition at the top.
Not only do the Houston Texans return an otherworldly tandem, and not only are the Denver Broncos coming off one of the greatest sack seasons by a team in NFL history, but the Baltimore Ravens are suddenly in the discussion, too, after trading for Trey Hendrickson .
Today's NFL landscape makes edge rushers more important than ever before. Containing the league's explosive passing attacks requires game-breakers, and the best are quickly becoming some of the most highly compensated players the sport has ever seen. Rostering one standout pass rusher is a necessity. Boasting two is no longer a luxury, but in many cases, the cost of entry into postseason contention.
Below are all 32 edge rusher situations in the NFL heading into the 2026 season, ranked from worst to best.
Key contributors: Chop Robinson , Josh Uche
The complete rebuild in Miami extends to the edge rushing unit. As a first-round pick two years ago, Robinson is the kind of young talent the Dolphins can build around if he begins to show signs of stardom. He has not taken that kind of step in the right direction, but his new coaching staff might be able to get him on track. Jeff Hafley is a bright defensive mind. If he cannot juice the potential out of Robinson, then maybe nobody can.
Key contributors: Jaelan Phillips , Patrick Jones II
If not for the injury Nic Scourton sustained on the first day of training camp, the Panthers would rank a healthy number of spots higher. Instead, his season is over before it even begins due to a torn ACL. Neither Phillips nor Jones is exactly reliable in terms of staying on the field, either, so the bottom has the threat of really falling out from underneath this group. Phillips is a plus starter when healthy, though, like he was all of last year.
Key contributors: John Franklin-Myers , Jermaine Johnson II , Jacob Martin, Keldric Faulk
Robert Saleh got the band back together. Each of Franklin-Myers, Johnson and Martin played for him during his New York Jets tenure. Perhaps their familiarity with each other and the bright moments they shared will make the unit better than the sum of its parts. If not, there is a first-round pick in Faulk behind them and ready to step into meaningful action as a rookie.
Key contributors: Boye Mafe , Demetrius Knight Jr. , Shemar Stewart , Myles Murphy
While the rest of the Bengals ' defense improved on paper this offseason, the edge rusher group said farewell to its leader, Trey Hendrickson. Mafe is an upside-oriented addition who will not fully replace Hendrickson's pass-rushing prowess, but who displayed flashes of greatness as a young starter for the Seattle Seahawks . The rest of the crew, plus second-round pick Cashius Howell , is extremely young. Cincinnati is banking on its last few drafts starting to pay off. It just might pay dividends, but it is impossible to know for sure until it actually happens.
Key contributors: Odafe Oweh , K'Lavon Chaisson , Dorance Armstrong , Charles Omenihu
Washington would like to see fresh faces inject new life into an edge rusher group that was arguably the team's biggest need. They figure to give starting jobs to a couple of players who have never held full-time No. 1 roles, which always comes with some volatility. Oweh and Chaisson are proven, veteran contributors who might be in for career years in those expanded roles. A healthy amount of playable depth behind them reduces plenty of risk.
Key contributors: Josh Sweat , Zaven Collins , Baron Browning , Jordan Burch , BJ Ojulari
This will be a difficult season for the Cardinals , who have as strong a chance as anyone to secure the No. 1 pick in next year's draft. That is not to say Arizona is entirely devoid of talent, however. Sweat is a Pro Bowl-caliber edge rusher coming off a 12-sack campaign, after all. Nobody helped him out disrupting quarterbacks last season, so the perceived depth in a rotation-heavy pass rush is a bit of a mirage, but there is reason to think Burch could develop in his second year, and that Ojulari can finally jump up to a starting caliber now that he is healthy.
Key contributors: George Karlaftis , Felix Anudike-Uzomah , Ashton Gillotte
The Chiefs could have benefited from investing in a free agent edge rusher, but instead used second-round draft capital on R Mason Thomas . For a team that needed to boost its pass rush and is trying to capitalize on Patrick Mahomes ' prime, that was a bit puzzling. The disruptive ability of Chris Jones from the interior defensive line will always mask some of the deficiencies on the edge, though, and Karlaftis is a solid force in that latter part of the defensive front.
Key contributors: Harold Landry , Dre'Mont Jones
The edge unit was far from a primary reason why the Patriots reached the Super Bowl last year. To get back to the top of the AFC, New England needed to retool that group. It acquired both a ready-made starter in Jones and a high-potential rookie in second-rounder Gabe Jacas to accomplish that goal. Depth is still a concern here, but the one-two punch of Landry and Jones is no worse than what the Patriots got from a group last year that won the conference. Landry needs to get his knee right for this to work, though. It bothered him for most of 2025 and remains an issue heading into training camp.
Key contributors: Will McDonald IV , Joseph Ossai , Kingsley Enagbare , David Bailey
Aaron Glenn revamped his defense as his job depends on it. The floor is seemingly higher in 2026 than it was during the dreadful previous campaign, but it is hard to argue that the ceiling is also raised. The Ossai and Enagbare additions are solid but nothing special. If the group improves dramatically, it will be because Bailey, the No. 2 pick, shines in his first year as a pro. An instant-impact standout in Bailey would be a pleasant running mate for McDonald and would form a riveting young duo.
Key contributors: Yaya Diaby , Al-Quadin Muhammad , Anthony Nelson , Rueben Bain Jr .
What if Al-Quadin Muhammad becomes more consistent? 7.5 of his 11 sacks last year came in three games, while he fell completely silent in a handful of others. That is the next step in proving his mid-career breakout is real. Whether it is him or rookie first-rounder Bain that locks down the No. 2 role, Tampa Bay will be in solid shape with Diaby holding down the other side. The fourth-year pro is extremely well-rounded as a pass rusher and run stopper and could have a long career ahead of him as a great (albeit short of elite) starting weapon.
Key contributors: Laiatu Latu , Arden Key , JT Tuimoloau , Micheal Clemons
Latu took the exact kind of second-year leap the Colts wanted from the former No. 15 overall pick and holds the potential to be the face of this defense for years to come. If Tuimoloau makes that same progress in his sophomore campaign, the edge rushing corps will be rolling. Key was a nice insurance policy to grab in free agency, as he can be a reliable part-timer next to Latu if JTT does not take off. Since 2021, Key has delivered no fewer than four sacks and no more than 6.5 in a season. Indianapolis knows exactly what it can expect.
Key contributors: Rashan Gary , Donovan Ezeiruaku , Malachi Lawrence
The post-Micah Parsons pass rush in Dallas is actually starting to come together quite well. That is not to say Jerry Jones made the right call moving on from his superstar last summer, but he at least made the most of the assets he received in return. One of those picks went toward grabbing Lawrence at No. 23 in April's draft. Between his potential, the strong…

title: Five Patriots with the most to prove at training camp after surprise Super Bowl run
summary: After going from 4-13 to AFC champions, the Patriots now have to prove last season was the start of something sustainable
full_text:
The New England Patriots bring a new level of expectations to the 2026 season. Their turnaround was quick, but whether they can maintain that momentum is the bigger question.
Heading into last year, quarterback Drake Maye was about to play his first full season as a starter. Mike Vrabel just took the job, and they were coming off a 4-13 season. This year, the Patriots are defending AFC Champions with Maye as the MVP runner-up and Vrabel earning Coach of the Year.
Was 2026 just a flash in the pan for the Pats? Or are they back to being a threat to the AFC, just as they were for two decades during the Tom Brady-Bill Belichick Era?
These questions will be answered in part by the performance of a few key players with a lot to prove. Some need to prove themselves after a bad playoff performance; others need to show they can bounce back from injury; some need to prove their contract is worth it; while others need to step up not only as leaders but as the star the team needs and lacked last season.
Here are the five players with the most to prove during training camp:
If you watched Super Bowl LX, or any of New England's playoff run, you know why Will Campbell is listed. He wasn't the same player after coming back from a MCL tear he suffered in Week 12 , and his performance dipped significantly when it counted most.
Campbell allowed 29 pressures during the playoffs, the most in the league since 2016. The 2025 No. 4 overall pick was credited with allowing one of the five Maye sacks in the Super Bowl and four total in the playoffs. Maye ate 21 postseason sacks, an NFL record.
This is the biggest of Maye's three years in the league. In his rookie season, he experienced growing pains, and last season, he adjusted to a new coach and exceeded expectations. This year, however, the pressure is on more than ever; the lights are bright, the schedule is more difficult, and with an upgraded roster, his play should naturally improve.
He won't get as many passes (no pun intended) for missteps this year as he had the first two years in the league. How he builds relationships with the new players, specifically A.J. Brown, will be paramount. Maye needs better results in the red zone, needs to take fewer sacks (which is also on his protection), and needs to improve ball security.
A trip to the Super Bowl is great, but the criticisms of the easy schedule are valid . Maye needs to prove that last year wasn't a fluke and that he can remain a top QB in the league. We've seen it before, where a quarterback explodes one year, then doesn't ever quite reach that same height in future years, and this is Maye's time to prove he won't be added to that conversation.
Wide receiver A.J. Brown heads to Foxboro after a rollercoaster experience with the Philadelphia Eagles . The Patriots desperately needed a reliable WR1 for some time, and Brown was brought in to be that guy. Their lack of a real star wideout lately has made both the teams and fans desperate for someone who can fill that role.
As Vrabel's former player with the Tennessee Titans , there is familiarity.
Brown needs to prove he was worth what the Patriots gave up to acquire him , a 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick
The Patriots ranked 23rd in receiving yards last season (4.459), but were tied for fifth in receiving touchdowns (31). Stefon Diggs reached 1,000 yards receiving last year, but before that, the last Patriot to hit the mark was Julian Edelman in 2019. Diggs is not currently on the team, and Brown is looking like the best long-term option for a reliable receiver.
Christian Gonzalez believes he is the best cornerback in the game and wants to get paid as such. This week, Patriots owner Robert Kraft said the team made a contract offer that would make Gonzalez the highest-paid cornerback in the league. Los Angeles Rams ' Trent McDuffie currently holds that title, with an average salary of $31 million per year.
Gonzalez is eligible for an extension and was training at the camp despite not yet agreeing to a new contract. He could hold out as he looks to get the deal done, and how both sides handle the negotiations as training camp takes place will be one to watch.
The 24-year-old allowed just 14 completions on 36 targets, marking the lowest completion percentage against (38.8 percent) for a cornerback in the playoffs since at least 2018.
The 2023 No. 17 overall pick has shown his ability to be a shutdown corner in the league, and if he gets paid, the pressure will be on even more.
The Patriots' wide receiver room also includes Brown, Romeo Doubs , DeMario Douglas , Mack Hollins, and Kyle Williams, and they have a reliable pass-catcher in tight end Hunter Henry . Boutte is going to need to do a lot to stand out in camp with such a crowded WR room.
There are frequent trade talks surrounding Boutte, as the 2023 sixth-rounder enters the final year of his rookie contract. Boutte has done well through the first few days of practice, and Vrabel said the trade rumors haven't impacted the 24-year-old's focus or performance, noting that he's "off to a good start."
His prior chemistry with Maye should help his case, and he has shown the work ethic to keep his roster spot.
Vrabel defied expectations and won Coach of the Year, but it wasn't without criticism. Like Maye, the easy schedule came up often when discussing Vrabel's success last year. With a more difficult one this year, he can prove that it wasn't due to the easy opponents.
The elephant in the room is the off-field drama involving Vrabel and NFL reporter Dianna Russini. Photos of the two together were made public, causing uproar across the league. Some even suggested the Patriots could fire him. The dust has settled somewhat, and Vrabel still has his job, but with the situation still top of mind for many, Vrabel has a lot to prove as he meets with the team and the media. The 50-year-old needs to ensure he still has the team's trust and respect despite the distraction.
author: Shanna McCarriston

title: Biggest training camp storyline for every AFC team: Patrick Mahomes' return, Cam Ward's Year 2 leap and more
summary: The biggest question facing every AFC team entering training camp, from QB battles to contract talks and key injuries
full_text:
You know when you walk into a department store and see "Back to School" gear on the shelves and realize the school year is right around the corner? Well, that's effectively what training camp is in the NFL . With all 32 teams reconvening and laying the foundation for the upcoming season, Week 1 will be here before we know it.
While the 2026 regular season is fast approaching, there's still a lot that needs to be ironed out. That's why we're going to comb through the AFC and highlight one major storyline looming over each team. It could be a contract negotiation, recovery from a prior injury or a good old-fashioned position battle. If you're curious about the big questions in the NFC, my colleague Garrett Podell has you covered here .
What are some of the biggest stories lingering in the AFC as camp begins? Let's discuss.
Storyline to watch: New pieces being added to the pass rush unit
Yes, all eyes will be on new head coach Joe Brady and how the former offensive coordinator differentiates himself from the previous regime after his promotion. Dig a little deeper, though, and how Brady -- along with defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard -- gets the new edge rushers to mesh with the returning pieces could be the key to Buffalo finally getting over the hump. According to TruMedia, the Bills ranked 24th in the league in total pressures (198) in 2025 and 20th in total sacks (36).
Injuries and player absences contributed to those lackluster numbers, with defensive tackle Ed Oliver and edge rusher Michael Hoecht both missing time. With both expected back for 2026, they'll join edge rusher Bradley Chubb -- who signed a three-year, $52 million deal in free agency -- and second-round defensive end T.J. Parker out of Clemson. There's enough talent for this group to become a more serviceable pass rush, if not a strength of the defense. That depends, however, on Brady and Leonhard putting all the pieces together.
Storyline to watch: When will Christian Gonzalez's extension happen?
New England is fresh off a Super Bowl appearance and an offseason in which it improved in several areas. The last order of business, however, is undoubtedly the most expensive. All-Pro cornerback Christian Gonzalez is extension-eligible but has yet to receive what will likely be a market-setting contract.
Over the weekend, Patriots owner Robert Kraft told reporters the team has been negotiating with Gonzalez's camp and has made an offer that would make him the highest-paid player at his position and the highest-paid player in franchise history.
"We love Christian Gonzalez. We love him as a player, as a person, and that's why we've made an offer to him to make him the highest-paid player to ever play that position in the NFL," Kraft said, via ESPN . "And coincidentally, it is the highest contract in Patriots franchise history. So we're glad we drafted him, he's developed here, and we hope he'll be with us for a long time."
If that's true (and there's no reason to think it isn't), what's the holdup? With Seattle's Devon Witherspoon also seeking a market-setting deal, could that be the obstacle preventing this contract from getting over the finish line?
Storyline to watch: Who emerges in the WR room?
Miami is coming off a transformative offseason that included hiring a new head coach (Jeff Hafley), general manager (Jon-Eric Sullivan) and quarterback ( Malik Willis ). On top of that, the Dolphins gutted their wide receiver room, cutting bait with veteran Tyreek Hill and trading Jaylen Waddle to the Denver Broncos .
Before suffering a gruesome season-ending injury last year, Hill averaged 147 targets per season. Over that same stretch, Waddle averaged about 94 targets per season and saw 100 targets over 16 games in 2025. That's a massive share now up for grabs, and Miami didn't exactly bring in players who will automatically command most of those looks.
Malik Washington is the key holdover. The Dolphins also signed veterans Jalen Tolbert and Tutu Atwell in free agency and drafted Caleb Douglas (third round), Chris Bell (third), and Kevin Coleman Jr . (fifth) this spring.
Someone from this group needs to emerge as Willis' top target if Miami wants a chance to be competitive in 2026.
Storyline to watch: What version of Geno Smith is New York getting?
There's a new quarterback under center in East Rutherford, but he's a familiar face to Gang Green: Geno Smith. He returns to the Jets -- who drafted him in the second round in 2013 and with whom he spent four seasons -- after a decade away.
Naturally, the question is what version of Smith the Jets are getting in his second stint. Will it be the player who revitalized his career in Seattle? Or will it resemble the quarterback who threw an NFL-high 17 interceptions for the Raiders last season?
It's worth noting Smith played behind one of the NFL's worst offensive lines in Las Vegas last season and was sacked a league-high 55 times. The Jets have a much better offensive line, which could help him return to his Seattle form.
There's only one direction for New York's passing game to go after it ranked last in the NFL in passing yards per game (140.3) in 2025..
Storyline to watch: Can Shemar Stewart break out?
The Cincinnati Bengals deployed a ton of resources and capital into improving the defense this offseason. They signed defensive tackle Jonathan Allen , edge rusher Boye Mafe and safeties Bryan Cook and Kyle Dugger in free agency. They also traded the No. 10 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft to acquire star defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence and used a second-rounder to select Texas A&M pass rusher Cashius Howell .
Those newbies will almost certainly help bring Cincinnati to a more respectable level, but the team's 2025 first-rounder, Shemar Stewart, could be the X-factor.
It was a rocky rookie campaign for Stewart after being the No. 17 overall pick. A contract squabble disrupted his offseason before a Week 9 knee injury landed him on injured reserve. In eight games, he tallied one sack and 11 tackles.
Stewart is looking for a reset entering 2026, and he has drawn praise throughout the offseason program. If he can carry that momentum into training camp and set a foundation for a bounce-back Year 2, he will take the defense to new heights.
Storyline to watch: Shedeur Sanders vs. Deshaun Watson
The Browns have one of the more notable quarterbacks battles in the AFC, with Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders set to compete for the Week 1 job.
Watson has seemingly gained momentum throughout the offseason and has the inside track entering camp. That said, the 30-year-old missed all of the 2025 season after re-rupturing his Achilles. Injuries aside, Watson's Browns tenure has been abysmal, especially considering the haul it took to acquire him.
As for Sanders, the 2025 draft pick started seven games during his rookie season, going 3-4 as the starter and completing 57% of his passes for seven touchdowns, 10 interceptions and a 68.1 passer rating. Not exactly sterling numbers from the Colorado product.
Todd Monken, who replaced the fired Kevin Stefanski, hopes one of these signal-callers separates himself as the deserved starter before the season opener.
Storyline to watch: Mike McCarthy era begins
After 19 seasons in Pittsburgh, the Mike Tomlin era came to an end following the 2025 season, and the Steelers have since turned to Mike McCarthy to begin the next chapter in franchise history.
While Tomlin never endured a losing season, his Steelers also had one of the lowest ceilings among contenders late in his tenure. McCarthy, who is 174-112-2 in 18 seasons as a head coach and owns a Super Bowl title, is now tasked with leading Pittsburgh deeper into the playoffs. How he lays the foundation for his first season will be one of training camp's most intriguing storylines.
That's especially true because his arrival also reunites him with Aaron Rodgers , who was his quarterback in Green Bay. How quickly the two get back in sync will be vital if the future Hall of…

full_text: Arizona Cardinals quarterback Carson Beck (19) practices during training camp at State Farm Stadium in Glendale on July 26, 2026. | Joe Rondone/The Republic / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Does it matter? That’s the question the first couple of days of training camp has yielded when it comes to quarterback Carson Beck. He has been… a third round rookie. That is most rookie quarterbacks are taken before they deserve to be taken as part of paying the quarterback tax, you pay it by having to over invest. So, for a player like Carson Beck, he probably wasn’t worth the 65th pick, but if the Cardinals wanted a quarterback they had to pay that price. That also means he likely wouldn’t light things up immediately, especially coming from a program that had just a lot more talent than their opponents most of the time. My thing is that the only negative about Beck being bad in camp is that it may make them not be overly confident in putting him in games if they get to the point of needing to see someone other than Jacoby Brissett. With Beck, the signs of needing time were there. He wasn’t elite at Georgia or even at Miami, really being more of a game manager on really good teams. Which is fine in the NFL, if you are on a really good team. Maybe the Cardinals first team offense will be that, and he can be the game manager that gives them a chance week-in and week-out. Yet, from the scenes at camp, it has not been that way. Carson Beck has had a lot of *big* misses early in camp. Like, 5+ yards off target. Something to keep an eye on. — Theo Mackie (@theo_mackie) July 26, 2026 Carson Beck has not completed a single pass in either day more than 5 yards down the field pic.twitter.com/IT6cRLLTLW — JaguarGator9 (@JaguarGator9NFL) July 26, 2026 So that really asks again… does it matter?

title: No 2026 International games? The Cardinals originated this
summary: In May, when the NFL schedule was revealed, several things jumped off the map. For one, the Arizona Cardinals didn’t have any prime-time games. Secondly, with nine international contests, the Cardinals were omitted from this series as well. And then, Las Vegas made Arizona the underdog in every regular-season game this year. Ouch. RELATED: CARDINALS […]
full_text: In May, when the NFL schedule was revealed, several things jumped off the map. For one, the Arizona Cardinals didn’t have any prime-time games. Secondly, with nine international contests, the Cardinals were omitted from this series as well. And then, Las Vegas made Arizona the underdog in every regular-season game this year. Ouch. RELATED: CARDINALS NAMED AFTER THE COLOR – NOT THE BIRD The Cardinals should have at least had a game in Germany or maybe Spain. The league is playing in Australia and in France for the first time, and yet the Cardinals weren’t even mentioned as participating in either contest. The Cardinals invented having the NFL play in stadiums not located in North America. It would have been symbolic for Arizona to go to one of these countries and bring the NFL game to a new fanbase. But the original club was not invited, nor was it even in the conversation. Apparently, losing 14 games in the prior season will do that. The year was 1976. The date was August 16. The St. Louis Cardinals played the San Diego Chargers in a forgotten Week 3 preseason matchup in Japan. It was the first-ever NFL contest of any kind that was played outside of the confines of North America. Expanding the game Outside of the United States and Canada, in the 1970s, the game of American Football was like Americans watching cricket. People across the globe had no idea how the game was played: the rules were confusing, players wore huge padded uniforms, helmets obstructed each player’s face, plus the game was full of violence and collisions. The NFL got the bright idea that the league should attempt to take its game to the world, considering that the entire globe was considered an untapped resource. The NFL has always been aggressive towards seeking out new money trails. But the rest of the world was considered a super highway instead of a trail. It just needed some recognition and exposure, and that would involve hosting live games. So, the owners discussed it. They threw out ideas. There was some positivity involved, but also many doubts. After all, football, known as soccer to fans in the United States and Canada, was a worldwide sport. It didn’t have to be introduced to any other country on this planet. Fans already knew the game’s rules, and everyone played the game as a kid. But not American Football. While soccer didn’t require a size metric, American Football players were big. They were viewed as gladiators going into battle instead of playing a sport. The NFL liked the idea of playing in other countries, but the concept needed to be tested before the league would go all in. Where should they start? The short distance to Mexico? Maybe South America? This game needed to be regionally close so that airfare for two complete teams, coaches, support staff, front office personnel, cheerleaders, and medical staff would be cheaper. And then, all of that equipment had to be shipped, which wasn’t going to be inexpensive either. Not to mention the most obvious: Initially having to worry about a language barrier. This made an English-speaking country a priority. Yeah, none of that happened. The first game was all the way in Tokyo, Japan. This meant none of the conditions the owners suggested were going to be followed. Asia? Exactly how did this go about? The Mainichi Star Bowl The United States was entering a bicentennial year in 1976. Numerous activities and events occurred nationally to celebrate 200 years since becoming a new country. It just so happened that the City of St. Louis had a relationship with a city situated in central Japan called Suwa, located just over two hours from Tokyo. A Japanese-American named Frank Takahashi was a produce farmer from the Los Angeles area. He had just seen the NFL start two new franchises in two new cities. He knew at some point the league would offer another round of expansion. Seattle and Tampa Bay cost $16 million each. Takahashi thought an NFL team would do well in Japan, most likely to settle in Tokyo. And he wanted to own it. The idea was submitted to the NFL owners. They liked the idea of expanding the league’s reach and popularity. An exhibition game was suggested and financed by Takahashi through efforts with the NFL. The Rams were located in Los Angeles Rams while just south was the San Diego Chargers. It was decided that the Chargers would become one team, and after looking at their 1976 preseason schedule, their game against the St. Louis Cardinals was the best option, especially since St. Louis had a relationship with Suwa. For three preseason games, the Cardinals wore a Suwa, Japan, patch on their jerseys. Takahashi figured if the game was a complete sell-out, he would break even. But the experience and exposure would provide him with the inside edge if a team was ever considered in Japan. He believed that once the league got over there for the preseason game, the topic would be discussed. And so would he. Back then, playing an NFL regular-season game was out of the question for anywhere other than their own stadiums. In fact, that suggestion would have been laughable. But a preseason game? Teams played in non-NFL cities all the time back in the day, such as Columbus, Akron, Norfolk, Jacksonville, Sacramento, Tulsa, San Antonio, Birmingham, Hartford, and Orlando, just to name a few. An exhibition game that did not count in the standings? Keep that conversation going while the room grabs some Cokes and mixes another cold one. The Cardinals were coached by Don Coryell, while Tommy Prothro was the head coach of the Chargers, with team owners Bill Bidwill and Gene Klein. Takahashi was able to secure sponsors, the Mainichi Daily News and the Sports Nippon Newspaper Company . So, the game was dubbed “The Mainichi Star Bowl,” even though it was an NFL game instead of college, and was strictly an exhibition. The Japanese did not care, plus it was something they had never seen before. After all, American football players were huge compared to the people of Japan. LINK: KORAKUEN STADIUM Korakuen Stadium in Tokyo was built in 1937 as a baseball stadium and home field to the Nippon Ham Fighters of the Pacific League. Michael Jackson and Madonna would later hold performances there. It held 45,000 for concerts and 38,000 for football, but decades later was demolished to make room for a high-rise, the Tokyo Dome Hotel. The Chargers flew out of San Diego, and the Cardinals left from San Francisco after a four-hour flight from St. Louis. Both planes refueled in Alaska. After all, it was a 13-hour flight. The Cardinals’ players, coaches, trainers, cheerleaders, and front office personnel all stayed at the “New Otani Hotel” with plenty of time to go sightseeing. The Chargers stayed at the “Grand Palace Hotel.” Players who didn’t want the local food ended up at a McDonald’s just down the street. Today, when an NFL game is played in an international city, the media is everywhere, and the locals and the hometown media photograph everything the players do. Back then, both rosters of players were just an oddity in the streets—very large men who obviously didn’t fit the surroundings. Players gave their hosts some impromptu football camps, which were interesting to see Japanese players in shoulder pads and helmets. Keep in mind, this was right in the middle of training camp, so the two teams practiced every day in full pads in the morning during their 8-day stay, then had free time to explore the city. The Cardinals had to get into their uniforms in their hotel rooms, parade through the hotel lobby, and then were shuttled on a bus. American Football players in full pads were an unusual sight, like Roman gladiators walking towards the arena – without the bus, that is. The playing field was Astro-Turf. Because it was a baseball stadium being used for only one football game, the lines used for football were lined with flour. It was played in humid, misty rain, and the cooking agent would cake and sometimes start to rise, which would clog up…

full_text: The perception of Tua Tagovailoa is that his sharp processing and accuracy can’t make up for his limitations as a quarterback. No matter how well-constructed an offense can be from a personnel and schematic standpoint, he will leave you wanting more. That is one of the biggest reasons why the Miami Dolphins failed to win a playoff game at their peak in the past five years. Those shortcomings will leave fans pondering how many games he could start in Atlanta. Michael Penix Jr. will return at some point. It’s hard to imagine him being completely disregarded, as he possesses the attributes and intangibles you want to see from a quarterback. That will leave Tagovailoa without much margin for error. Unless he regains his 2023 Pro Bowl form, the pressure will ramp up for Penix Jr. to be back on the field. That will take time due to the young quarterback’s devastating ACL injury from last November. It’s one of the main reasons why Tagovailoa will start plenty of games in Atlanta, regardless of his overall performance. In a close vote, more fans believe the former top five overall pick will start until November. Although many are optimistic he starts for most of the season, there is slightly greater belief in Penix Jr. taking over after a difficult stretch where the Falcons will play teams like the 49ers, Bears, and Bengals. This result is brought to you by FanDuel Sportsbook.

title: What Lamar Jackson’s film and record with the Ravens actually show
summary: Welcome back to former Raven Femi Ayanbadejo’s four-part series on Lamar Jackson. Part One examined why the narrative surrounding the two-time MVP requires a reset. In Part Two, Femi tests criticism of Jackson’s play against the film and data and resets the remaining goalpost where it belongs: the Super Bowl.  In December 2023, Fox Sports […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - APRIL 26: Lamar Jackson of Louisville poses after being picked #32 overall by the Baltimore Ravens during the first round of the 2018 NFL Draft at AT&T Stadium on April 26, 2018 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Tom Pennington/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to former Raven Femi Ayanbadejo’s four-part series on Lamar Jackson. Part One examined why the narrative surrounding the two-time MVP requires a reset. In Part Two, Femi tests criticism of Jackson’s play against the film and data and resets the remaining goalpost where it belongs: the Super Bowl. In December 2023, Fox Sports Radio host Monse Bolanos argued that Jackson did not deserve the MVP. “I want my quarterbacks to be quarterbacky,” she said. “To me, Lamar Jackson’s just a great athlete.” The backlash was swift. ‘Quarterbacky’ became somewhat of a rallying cry for the Ravens in press conferences and social media posts. Ray Lewis and LeBron James clowned the take. Jackson, as always, did his talking on the field, throwing five touchdowns and recording the third perfect passer rating of his career. The word exposed a framing that has followed Jackson since before he was drafted: the tendency to strip him of intellectual credit and reduce him to his physical gifts. When another quarterback escapes pressure, it is called creativity or processing. When Jackson does it, the play is often described as instinct, as though elite cognition and elite athleticism cannot occupy the same body. Jackson is the “and.” Instinct and intellect. Improvisation and structure. Creativity and discipline. The Common-Denominator Argument This past June, Emmanuel Acho argued that Baltimore had again changed coordinators while its postseason results remained the same, making Jackson the common denominator. The phrase sounds conclusive, but it confuses continuity with causation. Jackson is a common denominator, but not the only one. Identifying him as present in every loss does not establish how much responsibility he carries for each one. As the face of the franchise, he takes blame for the team’s shortcomings without a full accounting of his actual responsibility for each. When it comes to coordinators, Jackson is actually the common denominator of success. In Greg Roman’s first full season as OC, he led the Ravens to the No. 1 seed in the AFC and earned a unanimous MVP. After Todd Monken was hired in 2023, he repeated the feat (with 49 of 50 MVP votes). Those offenses were not identical. Roman emphasized the zone-read game and a record-setting rushing attack. Monken expanded the route tree, spacing, progression game, and Jackson’s responsibility as a passer, even while Baltimore remained committed to the run. Jackson thrived in both systems – better yet, both systems thrived because of Jackson. The playoffs require a more exact audit. In his first two losses to the Chargers (2018) and the Titans (2019), Jackson’s late production did not erase slow starts, turnovers, and missed opportunities. His pick-six against the Bills in 2020 was decisive. And though Baltimore’s abandonment of the run is partially to blame for the heartbreaking 2023 AFC Championship loss to the Chiefs, Jackson also pressed, held the ball, and threw a costly end-zone interception. Those are not imaginary failures. They belong in his evaluation. Other losses require shared attribution. Protection, play selection, penalties, drops, fumbles by teammates, and defensive performance also shape elimination games. “Common denominator” is a starting question, not a completed analysis. The responsible conclusion is that Jackson has contributed materially to several playoff losses without being the sole explanation for Baltimore’s postseason record. What the Regular-Season Record Shows Jackson ended the 2025 season tied with Aaron Rodgers for the highest qualifying career passer rating in NFL history at 102.2. In 2024, he produced a 119.6 passer rating from the pocket. He shares the record of four qualifying perfect-passer-rating games with Peyton Manning and Ben Roethlisberger. He is the first quarterback to throw at least 40 touchdown passes with fewer than five interceptions in a season. In other words, his passing production is not simply the byproduct of scrambling. In Jackson’s 2019 MVP season, 25 of his 36 touchdown passes came from the pocket. Warren Sharp’s charting showed Jackson leading quarterbacks from the start of 2024 in touchdown passes traveling more than 10 yards through the air, while also ranking first in red-zone passing efficiency and EPA per attempt on throws released within 2.5 seconds over the same period. Film provides the mechanism behind the numbers. Jackson manipulates second-level defenders with his eyes and legs, resets throwing platforms without surrendering vision downfield, and turns simulated pressure into favorable space. Under Monken, he showed greater patience through full-field concepts and more willingness to win from inside the structure. His mobility changes coverage rules, but exploiting the resulting leverage still requires recognition, timing, and accuracy. Athletic stress creates the question. Quarterback play supplies the answer. That distinction matters when commentators treat the effect of Jackson’s legs as evidence against his passing. A quarterback does not lose intellectual credit because one elite trait creates opportunities for another. Every great player forces defenses to overreact to what he does best. Durability in Context Joe Burrow is an exceptional quarterback and belongs in any discussion of the league’s elite. Durability, however, is part of quarterback value. From his 2020 debut through the 2025 regular season, Burrow missed roughly one-third of Cincinnati’s games because of injury. Jackson missed less than 10 percent of Baltimore’s regular-season games because of injury over his career through 2025 and has not undergone surgery. This comparison does not diminish Burrow. It demonstrates how selectively availability enters quarterback debates. Jackson’s open-field style is regularly presented as a durability liability even though his actual injury history has been less severe than that of several celebrated pocket passers. Where the Criticism Is Valid Jackson’s postseason record is 3-5. His postseason passer rating is 84.6, far below his regular-season standard. Across eight playoff games, he has thrown 10 touchdown passes and seven interceptions, taken 29 sacks, and committed additional fumbles. The exact fumble total varies by statistical classification, but the conclusion does not: his elimination-game ball security has been materially worse than his regular-season norm. The performance is not static. In his four most recent playoff games through the 2024 season, Jackson completed 70 percent of his passes, produced seven passing touchdowns against two interceptions, and posted two of the best postseason performances of his career. That improvement matters. So does the fact that Baltimore did not finish the job. The fairest critique is specific: Jackson has sometimes pressed when the game turned against Baltimore, held the ball while searching for an explosive answer, and exposed the offense to sacks or turnovers. The coaching staff has compounded that problem by departing from its identity in critical moments. Both can be true. Accountability does not require assigning every failure to one person. It requires identifying what that person controlled. Jackson does not need to prove that he can play quarterback, win from the pocket, master different systems, or produce historically efficient seasons. The unresolved requirement is narrower and more demanding: carry his regular-season decision-making and ball security through four championship-level postseason performances. That is a legitimate question. But really, it’s the only one left.
author: Femi Ayanbadejo

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 training camp position battle primer: LB
summary: In the last installment of this series, we covered the defensive line — Ed Oliver’s every-down workload and the battle behind Deone Walker on the Buffalo Bills’ roster. Now we move to the second level of Jim Leonhard’s new 3-4 system, where two rookies have real runways to snaps and Terrel Bernard’s own health might […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - DECEMBER 21: Terrel Bernard #8 of the Buffalo Bills returns a fumble during the second quarter against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on December 21, 2025 in Cleveland, Ohio. The fumble was ruled an incomplete pass. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images In the last installment of this series, we covered the defensive line — Ed Oliver’s every-down workload and the battle behind Deone Walker on the Buffalo Bills’ roster. Now we move to the second level of Jim Leonhard’s new 3-4 system, where two rookies have real runways to snaps and Terrel Bernard’s own health might end up deciding who plays where. Kaleb Elarms-Orr is fighting for a starting job and auditioning as Buffalo’s answer at Bernard’s own spot if things go wrong. T.J. Parker’s path isn’t as open, but it isn’t closed either. As training camp opens today, we dive into the linebackers — a group that bears watching throughout the rest of summer. Bills’ LB depth chart entering camp Inside Linebacker: Terrel Bernard, Dorian Williams, Kaleb Elarms-Orr, Joe Andreessen, Keonta Jenkins, Demetrius Flannigan-Fowles, Theron Gaines, Jimmy Ciarlo Outside Linebacker (EDGE): Greg Rousseau, Bradley Chubb, T.J. Parker, Michael Hoecht, Javon Solomon, Mike Danna, Andre Jones Jr., Cade Denhoff Inside Linebacker: Kaleb Elarms-Orr vs. Dorian Williams This is the battle to watch all camp, and it’s a two-layered one. On the surface, it’s about who starts next to Bernard. Beyond that, it could be about who becomes Buffalo’s answer at Bernard’s own spot if his health issues continue trending the wrong way. Elarms-Orr has impressed the coaching staff from the moment he arrived, has said openly that he’s targeting the starting job from day one, and has already gotten first-team looks during minicamps — opportunities that exist in large part because Williams’ injury opened that door for him. I believe he has everything needed to win this outright as a rookie. But Williams isn’t handing this over easy. He brings traits that fit what Leonhard wants defensively, and a healthy Williams is a real problem for a rookie trying to take his job. Either way, this camp carries double duty for Elarms-Orr: he’s competing to start now, and effectively auditioning to be the answer at Bernard’s spot too if the captain’s body doesn’t cooperate. That dual-stakes situation is exactly why I have this at the top of my watch list all camp. The Terrel Bernard Factor Speaking of Bernard, the talent was never the question. Health is. Bernard has put together genuinely elite stretches before — in 2023 and 2024 he was playing at as high a level as any linebacker in the NFL — but he’s also spent long chunks of recent seasons playing through injuries and taking on blockers in space with little help clearing a path in front of him. Does Leonhard’s scheme actually change that? Does it let him play cleaner and finally stay on the field for a full season? Or do we watch the same pattern repeat, with Bernard doing more than his share of the dirty work because the players ahead of him aren’t doing theirs? Scheme fit can only do so much here — a lot of this still comes down to luck. It’s exactly why Elarms-Orr’s camp matters as much as it does for the rookie. Joe Andreessen is the presumptive first man off the bench right now when thinking green dot, but “presumptive” is doing a lot of work in that sentence. He still has to prove it in these same camp battles. Keonta Jenkins, Demetrius Flannigan-Fowles, Theron Gaines, and even Jimmy Ciarlo (more of a special-teams piece than a defensive one), are all fighting to show enough in hopes of earning a depth spot, or, for some of them, just a practice squad look. If Bernard can’t stay on the field and this Williams-Elarms-Orr battle doesn’t produce someone ready to step up and hold the job, I wouldn’t rule out Buffalo circling back to Matt Milano or Shaq Thompson on a short-term, hole-filling deal. Neither has retired, and neither has signed elsewhere. That’s not the plan right now — it’s the contingency if the plan doesn’t work. Cuts here: I’d expect just four ILBs making the team, with a couple of them (at least) being carried on the practice squad. Right now I’d keep Jenkins on the 53. Andreesen, Jenkins, Flannigan-Fowles, and Gaines fight for this last spot, and also with Ciarlo for a practice squad spot. Positional battle interest level: High Outside Linebacker: The starters and T.J. Parker’s real opportunity There isn’t much debate on paper here. Rousseau and Chubb should be the undisputed starters at outside linebacker in this 3-4, full stop. The question is durability, not talent. The rookie clearly isn’t walking into a starting job — Chubb is genuinely better than he gets credit for right now, in my opinion, and he’s not losing his spot to a rookie based on merit alone. But Chubb also comes with his own physical questions, and that’s where Parker’s real opening lives. If Chubb deals with anything physically this season, I could see Parker not just stepping into snaps but out-snapping the starter across from him. That’s a real possibility, as long as he’s ready, even without a clean path to a Week 1 starting job. The rotation behind starting OLBs Michael Hoecht, working his way back from a torn Achilles, is the other complementary piece I expect the Bills to lean on, alongside Parker. That’s the quartet I think Buffalo trusts to generate pressure off the edge in 2026: Rousseau, Chubb, Parker, and Hoecht. He seems to be closer to his return than people believe, but if he really needs more time, there are some options. Javon Solomon is fighting to establish his value in a scheme that fits his style better than the old one did, and he’s someone who could push for real snaps if he shows well early. Mike Danna is the steadying veteran presence here — extremely experienced, and he sets a real floor for this group. If the Bills chose the conservative route with Hoecht, he’s a lock to make the team. Andre Jones Jr. and Cade Denhoff round out the group. I’m not expecting much beyond them showing enough effort to make a case for a practice squad spot, but the top four in this room feels well settled and unlikely to change much between now and Week 1. Cuts here: Jones Jr. and Denhoff are the ones I’d flag as the longest shots to make the initial 53, more likely candidates for the practice squad if either sticks around at all. Solomon has to show more or his spot on the 53-man roster could be in danger. Positional battle interest level: Medium Final Thoughts Two rookies, two very different runways. Elarms-Orr’s path to real snaps is wide open — he can win a starting job outright and double as Buffalo’s insurance policy at Bernard’s spot in the same camp. Parker’s path is narrower on paper, but Chubb’s own durability questions mean the opportunity is still there if things break right. Bernard can still be the engine of this defense when healthy — the real question is whether he stays that way, and whether Leonhard’s scheme gives him the help he hasn’t always had. Catch up on the series: Part 1: QB, RB and OL Part 2: WR and TE Part 3: Defensive Line Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: RB Ty Johnson
summary: The Buffalo Bills had a devastating rushing offense last season. Their top dog led the entire league in rushing yardage, becoming the first Bills player to earn that honor since NFL Hall of Fame running back O.J. Simpson did it during the 1976 season. The players who served as backups last season weren’t slouches, either. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 04: Ty Johnson #26 of the Buffalo Bills runs for a touchdown in the second quarter against the New York Jets at Highmark Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills had a devastating rushing offense last season. Their top dog led the entire league in rushing yardage, becoming the first Bills player to earn that honor since NFL Hall of Fame running back O.J. Simpson did it during the 1976 season. The players who served as backups last season weren’t slouches, either. With all of Buffalo’s top running backs returning this season, there’s a natural inclination to run it back with the same group. Do the financials make sense — and should that matter in making the decision? In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a running back whose role might seem small, but whose absence during the postseason was definitely felt. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Ty Johnson Number: 26 Position: RB Height/Weight: 5’10”, 210 pounds Age: 28 (29 on 9/17/2026) Experience/Draft: 8; selected by the Detroit Lions in the sixth round (No. 186 overall) of the 2019 NFL Draft College: Maryland Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 8/21/2023 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Johnson enters the final year of the two-year deal he signed prior to last season. For the 2026 NFL season, Johnson’s cap hit is $3.275 million. Buffalo can release Johnson prior to Week 1 and carry a dead-cap hit of just $820,000. As a vested veteran, his base salary ($2.22 million) becomes fully guaranteed if he’s on Buffalo’s roster for Week 1, however. 2025 Recap: Johnson had basically the same role in Buffalo’s offense during the 2025 season as he did during the 2024 season. He did see a slight uptick in playing time, as he increased his offensive snap count from 316 snaps to 335 and his touch total from 59 touches in 2024 to 74 touches in 2025. Johnson carried 50 times for 200 yards and three touchdowns last season, adding 24 catches for 263 yards and two more receiving scores on 33 targets. He appeared in all 17 regular season games for the second straight season, but a high ankle sprain suffered during the regular-season finale made it so that he missed both of Buffalo’s postseason games. Johnson also did some work on special teams for the Bills, totaling two tackles and returning 11 kickoffs for 240 yards (21.8 yards per return). Positional outlook: Johnson is one of five running backs on the current roster. James Cook III, Frank Gore Jr., Ray Davis, and Ian Wheeler are the others. 2026 Offseason: Johnson is fully healthy, having participated all offseason, and he’s ready to go for the start of training camp. 2026 Season outlook: Buffalo has to decide a few things as it relates to Johnson this season. First, what is his role in the offense. Second, is that role worth a top-20 cap hit on the club? While Johnson was angling towards being the primary kickoff return man, he was surpassed by Ray Davis last season in that role. Davis is also a very good backup running back, and James Cook proved that he could be a workhorse by leading the entire NFL in rushing yardage. Is there room for Johnson on the roster, or should the Bills go with a younger, less expensive player in his place? There is definitely room for Ty Johnson on the current Buffalo roster, and it’s hard to say that he isn’t head-and-shoulders better than at least Gore Jr. Perhaps Wheeler will come in and show explosiveness and ability in the passing game to make his case for Johnson’s role, but given the success that No. 26 has had in that role over the last two-plus seasons, it’s hard to see anyone on the current roster pushing him off of it. Even if we’re looking at finances only, Johnson’s cap hit doesn’t make me shy away from keeping him. If they release him, the team would have to eat that $820,000 dead-cap charge and keep one of Gore Jr. or Wheeler, whose cap hits are $885,000. Is it worth saving $1.5 million to downgrade a spot on the team that will see guaranteed use? Unless that $1.5 million is going to go to use this year at another position of need, I don’t know how I feel about it. Johnson’s cap hit has him at RB35, which is probably a little rich for his actual output. However, he’s a solid contributor in multiple phases of the game. He’s likely going to be on the team, and he’ll likely see plenty of run on third downs and in spelling Cook this season.

title: Bills Mafia should have seen “Nickel City” uniform coming
summary: It’s pretty wild how the Buffalo Bills kept the new Nickel City gray unis under wraps if I’m being candid. I wrote this post accusing them of stealing my idea, and that post was in mid-April. That’s notable because at the time, there wasn’t even a whisper really about new uniforms and in just over […]
full_text: It’s pretty wild how the Buffalo Bills kept the new Nickel City gray unis under wraps if I’m being candid. I wrote this post accusing them of stealing my idea, and that post was in mid-April. That’s notable because at the time, there wasn’t even a whisper really about new uniforms and in just over three months here they are. That said, astute fans of the Buffalo Bills and their uniforms maybe should have seen these coming. How did we miss this trend? Real fans of the Buffalo Bils that have been following the modern era uniforms know that they all draw their inspiration from the same source. The Smurfs. Yes. The Smurfs. All Bills uniforms can be broken down into their Smur-errific varriant. Don’t believe me? Let’s give it a whirl. True Smurf/Classic Smurf Traditionally, Smurfs wear white pants, have blue skin, and white hats. The resemblance is uncanny. The Smurfette look One iconic Smurf happens to reverse the look a bit. James Cook is looking good with Smurfette’s iconic white hat, white top/dress, and blue leg look. See? I’m not crazy, there really is a good connection to Smurf-dom. Naked Smurfs Two thoughts. Yes, this wouldn’t quite be a naked Smurf as he’s still wearing his hat, but it’s nude enough. Secondly, if you thought I was going to post an image of an actual nude Smurf, you have the wrong website and I’m not sure I want to know what the “right” one would be. Papa Smurf I don’t believe the Buffalo Bills have done a proper Papa Smurf (red helmet, blue jersey, red pants), but I have to imagine that someone as dapper as Papa Smurf has various outfits for different occasions. Now to be fair, they technically have all the components, but they’ve yet to put them all in on one uniform (and I’m not sure they’d be allowed to honestly). But there’s variants of Papa Smurf. In order of the images above, I call these… Half-Daddy Smurf (traditional male Smurf with the bare torso, but only half the attire says “Papa”) Semiformal Papa (white and red tux/suit) Bathrobe Papa Actually, the one variant could be Painter or Slouchy Smurf. Karate Smurfs Now we’re getting into the deeper-dive stuff. I used the Rivalries jerseys here, but any all whites will do (I just like the extra sparkle). It may have only been one episode, but there was a time when the Smurfs put on all whites to learn karate. Right Skare, but none of the Smurfs wore gray Well, you’re just not looking hard enough. The Smurfs were not just the cartoon I grew up with. Various cartoons have occurred over the years, and there have even been comic books. Let me introduce you to the “Gray Smurfs” and the “Pluffs.” Who the heck are the Gray Smurfs and the Pluffs? The grays are from a comic book aptly called “The Smurf Menace.” The Pluffs are from a more recent cartoon. In both cases, the gray variants of the Smurfs are opposite of the regular ones. Handy Smurf can build or fix pretty much anything. Gray Handy is more likely to break things. So if you’re wondering what the future of Buffalo Bills uniforms might have in store for us, we might want to start doing some deep dives into Smurf lore. We don’t want to be caught off guard again. Sabres crossover Smurf?

title: Buffalo Bills training camp will be a major regional draw in 2026
summary: The results of our latest Reacts poll are in, and the numbers reveal a few interesting things. This past week, we asked Rumblers if they were going to Buffalo Bills training camp in 2026 or not, or if they simply hoped to go and hadn’t yet found tickets. If you’ve been to Bills camp before, […]
full_text: The results of our latest Reacts poll are in, and the numbers reveal a few interesting things. This past week, we asked Rumblers if they were going to Buffalo Bills training camp in 2026 or not, or if they simply hoped to go and hadn’t yet found tickets. If you’ve been to Bills camp before, you know how busy it can get on the east side of Rochester at this time of year. Since Josh Allen’s rise to stardom, getting tickets to training camp (and even getting somewhat close to the action on the field) has proven nearly impossible for most fans who don’t have season tickets (or corporate sponsor perks). The Bills are big business in Rochester during training camp, and every other day of the year. Midsummer is a tough point in the calendar, where those who work in the corporate world are often limited by their bank of vacation days. Many folks have used up a healthy amount of those days by now, having spent time with family and friends around the paid summer holidays or on planned trips. That means for those Bills fans living far away from Western NY, there’s a need to carefully plan if the goal is to be in Rochester, NY at the end of July. It’s a commitment that’s also impacted by fans’ regular-season plans. Based on the results of our poll, it’s fair to guess that most people planning to attend camp are local or within a reasonable day’s drive of St. John Fisher University. Regional fandom is the lifeblood of any sports team. Our poll returned with 52% of voters saying “no” to attending training camp. Mind you, this number could also represent those who do live close enough to attend, or who could have tried for tickets and just didn’t make the effort. Yet 52% is a sizeable majority in this poll, which still makes me think we’re seeing regional results at play where many voters simply don’t live close enough to make it work. Conversely, 39% of voters say “yes” they’ll be attending camp. Buffalo Rumblings meetup, anyone? To me, the most interesting figure is the 9% of voters who said “yes, if I get tickets.” These are the fans who could change the “yes” votes to as much as 48% if lucky to get tickets, or raise the “no” votes to as much as 61% if unable to secure passes. Wanting to go to camp and missing out on tickets stinks. It wasn’t that long ago that almost everyone who wanted to go was able to do so, but Josh Allen and winning changes the formula. As someone who has struggled to get tickets every summer since the drought was broken, I have the following advice to offer: If you’re close enough to go on a moment’s notice, do so. Get there well before camp opens up for the day and stand at entrance gate, where sometime people will have extra tickets to pass along. There are even cases where people have their unused ticket scanned for anyone who shows up without one. It doesn’t hurt to ask, which includes the ticket-scan folks. If you’re having FOMO, let it go. Training camp has become a massive event, and fans’ access to the team has changed as a result. The people who are there as guests of corporate sponsors tend to get the best experience, which includes heightened opportunities to interact with players and obtain autographs. To those attending for the first time, it can be difficult to find a place to sit around the action. There’s plenty of space to stand along fencing, and it helps to follow along to see what player groups are going where and for what purpose. I recommend bringing one of those cinch-sack backpacks. As a final bit of advice, if the bus trip and waiting to be picked up isn’t for you, you can drive right to camp and park where local residents have opened their property to campers. As recently as 2025, that would cost you $20 a trip. Time will tell if people have raised their prices for 2026. Think you’ve got what it takes to make a play with the Buffalo Bills in 2026? Head over to FanDuel Sportsbook now to put it to the test !

title: Buffalo Bills’ new uniform should have leaned into AFL roots
summary: With the Buffalo Bills unveiling their new “Nickel City” alternate uniforms, complete with a never-before used Bills Blue helmet, one thing was clear: They were ready to lean into Western New York’s heritage, its ethos. It’s impossible to dislike the intent, and you can be sure well-represented meetings were had about leaning into the historic […]
full_text: Sep 1, 2016; Detroit, MI, USA; Detroit Lions defensive tackle Stefan Charles (96) grabs Buffalo Bills quarterback Cardale Jones (7) by the helmet during the fourth quarter at Ford Field. Lions win 31-0. Mandatory Credit: Raj Mehta-Imagn Images With the Buffalo Bills unveiling their new “Nickel City” alternate uniforms, complete with a never-before used Bills Blue helmet, one thing was clear: They were ready to lean into Western New York’s heritage, its ethos. It’s impossible to dislike the intent, and you can be sure well-represented meetings were had about leaning into the historic culture of Bills Country. I’m somewhere down the middle with these new threads. By now I’ve seen the basic run of commentary, where many folks dislike it and say it’s too close to something the Detroit Lions would wear. I’m here to say that’s exactly what they should have done, leaning in harder and with a modern take on the team’s beginnings. It’s true that the NFL’s uniform policy grows more complex by the season. There are different sets of rules and regulations that are attached to teams’ pursuit of heritage (aka throwback) uniforms. Every NFL team is allowed to introduce new uniforms that aren’t throwbacks given they don’t deviate from the color palette of the franchise. It’s a far cry from uniform policies even 10 years ago. Now, the NFL understands that variety is the spice of life in uniforms, and it does well at checkout. I’m not here to say these Nickel City uniforms shouldn’t have been made. The NFL and Bills are a business, and new uniforms play a role. Instead I wish these came out a bit down the road, perhaps with some refinements such as a voice of reason explaining why a charging Bills logo should not lose the bison and connect the charge streak into a boomerang. Seeing these new uniforms does disappoint me only because they were so very close to finally honoring one of the team’s significant AFL uniforms that’s never received a throwback tribute in any form. For anyone who’s read my work here with Buffalo Rumblings long enough, they likely understand my affinity for the Bills’ first uniforms, as strange as they may appear to anyone new to their existence. Those inaugural uniforms were leftovers that founding owner Ralph C. Wilson Jr. borrowed from the Detroit Lions, which you can see in the following images: What you see is a Honolulu blue/silver/white uniform. Yes, as I noted above, those are in fact Lions threads. Check out the silver pants with blue/white stripes, and a simple white jersey with blue numbers on the front, back, and shoulders. Then there’s the simple white socks with blue stripes, and black shoes. Finally, that helmet. It’s simple with zero in the way of stripes or logos — a silver expanse dressed up with blue numbers above the ear holes. These uniforms were what the Buffalo Bills entered professional football wearing, and their Detroit roots was a natural connection for Wilson. The league would never allow teams to share uniforms today, but things were very different nearly 70 years ago. Understand, it isn’t that the team cannot still properly reproduce these uniforms, but we would all likely bet that doing so in the near future is far from guaranteed after this week’s uniform reveal. With the new alternates, perhaps it allows them to rethink any prior conversations about their inaugural uniforms. They’ve already fully embraced the grey, which is in the same family as silver. The 2026 season is being marketed as the inaugural season in the new Highmark Stadium. It made all the sense in the world to me that they might have rolled out a new interpretation of those first AFL uniforms — the ones that allowed the Bills to get where they are today. Instead of franchise heritage, they chose regional heritage, and that’s commendable. Besides, there’s always next season!

title: Highmark Trail at Bills’ new stadium offers unique experience
summary: If you haven’t heard, the Buffalo Bills will be playing their home games in a new stadium this season. Along with the new stadium, there’ll be plenty of new things to check out. The Bills commissioned numerous art installations to put around the stadium for instance. The large, broken folding table for instance. Cool new […]
full_text: If you haven’t heard, the Buffalo Bills will be playing their home games in a new stadium this season. Along with the new stadium, there’ll be plenty of new things to check out. The Bills commissioned numerous art installations to put around the stadium for instance. The large, broken folding table for instance. Cool new seat colors. There was some controversy on the design of a trio of giant bison statues, that will be the centerpiece of an area called the “Family Circle.” That’s where our journey begins… Highmark Trail The bison statues are installed, but as you can see from the exposed panels, there’s a little work to be done. Which is why I took this picture through a chain link fence. In the family circle area, you can see what is essentially a smaller and walkable version of the ring of honor from the old stadium. Unless something changes, as far as I can tell this area will be permanently available to the public. You’re reading that right, this area can be visited by anyone at any time. Incidentally, not to reignite the O.J. dialogue, but having his name up here would be a surefire vandalism target I’d imagine (perhaps another reason to not include him). I wasn’t paying a ton of attention to the sign markers at this stage of the trail walk, as we were only there for this… pic.twitter.com/yZmHrT8kTt — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 27, 2026 This is a snippet of the Musical Rush section on the trail. This has been publicized by the team, but I don’t think it’s possible to do this justice unless you’re there. Here’s the on-site description, with some Skare notes to follow. That’s not a bad way to describe it. For my attempt to do it right, the major yard markers have speakers. But all the yard markers have motion sensors. The major line and the several to either side of it all play from the same speaker. If you have multiple people, or quickly move between lines, you can mix the sounds to your liking. Iconic sounds are captured, including something that’s not exactly Mr. Brightside, but well… you’ll recognize it for sure. The Musical Rush area kept four of us entertained for quite some time. So far the bisons and the Musical Rush area are the only installations on the 1.4 mile walk, but there’s evidence of more to come. And did you notice that the signs have little cutouts in the shape of the charge stripe? As you can see from the signs, there’s plenty of evidence that this will be used to encourage wellness activities. Three of the signs suggest there will be fitness related installations. The 40-yard dash is intriguing. Will they just have start and stop lines? Or are they dreaming bigger. The powerlifting section surely won’t be a weight bench just hanging out waiting for someone to forget their spotter and remember their lawyer. The blank sign could be, well… anything. You could argue that there’s not a ton of reason to visit just yet, but I’d disagree. Some of the views of the new stadium are stunning. Wrapping up, I was a little surprised to see how much landscaping went into the design as well. You might notice small ponds in the background in a couple pictures. These were prominent on the back end of the stadium and are already attracting wildlife. I firmly scolded some geese for leaving some droppings on the trail. Grasswork is still coming in, but a robust sprinkler system suggests the Bills want it green and attractive. The family circle and area near the permanent fencing for the stadium all had attractive plants and greenery as well. The purpose seems to be clear: Get fans around the stadium grounds as much as possible. After taking a stroll along Highmark Trail, I think they’re onto something.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: ILB Joe Andreessen
summary: The Buffalo Bills haven’t shied away from bringing small-school players into the fold of late. They really haven’t been shy about looking 30 minutes up the Thruway by scouting and signing players from The University at Buffalo. Whether we’re talking about Cam Lewis, Ja’Marcus Ingram, or Tyree Jackson, the Bills have had plenty of representation […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 04: Linebacker Joe Andreessen #44 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates during the first quarter against the New York Jets at Highmark Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. The Bills defeated the Jets 35-8. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills haven’t shied away from bringing small-school players into the fold of late. They really haven’t been shy about looking 30 minutes up the Thruway by scouting and signing players from The University at Buffalo. Whether we’re talking about Cam Lewis, Ja’Marcus Ingram, or Tyree Jackson, the Bills have had plenty of representation from UB of late. There’s another player that we left out of that grouping, and that’s because he’s the subject of today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days.” _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Joe Andreessen Number: 44 Position: ILB Height/Weight: 6’1”, 240 pounds Age: 26 (27 on 2/7/2027) Experience/Draft: 3; signed with Bills following the 2024 NFL Draft College: University at Buffalo Acquired: UDFA signing Financial situation (per Spotrac): Andreessen enters the third and final year of his rookie deal, which is worth $2,832,500 overall. For the 2026 season he carries a cap hit of $1,075,834 if he makes the 53-man roster. Buffalo would carry a dead-cap charge of $834 if they were to release him. 2025 Recap: Andreessen continued living out his dream of playing for his childhood favorite team, making Buffalo’s 53-man roster once again. He played in all 17 regular-season games, starting two, amassing 35 tackles, two tackles for loss, and two quarterback hits. Although he played in more games overall, he actually totaled fewer snaps on defense last season, as his defensive snap total fell from 114 as a rookie to just 96 last season. However, he became an indispensible part of the Bills’ special teams unit, playing on 341 snaps in that phase. That was more than anyone on the Bills’ roster. Andreessen was credited with 23 tackles on special teams, which was tops among Bills players and second only to a former Bills player — Del’Shawn Phillips, who had 24 special teams tackles — in the entire NFL. Andreessen also had two tackles in the postseason, both of which came on special teams. Positional outlook: Andreessen is one of seven players listed at inside linebacker on the current roster. Terrel Bernard, Jimmy Ciarlo, Dorian Williams, Demetrius Flannigan-Fowles, Theron Gaines, and Keonta Jenkins are the others. Another linebacker, rookie Kalen Elarms-Orr, is listed merely at linebacker, but he is expected to play inside linebacker. 2026 Offseason: Andreessen is healthy and competing for time on defense during offseason workouts. 2026 Season outlook: Andreessen is far beyond a cute story at this point, as he is legitimately one of the best special teams players in the NFL. He is a far more dynamic athlete than many people realize, as he is fast (4.64-second 40-yard dash, 4.22-second 20-yard shuttle), strong (32 reps of 225 pounds on the bench press), and explosive (38” vertical and 10’2” broad jump). His Relative Athletic Score, or RAS, was a 9.35 based on his Pro Day results. In short, Andreessen is a dynamic athlete, not just some local kid living out a dream. Could a move to a more attack-oriented defense help him to earn more time on the field? It absolutely can. However, he still needs to be better in coverage, because he was a liability in his limited snaps in that phase of the game over the last two seasons. I assume that the Bills will slate Terrel Bernard in as one of the starters at inside linebacker, but Andreessen will have a shot to join him if he can beat out Dorian Williams and Kaleb Elarms-Orr. Given that we really have no idea how new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard will deploy his linebackers, there’s also a chance that Andreessen might see time on defense in unique packages and situations, as well. At worst, Andreessen is set to reprise his role as a demon on special teams. At best, a shift in scheme allows him to unlock the best version of himself, parlaying his elite athleticism into at least a two-down tackling machine. Either way, there’s little to no chance that the 53-man roster doesn’t include “Buffalo Joe” this season. He’s as close to a lock as there is for someone who isn’t a shoo-in for a starting role this season.
