summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - AUGUST 29: Mario Addison #97 of the Carolina Panthers looks on before their preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Bank of America Stadium on August 29, 2019 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jacob Kupferman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #46. Mario Addison I think you’d be hard pressed to find a more self made player than Mario Addison. He’s never had any prestigious pedigree or flash to his game, but he steadily improved as a football player to become an unlikely high level contributor for a number of years. He might not be a household name, but he was quietly a very good player for a pretty long time. And I bet you can’t guess where he ranks all time among Panthers in sacks. Addison was barely recruited out of high school and spent two years at junior college before transferring to noted football power Troy University. There, he had to redshirt a year before playing as a reserve player as a fourth year junior. He was able to break out just enough in his one season as a starter to get looks from NFL teams. He signed on with the Bears as an undrafted free agent, and while he made the team as a rookie, playing time was sparse, and he was ultimately cut. He bounced between practice squads and active rosters across four teams in his first two seasons. The last of those was the Carolina Panthers. Addison latched on as a rotational pass rusher and was quite productive in his somewhat limited playing time. He became a full time starter for the first time in his NFL career at age 30, and he responded by tallying 11 sacks and two forced fumbles for a Panthers team that went to the playoffs in 2017. He followed that with 9 sacks the next year and 9.5 the year after. He totaled at least six sacks in his last six years in Carolina and at least nine in his last four, the last three of which he was a starter. Addison departed after the 2019 to reunite with Sean McDermott and seemingly every other departed Panthers defender with the Buffalo Bills. He spent two seasons there before ending his career with a single season in Houston. Addison’s ascension is truly as gritty as they get. He incrementally improved basically from the time he was a senior in high school all the way through his first starting gig in the NFL at age 30. You almost never see that. His steady improvement, longevity, and consistent production led him to rack up 55 sacks in a Panthers jersey. That’s fourth in team history, just a half sack behind Mike Rucker. He’s a great story, and he was a great player. For that, he comes in at number 46 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 47 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - DECEMBER 04: Michael Vick #7 of the Atlanta Falcons evades a tackle by Will Witherspoon #54 of the Carolina Panthers during a game on December 4, 2005 at the Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Sporting News via Getty Images via Getty Images) | Sporting News via Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #47. Will Witherspoon Among the litany of great Panthers linebackers in their relatively short existence, Will Witherspoon was often overlooked. The Panthers selected Witherspoon in the third round of the 2002 NFL Draft. That particular draft had a handful of major Panthers players who helped the team reach the Super Bowl the following season including Julius Peppers and Deshaun Foster in the first two rounds. Witherspoon was originally a middle linebacker and backed up 2001 first round pick and current Panthers GM Dan Morgan. Morgan suffered some injuries in the 2002 season, allowing Witherspoon to rack up 15 appearances and eight starts in the middle of the defense. Witherspoon showed so much promise that he was moved to the weak side linebacker position the following year so he and Morgan could be on the field together. That decision paid off both personally and for the team itself as Witherspoon and Morgan were monsters in the second level of the Panthers defense that helped take them to the Super Bowl. Witherspoon’s third season was arguably his best. He logged 103 tackles, three sacks, four interceptions, and 14 passes defended. With Dan Morgan battling injury after injury year after year, Witherspoon was a consistent force on the defense for his entire four year stint with the Panthers. Unfortunately for the Panthers, that meant Witherspoon became a highly coveted free agent after his rookie contract expired. Witherspoon ultimately signed a massive six year, $33 million contract with the St Louis Rams (the equivalent of about $16 million per year in today’s NFL). The Panthers could not match that offer, so Witherspoon played middle linebacker for the Rams until the middle of the 2009 season when he was traded to the Philadelphia Eagles for a wide receiver and a fifth round pick. After spending three seasons with the Tennessee Titans, he followed coach Jeff Fisher to St Louis for a second tenure with the Rams. That ended up being his final season in the NFL. While his time in Charlotte was relatively short, his production and impact during one of the best stretches of Panthers football ever earned him this spot on our countdown of the Top 100 Panthers.

summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys. The Chicago Bears have held training camp at Halas Hall for a few years now, and this will be the second year in a row I failed to get any tickets. It’s a bummer because even though it’s just a football practice, there’s something neat about watching your favorite team in that setting. My first camp was during the Jon Fox era, back when the Bears held it at Olivet Nazarene University in Bourbonnais, Illinois. I’m not sure what finally motivated me to make the two-hour drive down after so many years of having no interest, but once I experienced it, I regretted not going sooner. I was into photography back then, and I took a ton of pictures that I shared here and on social media. The social media aspect of camp is huge, and while I never shared any videos (even though I was accused of it!) , firing off Tweets about what’s happening is great for engagement. I got to meet some of my Windy City Gridiron colleagues in person for the first time at camp, and I also met several other fans and Bears media personalities there. In those Bourbonnais days, there was no cap on how many fans could attend, but since the switch to Halas Hall, there’s a limited number of free tickets available, and they go fast! If you have tickets you can’t use, feel free to use the message boards here to give them away to your fellow WCG members. Vote in this week’s Reacts survey question below (or in The Feed section), but also share with us your favorite training camp story in the comment section below.

title: Chicago Bears Training Camp ‘26 Opening Press Conference
summary: Chicago Bears GM Ryan Poles and Head Coach Ben Johnson met with the media today to open up training camp. Here are some noteworthy nuggets. Kyler Gordon / PUP Kyler Gordon was the talk of the town today as he continues to not be healthy enough to play. Spidey opens up training camp on the […]
full_text: LAKE FOREST, ILLINOIS - JUNE 10: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears speaks to the media before the Chicago Bears Minicamp at Halas Hall on June 10, 2026 in Lake Forest, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images Chicago Bears GM Ryan Poles and Head Coach Ben Johnson met with the media today to open up training camp. Here are some noteworthy nuggets. Kyler Gordon / PUP Kyler Gordon was the talk of the town today as he continues to not be healthy enough to play. Spidey opens up training camp on the Physically Unable to Participate list. Ryan Poles and Ben Johnson were understandably frustrated. According to them, he has done everything he has needed to do this off-season to prepare and get healthy, but when asked about what his message has been to Kyler Gordon, Ben Johnson succinctly said: “Get healthy.” A healthy Kyler goes a long way for this team. But your best ability is availability, so it remains to be seen if he sees out his recently inked contract just a year ago. Joining Kyler on PUP are TJ Edwards, Elijah Hicks, Keyshaun Elliott, and Montez Sweat, but none of them are expected to be long-term. For more on the Bears’ roster moves today, you can click here . Darnell Wright The young stalwart at RT was also discussed today, specifically regarding his contract extension. According to Poles, that is something they are working on and they have a “window of time” they are focused on getting it done. But it remains to be seen if the window is now. With Vikings RT Brian O’Neill signing a lucrative contract to open up camp in Minnesota, there is now a reasonable floor for Wright’s next deal. 4 years $96million While Poles “doesn’t want any distractions” regarding the contract and dragging it on into the season, he also said Wright “is a guy we want here for a while.” So hopefully we hear some news in the coming days or weeks for one of the best tackles in the league remaining in Chicago. Left Tackle Competition I found it noteworthy to hear both Poles and Ben to highlight this position and how each player is looking healthy and ready to compete. Loved the mention of Theo Benedet as a player to watch and how Jedrick Wills has gained double digit lean mass weight. Braxton is the healthiest he’s been since his rookie season and seems to be the frontrunner but some encouraging update on Ozzy and even a positive mention of Kiran. Center Competition It sounds like Garret Bradbury will not be given the job to start the season. While he obviously has a leg up from an experience standpoint, rookie Logan Jones will have every opportunity to compete for the starting gig. Poles touted the “knowledge and wisdom, especially with a young QB behind him” in regards to Bradbury, but the “hunger” of Jones will be something to watch. I will add his athleticism and headiness for a young player. Miscellaneous Thoughts and prayers for former Bears OC Eric Bieniemy and his wife Mia as she is in stable condition following a tragic shooting. Hats off to the Bears camp crew for preparing for camp. Sounds like there is some brand new bells and whistles this year with new fields, new “state-of-the-art” film setup on each field. Luther Burden III got yet ANOTHER glowing endorsement. This time from Ryan Poles. All Edge rushers will be entering camp healthy (I do not consider Sweat’s “illness” as unhealthy), including Dayo Odeyingbo who finished the season on IR. Caleb has Ben’s FULL trust and vote of confidence as a player and QB for this offense. “He can do everything,” coach said matter-of-factly.

title: Pre-Training Camp Chicago Bears 53-Man Roster Projection
summary: Training camp is finally here, and the Chicago Bears’ veterans are set to report on Wednesday before kicking off the practice festivities later in the week. Coming off an 11-6 season and their first NFC North crown in seven seasons, the “surprise” Bears are no more. Expectations are high, and the “next step” is there […]
full_text: Jun 11, 2026; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears offensive lineman Caden Barnett (76) runs on the field during Minicamp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images Training camp is finally here, and the Chicago Bears’ veterans are set to report on Wednesday before kicking off the practice festivities later in the week. Coming off an 11-6 season and their first NFC North crown in seven seasons, the “surprise” Bears are no more. Expectations are high, and the “next step” is there for the taking. Although Super Bowls can’t be won or lost in training camp or the preseason, last year was a prime example of how important the foundation of a team is. Fans should expect that to be established over the next month and a half. While the team still has clear gaps, coaching will drive further development. Before enjoying all of the fun that comes with the training camp and preseason, let’s give this roster one final projection before the action begins. Quarterback (3): Caleb Williams, Tyson Bagent, and Case Keenum Because of the contracts handed out to Bagent and Keenum, barring an injury, this group is set in stone. The big focus will be on Williams taking another sizable leap forward in Year 3, and keeping the quarterback room the same from a year ago is a good first step to making that happen. The only question is whether or not they’ll keep a quarterback on the practice squad. Practice Squad: Miller Moss Running Back (3): D’Andre Swift, Kyle Munangai, and Brittain Brown The top two spots of the depth chart are good to go, but past that, it’s all a mystery. Chicago is set to open camp with six names at the position. The more pressing question is how many they’ll choose to keep on the final roster. Some view Roschon Johnson as the favorite for the RB3 spot, but considering his injury history, I find it hard to believe that he’s their preference. If they opt to keep four, maybe Johnson’s chances improve, but assuming they keep three, my prediction is that the final spot comes down to a choice between Salvon Ahmed and Brown. Practice Squad: Salvon Ahmed and Coleman Bennett Tight End (3): Colston Loveland, Cole Kmet, and Sam Roush Since taking over as the head coach last offseason, Ben Johnson has put a strong emphasis on reworking his tight end room. It started with last year’s No. 10 overall pick and continued in April with Roush and the undrafted free agent signing of Hayden Large. In addition to the three names projected to make the roster, Large, veteran Stephen Carlson, and Nikola Kalinic will be challenging for a final roster spot if the team keeps four. Worst case, don’t be surprised to see a pair of tight ends on the practice squad. Practice Squad: Hayden Large and Stephen Carlson Wide Receiver (5): Rome Odunze, Luther Burden III, Kalif Raymond, Jahdae Walker, and Zavion Thomas No DJ Moore, no problem? That’s what the Bears are hoping for, and assuming all goes well, that should be exactly the case. Odunze and Burden will be their top two receivers, but the added speed of Raymond and Thomas should not be overlooked. Depth is the bigger question here, which is why they could keep six. That said, Johnson’s value on tight ends in 12 and 13 personnel could lessen the need to keep an extra receiver. If they do, keep an eye on Scotty Miller, Maurice Alexander, and potentially Kaden Davis for that final spot, as all three would provide quality special teams value. Practice Squad: Scotty Miller and Kyron Hudson Offensive Line (10): Braxton Jones, Joe Thuney, Garrett Bradbury, Jonah Jackson, Darnell Wright, Logan Jones, Luke Newman, Theo Benedet, Jedrick Wills Jr., and Jordan McFadden Ideally, Drew Dalman wouldn’t have retired, and Ozzy Trapilo would be fully healthy heading into camp. Unfortunately, neither situation is true, and that’s just something the Bears have needed to deal with. On the plus side, they have a very good group of starters and the best depth we’ve seen in quite some time. No matter who wins the starting left tackle and center competitions, they should be in good hands. How the depth plays out behind the starting five will be interesting, along with how many bodies they choose to keep. There are plenty of rosterable names and simply not enough spots. Practice Squad: Caden Barnett, Jaren Kump, and Mason Murphy Defensive End (5): Montez Sweat, Austin Booker, Dayo Odeyingbo, Shemar Turner, and Daniel Hardy For a second straight season, the team’s front office has left fans wanting more off the edge. Barring a surprise move (or an injury that necessitates one), it feels like the coaching staff is content to roll into the season with what they have. Odeyingbo’s participation in veteran mini-camp was quite the surprise, and the hope is that Turner will be ready for the start of training camp. Sweat is a quality player, but he’ll need someone to step up on the other side of him. This group doesn’t have much upside, but the hope is that with better health, they’ll have a safer floor in 2026. Practice Squad: Jonathan Garvin Defensive Tackle (5): Grady Jarrett, Gervon Dexter Sr., Neville Gallimore, Jordan van den Berg, and Kentavius Street Even if the Bears didn’t spend big resources at the position, it’s clear that the emphasis on tackle was simply to acquire better scheme fits for Dennis Allen’s unit. Jarrett and Dexter project as the team’s starters, but Gallimore should see a valuable role. How the final spot (or two) play out will be interesting to monitor with veterans like James Lynch and Street locked into battles with rookies Jayden Loving and van den Berg. Similar to edge rusher, the hope is that the floor has been raised, even if the ceiling remains concerning. Practice Squad: Jayden Loving Linebacker (6): Devin Bush, DeMarco Jackson, T.J. Edwards, Ruben Hyppolite, Keshawn Elliott, and Jack Sanborn Following Tremaine Edmunds’ release, the focus at linebacker has been on speed and playmaking ability. Bush brings both, and the hope is that with more experience in a starting role, Jackson can continue to ascend. The two big questions in this group are simple: Who starts alongside Bush? Jackson fits the physical profile better, but Edwards is regarded as a leader. How will the depth spots shake out with Hyppolite, Elliott, Sanborn, and the Sewell brothers all vying for two, maybe three spots? Overall, it’s easy to see why this group should be better suited than they were a year ago, but as we’ve seen during the offseason program, health will be key to getting the most out of this unit. Practice Squad: Nephi Sewell Cornerback (6): Jaylon Johnson, Tyrique Stevenson, Kyler Gordon, Malik Muhammad, Terell Smith, and Josh Blackwell If healthy, this group has a chance to jump right back into the “very good” category. At their best, both Johson and Gordon are top names at their positions. Stevenson comes into a contract year with plenty to prove, and the competition for starting snaps opposite Johnson should be a healthy one with Muhammad and Smith vying for a role. Smith is not a lock to make this roster, but if he can prove he’s healthy, his upside is far greater than what Jaylon Jones can provide on the field. Finally, barring a surprise, Blackwell projects as the special teams ace and backup nickel to Gordon. Practice Squad: KC Eziomume and Dallis Flowers Safety (4): Coby Bryant, Dillon Thieneman, Cam Lewis, and Elijah Hicks Heading into free agency, the Bears didn’t have any of their four safeties from 2025 under contract. When all was said and done, they parted ways with three of the four, including both starters. While it’s fair to assume that they’ll miss Kevin Byard’s play-making ability and veteran leadership, it’s also easy to see what they are going for with their new starting tandem of Bryant and Thieneman. Versatility is key, and so is speed. Lewis should double as a backup safety and a potential option as a backup nickel. Hicks is back for a fifth year in Chicago. There’s not much…

title: Are the Chicago Bears Going to Suffer From Regression in 2026?
summary: Hello, Chicago Bears fans! There is a certain argument that purports to be rooted in one of the fundamental laws of statistics, namely regression, that casts doom and gloom upon the horizon of the Chicago Bears, forecasting a return to mediocrity in the 2026 season.  Once such example, and the social media feeds on the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Jaylon Johnson #1 of the Chicago Bears gets set during the second quarter of an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello, Chicago Bears fans! There is a certain argument that purports to be rooted in one of the fundamental laws of statistics, namely regression, that casts doom and gloom upon the horizon of the Chicago Bears, forecasting a return to mediocrity in the 2026 season. Once such example, and the social media feeds on the NFL and the Bears are quite full of them, is seen here from Carson Caldwell on X: Bears regression in 2026-27 is going to hit like a truck🤯 • 11 wins, but only a +26 point differential • Expected record was just 9.1–7.9 • NFL-best +22 turnover margin, even if they remain good at taking the ball away and get like a +10 thats still 12 less possessions… pic.twitter.com/LprPTILEsZ — Carson Caldwell (@caldwellcorner_) July 27, 2026 Before I address this argument in the context of the Chicago Bears, let us talk about what regression is, as opposed to this distorted version employed by Mr. Caldwell. I think part of the problem comes from the colloquial definition of regression, as Merriam-Webster defines it: a return to an earlier, worse, or less advanced state. We are ingrained from common usage of regression and “to regress “to think of it as to, essentially, “get worse” or go backward. If we were to talk about the Chicago Bears’ offense “regressing,” we would naturally take that to mean that the Bears’ offense had taken a step back from its current level of success and achievement. Such use of the word “regress” is not wrong – it is an accurate invocation of the definition and usage of the term in common parlance. But it is not what we mean when we talk about “regression” as a statistical phenomenon with regards to sports performance and statistics. So, what is regression in that sense? The common example we use in statistics classes (FYI, I have a Master’s in Statistics and have taught statistics for over 20 years) is height, as Sir Francis Galton observed it as a phenomenon in the 19 th century while studying population statistics. The average height for men in the United States is about 5 feet 9 inches, and for women, approximately 5 feet 4 inches. Let’s assume, though, an NFL linebacker gets married to a WNBA basketball player. Our NFL linebacker is 6 feet 4 inches, and our WNBA player is 5 feet 11 inches. Both represent extreme “outliers” in terms of height – about 2.5 standard deviations above the mean for both, or approximately the 99.4th percentile (they are both taller than all but 0.6% of the population of humans). What are they outlying from? The mean – the average we have already described. So, let’s say our married couple have a boy. What height should we expect the boy to reach in adulthood? Many of you may expect two outliers who have a child are likely to produce an even greater outlier – a 6’11” future NBA center, perhaps. Or perhaps you have reasoned that the boy will be equivalent to the height of their parents (say, 6 feet 5 inches). Well – your intuition that the expected height of the boy is likely to be determined by the height of his parents is correct – we know that from genetics. But in fact, due to regression to the mean, which is 5 feet 9 inches for men, we would expect the boy to likely be approximately 6 feet 1.5 inches tall – shorter than both his mother and father in terms of their unusualness – the boy would only be approximately 1.25 standard deviations above the mean, or in the 88.44th percentile in height. Still an unusual height – but not as unusual as his parents. Regression is fundamentally an observation that unusual things are unusual for a reason. And if the unusual becomes commonplace, then it is no longer unusual. In height, a man or woman who is unusually tall who have children would be expected to have children less unusual than themselves – the progeny would ‘regress’ to the mean of the human population in height. But there is another side to this story. Let’s say our man was, in fact, 5 feet 2 inches, and our woman was 4 feet 7 inches – unusually short. Our male is approximately 2.5 standard deviations below the mean height for men (a bottom 1% of the male population in height), and our female is actually 3.3 standard deviations below the mean height for women. Regression to the mean here works in the positive direction. Their children would be expected to be taller than their parents. In fact, we would expect the male child of this couple to be approximately 5 feet 3.5 inches tall, or 1.87 standard deviations below the mean (about the 3rd percentile – only 97% of the male population is taller). Positive regression relative to a “low” outlier is just as valid a form of “regression” in the statistical sense as is negative regression relative to “high” outliers. It is a testament to the power of the center – a return to the normal after something unusual happens. And it is positive regression that is most often left out of these pessimistic takes on the Chicago Bears for the 2026 season. It is, of course, easy to look at the ways that the Bears were unusually successful in the 2025 season and to confidently predict that the Bears are unlikely to reach those heights again. The two most commonly cited examples are the fact that the Bears’ defense led the league in turnover margin in 2025 (+22) and that the Bears won many games that were close and late (they were, in fact, 8-5 in games decided by one score). We see one of these explicitly in the Caldwell tweet, and the reference to point differential is an implicit way of referring to the Bears’ success in close games. And as such – the point is fair enough. We should expect the Bears to regress in turnover margin. We would expect the Bears turnover margin in 2026 to be drawn back towards the average (which is zero) and for the win rate in close games to be pulled back towards the mean (which is 50%). And this is where our interlocuters (many of which just so happen to be Green Bay Packers fans) end their inquisition into the Bears’ prospects and pronounce the Bears doomed to a “regression” – in win total and perhaps even a losing season this year. But there is a fundamental flaw in this analysis, and I bet you can now, having a full understanding of what regression is in the statistical sense, deduce it. That’s right – they are ignoring that the 2025 Chicago Bears were negative statistical outliers in several important categories related to winning games in the NFL. Let me count the ways. The Chicago Bears were 27th in the NFL in rushing yards allowed per game, giving up 134.5 yards per contest. The Bears were 22nd in the NFL in total sack production with just 35 total sacks, tied with the Cincinnati Bengals. The Bears were 21st in opposing passer rating, they allowed 32 passing touchdowns, and in total defense rank the Bears were 29th. Huh, well, maybe the Bears were just bad on defense. And sure – they were. They were unusually bad on defense. You cannot rely on negative regression to the mean when talking about the areas where they were unusually good without also accounting for positive regression in the areas where they were unusually bad. The Chicago Bears doomers only look at one half of the equation. One-half of the story of regression to the mean. They assume the Bears will be frozen in amber on the things they were unusually bad at, while experience statistical regression on the things they were unusually good at. As the meme goes: that’s not how this works. That’s not how any of this works. And it doesn’t stop with the defense. The Bears were only 21 st in fourth-down conversion percentage – they converted only 51.7% of their attempts. Failure to convert those fourth-downs are effectively turnovers. So fully accounting for regression means tallying the…

title: Chicago Bears 2026 Training Camp Position Breakdown: Wide receiver
summary: The Chicago Bears traded DJ Moore away this offseason, partly for money reasons, but also with the expectation that their young receivers are all ready to step up in 2026. Moore was Chicago’s number one wideout all three years he was a Bear, averaging 81 receptions and 1,004 yards, and he never missed a game. […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 10: Luther Burden III #10 of the Chicago Bears runs with the ball during an NFL wild card playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears traded DJ Moore away this offseason, partly for money reasons, but also with the expectation that their young receivers are all ready to step up in 2026. Moore was Chicago’s number one wideout all three years he was a Bear, averaging 81 receptions and 1,004 yards, and he never missed a game. Ben Johnson’s offense may not feature any one receiver, but they’ll still need to replace Moore’s 979 snaps. Roster Locks Luther Burden III figures to be the biggest beneficiary of Moore not being in Chicago, as he’ll slide into a full-time starter role now. Last year, as a rookie, Burden played in 15 games with 5 starts, and he caught 47 passes for 652 yards. He’s been mentioned as a breakout player by several analysts this offseason, which I agree with. There’s just something different about the way Burden moves on a football field, and I expect him to get at least 80 touches this season. “He makes the first guy miss every time. That’s his trait,” quarterback Caleb Wiliams said about Burden on a recent appearance with Kay Adams. “He catches everything. Easy passes. Hard passes. He’s a friendly receiver; is what we call it as a QB. His route running and things like that, he’s super friendly. And when you get the ball in his hands, he makes that first player miss quite often.” Rome Odunze was the 10th overall pick in 2024, and early on last year, he looked like a potential breakout star, but injuries derailed his sophomore season. After his hot four-game start to open the year (20 catches, 296 yards, 5 TDs), he missed five games and finished with 44 receptions for 661 yards and 6 touchdowns. Kalif Raymond (5’9, 180) figures to start the season as the WR3, but the Bears are very high on 2025 UDFA Jahdae Walker (6’3″, 206). They kept Walker on the 53-man roster all season, and while they tried to make a special teamer out of him early, they eventually started giving him some offensive reps, and in weeks 16, 17, and 18, he played 78 snaps on offense and had 6 receptions for 87 yards and 2 TDs. As Walker and Raymond are physically different receivers, it may be a matchup game to see who plays more. The Bears will likely bring rookie third-round pick Zavion Thomas around slowly, but he should be in the mix as a returner immediately. His 4.28 speed popped this offseason at Halas Hall, but head coach Ben Johnson has already discussed what he needs to see before making Thomas a consistent part of the offense. “If we can harness all of this energy and make sure that we can trust him and he’s going to align where he needs to and run the route the way we need him to, that we really could use him and he could be a big weapon for us this year.” A Good Bet To Make It The Bears carried six receivers on the 53-man roster last year, so if the five above are locks, there’s only room for one more. Considering he appeared in 13 games last year for the Steelers, and 93 total in his seven-year career, 29-year-old Scotty Miller makes sense. He doesn’t have a ton of special teams experience, but in 2022 and 2023, he logged 240 snaps in the third phase. Roster Bubble/Practice Squad Maurice Alexander has been with Ben Johnson for a few years now on his offense’s practice squads. He appeared in one game last year. Kaden Davis spent parts of the last two years on the Browns’ practice squad, where he was elevated for three games. The Bears are his eighth professional stop since being a 2022 Broncos UDFA, and that includes a few months in Detroit with Ben Johnson in 2024. JP Richardson was a 2025 UDFA, and he returns after spending last season on the practice squad while being elevated for one game. The Bears have two rookie UDFA’s this offseason: Kyron Hudson (6’1″, 212) and Omari Kelly (5’11”, 190). Hudson was at USC for two years with Caleb Williams, and in 2025, while at Penn State, he caught 23 passes for 288 yards. Kelly was also in the Big Ten last season, and he had 47 receptions for 626 yards for Michigan State. Do you see any surprises at receiver for the Bears this seaosn?

It’s the unofficial/official start to the 2026 season. Training camp will launch us into the preseason, and the preseason brings us to Week 1. The Bengals took some big swings this offseason, including trading the No. 10 overall selection in the draft to the Giants for Dexter Lawrence. With the talent level on the offense, a stable offensive line and a defense that looks very different on paper, there is a high level of excitement in the city despite the fact they’ve missed the playoffs for three consecutive seasons. Here are some story lines as the Bengals get back into fighting shape: Paul Dehner Jr. reported back on the Bengals’ annual media luncheon. Yes, optimism rolls in as thick as the July humidity at the start of training camp every year, but undeniably, this year felt different than most and certainly a significant departure from the last three seasons filled with contract squabbles and Burrow rehabs. With the news the Eagles extended defensive tackle Jalen Carter to a massive extension, Yahoo Sports’ Duncan Day says the Bengals got a sweetheart of a deal with Lawrence. Carter, who is a few years younger, is making an average of $10 million more annually. PFF’s 2026 Cincinnati Bengals season preview is out. Were it not for an injury that sidelined Joe Burrow from Weeks 3-12 last season, the Cincinnati Bengals could have made a serious playoff run despite their struggles on defense. While they are running it back with the same head coach and coordinators, they made significant additions on defense this offseason, and expectations are high for the 2026 season. While Bengals owner Mike Brown didn’t take questions from the media during their annual luncheon on Monday like he usually does, The Cincinnati Enquirer ’s Jason Williams notes his presence is still very much felt in the building . The Baltimore Ravens have signed another former Bengal. Offensive lineman Hakeem Adeniji , who started in the Super Bowl for Cincinnati at right guard, has signed with the Ravens. Since playing in front of Burrow, he has signed one-year deals with Vikings, Browns and Cowboys before returning once again to the AFC North. title: ESPN ranks Bengals ‘under-25 team’ 20th in the NFL
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals front office has been working to fill the roster holes with younger pieces moving into the next chapter of the Joe Burrow era. The Bengals have drafted multiple pieces that have seen significant playing time very quickly, which naturally brings some growing pains for the roster. But going into 2026, the young […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals front office has been working to fill the roster holes with younger pieces moving into the next chapter of the Joe Burrow era. The Bengals have drafted multiple pieces that have seen significant playing time very quickly, which naturally brings some growing pains for the roster. But going into 2026, the young section of the roster is taking steps forward, and ESPN now has the Bengals ‘under-25 team’ ranked No. 20. ESPN’s Aaron Schatz wrote, “The Bengals climbed up a bit in these rankings despite graduating most of their secondary. The youth that remains begins with the offensive line, as right tackle Mims and left guard Dylan Fairchild are both 23. So is guard Jalen Rivers, who started seven games last season because of injuries on the line. And fourth-round center Connor Lew will be 21 in August. The other position with a lot of youth is edge rusher: Myles Murphy is 24, and Shemar Stewart is 22; 2026 second-round pick Cashius Howell is 23. Behind those players, you’ll find linebacker Barrett Carter, who started 12 games as a rookie and doesn’t turn 24 until October, and 22-year-old third-round rookie cornerback Tacario Davis.” Schatz has starting right tackle Amarius Mims listed as the Bengals’ ‘blue chip’ piece for their under-25 team, which makes sense considering his stellar play the past two seasons. Again, it is safe to say the young pieces of the Bengals roster are improving and will carry a crucial load this upcoming season if Burrow and company hope to snap a 3-year playoff drought.

title: Al Golden embraces Zac Taylor’s challenge to maximize Bengals’ defensive talent
summary: One of the biggest themes emerging as the Cincinnati Bengals enter training camp this summer isn’t about installing a new defensive scheme; it’s about making sure every talented player is put in the best position to succeed. Defensive coordinator Al Golden said head coach Zac Taylor challenged every assistant coach before camp with a simple […]
full_text: One of the biggest themes emerging as the Cincinnati Bengals enter training camp this summer isn’t about installing a new defensive scheme; it’s about making sure every talented player is put in the best position to succeed. Defensive coordinator Al Golden said head coach Zac Taylor challenged every assistant coach before camp with a simple but important question: Are we getting the most out of our best players? Al Golden says Zac Taylor challenged his coaches to make sure they’re using the great talent on the roster “accordingly” throughout the season starting in camp. pic.twitter.com/NHLsWwNfxJ — Mike Petraglia (@Trags) July 27, 2026 For Golden, that challenge carries particular significance. His defense struggled with consistency last season and was the main reason why the Bengals failed to make the playoffs for the third straight season. With eight new faces going into camp, this group now features a blend of proven veterans and intriguing young talent. Rather than forcing players into rigid roles, the emphasis is on discovering how each defender can make the greatest impact. “Training camp is about how we come together as a collective, who emerges as leaders, where are the position battles, how do they play out,” Golden noted. “Take a deep breath and say, the guys with the most talent, are we using them accordingly, are we getting the most out of what they do best? That’s what we have to get done here in the next six weeks.” Golden’s comments suggest that process will continue well beyond the preseason. The goal isn’t simply to identify the most talented players; it’s to make sure those players are consistently being used in ways that allow them to perform at the highest level. For a defense looking to take a major step forward in 2026, that philosophy could prove just as important as any new blitz package or coverage adjustment. The Bengals believe they have the talent. Now, the coaching staff must accept Taylor’s challenge to maximize it. And, as Golden made clear, that work starts now.

title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: The start of training camp
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are back to work this week as training camp officially gets underway. Their first practice is scheduled for Wednesday (7/29), kicking off the process of trimming the roster from roughly 90 players down to the final 53. It also marks the end of the NFL’s annual summer lull. After weeks of almost nothing happening […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - JANUARY 04: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) looks at the scorebord during the game against the Cleveland Browns and the Cincinnati Bengals on January 4, 2026, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals are back to work this week as training camp officially gets underway. Their first practice is scheduled for Wednesday (7/29), kicking off the process of trimming the roster from roughly 90 players down to the final 53. It also marks the end of the NFL’s annual summer lull. After weeks of almost nothing happening throughout June and July, football is finally back. Thank the football gods. Here are a few storylines to watch as camp opens. Defensive line depth The Bengals completely rebuilt their defensive front this offseason, adding Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe and Jonathan Allen, while also drafting Landon Robinson and Cashius Howell. Even with B.J. Hill expected to begin camp on the PUP list, there’s little reason to panic because of how much depth Cincinnati added. The biggest question may not be who starts—it may be who gets cut. There are only so many roster spots available, and at least one talented defensive lineman is likely to be left looking for work elsewhere. Late free-agent additions Last August, the Bengals signed Dalton Risner late in the preseason. He eventually took over the starting right guard job, earned a new contract and helped give Joe Burrow the same starting offensive line in consecutive seasons for the first time in his career. Could lightning strike twice? The Bengals largely bypassed linebacker in both free agency and the draft, and there are still veterans on the market who could help. Cornerback is another position worth watching. Cincinnati signed Ja’Sir Taylor and drafted Tacario Davis, but is that enough? If the Bengals make another veteran addition before Week 1, linebacker or cornerback seems like the most likely destination. Running back is also a possibility, although it feels like more of a long shot. An evolving training camp philosophy One of the defining characteristics of the Zac Taylor era has been slow starts. The Bengals have tried to address that by changing their approach to training camp, including playing starters during the preseason. Even so, the only time they’ve been better than 2-2 through the first four weeks came during their Super Bowl run in 2021. This roster is far too talented to spend another season digging itself out of an early hole. Will the coaching staff continue tweaking its training camp approach in hopes of finally getting off to a fast start? We’ll find out soon enough. Who’s next for an extension? Several key contributors are entering the final year of their contracts in 2026. Dax Hill, DJ Turner II, Andrei Iosivas, Jordan Battle, Chase Brown and others are all scheduled to become free agents after the season. The Bengals will undoubtedly extend some of them—but certainly not all. Who will be wearing Bengals stripes for the final time? The battle for WR3 Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins have WR1 and WR1A locked down, but who claims the third receiver role? The Bengals have rotated players such as Andrei Iosivas and Charlie Jones into that spot, while Mike Gesicki has also absorbed plenty of receiving opportunities from the tight end position. Still, no one has firmly established themselves as the clear third option behind one of the NFL’s best receiving duos. Training camp could change that. The tight end rotation This position group is especially intriguing because of Erick All Jr.’s return from the knee injury that has sidelined him since Week 9 of the 2024 season. Gesicki is essentially a wide receiver playing tight end, while Drew Sample is one of the league’s better blocking tight ends. All has the potential to provide the best of both worlds. If he can stay healthy, could he completely change the dynamic of Cincinnati’s offense? More storylines will emerge as training camp unfolds, but these are a few of the biggest heading into Week 1. title: Duke Tobin does not anticipate DJ Turner or Dax Hill skipping practice amidst ongoing contract talks
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have a good problem most teams would take. They have two young corners worthy of re-signing for a second contract. DJ Turner (a second-round pick in the 2023 draft) and Dax Hill (a first-round selection from the 2022 draft) are both quality starters—especially Turner, who has received the underrated tag pretty frequently […]
full_text: Cincinnati cornerback DJ Turner (0) takes the field during minicamp, Tuesday, June 16, 2026, at Kettering Health Practice Fields in downtown Cincinnati. | Frank Bowen IV/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Cincinnati Bengals have a good problem most teams would take. They have two young corners worthy of re-signing for a second contract. DJ Turner (a second-round pick in the 2023 draft) and Dax Hill (a first-round selection from the 2022 draft) are both quality starters—especially Turner, who has received the underrated tag pretty frequently this offseason. However, it is still a problem when you need to re-sign them. The Bengals have been spending quite a bit, and while they could re-sign both players. The team would be left without the wiggle room it usually would like to have. We’ve seen players like Trey Hendrickson, Jessie Bates, and Ja’Marr Chase all skip portions of training camp as they entered the last years of their respective contracts. The Bengals aren’t expecting that this time around. “When you draft guys like that that come in and find roles and elevate their game and elevate the people around them. Those are guys you want to be around,” Director of Player Personnel Duke Tobin said of the cornerback duo . “And I’m not going to make any predictions about future contracts. We have everyone signed up right now, which is really good. It’s a good feeling. I think everyone is locked in on the season, and we’ll see what the future holds. But right now, our focus is winning and winning now.” “I’m not going to give any potential contract details or anything like that. Everyone’s under contract, and we want the good players to stay here long term. That’s always the way we’ve been.” Tobin’s last line is certainly one most fans will scoff at considering the team’s track record. It also seems like this is mostly from the team’s perspective that they do not expect any hold-ins or hold-outs. They would probably have a good idea, though, given they are negotiating with these players’ agents. Still, hold-ins and trade requests remain the only leverage a player looking for a new deal has without sacrificing (potentially) tons of money in the process. We did see Tee Higgins practice during training camp the year that he would eventually play on the franchise tag. However, that has been more of the exception than the rule around the NFL. Ultimately, it is up to each player to do what they think is best for their situation. You could argue that playing out the contract and performing well would let you hit the market with some momentum. But you could just as easily suffer a major injury and then need to prove yourself all over again if you are even able to play at that level again. We will see how Turner and Hill decide to handle their business. "We want the good players to stay here long term." "I'm not going to make any predictions about future contracts. title: Cleveland Browns training camp 2026: OL preview, Part 2 – Who starts at offensive guard, center?
summary: Next up on our Cleveland Browns training camp preview for the offensive line position is the interior: guard and center. Although we feel confident in one of the positions, training camp will help decide who starts in the other two spots. Fans have already made their voices heard. 6. Elgton Jenkins – Starting OG/C Height: […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - MAY 20: Elgton Jenkins #74 and Zion Johnson #77 of the Cleveland Browns run a drill during the Cleveland Browns OTA Offseason Workouts at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on May 20, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Next up on our Cleveland Browns training camp preview for the offensive line position is the interior: guard and center. Although we feel confident in one of the positions, training camp will help decide who starts in the other two spots. Fans have already made their voices heard . 6. Elgton Jenkins – Starting OG/C Height: 6-5 | Weight: 310 lbs | Age: 30 Experience: 8 years | College: Mississippi State With the Browns not retaining C Ethan Pocic in free agency, they needed to give themselves an option on the market. They did so with veteran Elgton Jenkins , signing him to a 2-year, $24 million deal. A second-round pick by the Packers in 2019, Jenkins proved to be durable, starting 94 games. He made the Pro Bowl as a guard in 2020 and 2022, and was then moved to center last year. There were reports that he wasn’t necessarily thrilled with playing center, when thinking about the better salaries that guards make as free agents compared to centers. That might be moot at this point, considering he’s under contract. Jenkins’ experience at guard has primarily been at left guard, but it sounds like Zion Johnson is locked up there. I’m sure Jenkins can play the right side just fine too, but my thought process heading into camp is that Cleveland will be able to get the best five offensive linemen on the field if Jenkins is at center, and someone else plays right guard. Barry Shuck also has an article all about Jenkins’ background here . Final Roster Odds: 100% 7. Zion Johnson – Starting OG Height: 6-3 | Weight: 315 lbs | Age: 26 Experience: 5 years | College: Boston College Zion Johnson was a first round pick by the Chargers in the 2022 NFL Draft, starting 65 games in that stretch. He has primarily played left guard, and that’s the starting job he’s expected to take on with Cleveland. When you look at his PFF rankings for the past few years, though, it doesn’t seem like a slam dunk signing for Cleveland. Johnson struggled a bit with the Chargers last year, ranking as the league 53rd best guard. Johnson has a bit of a reputation of struggling in pass blocking, with the ability to be a mauler in the run game. There’s also been some consistency issues over the course of his career. On the surface, the Browns definitely overpaid for Johnson’s 3-year, $49.5 million deal. They are banking on him being a better for for what offensive line coach George Warhop and head coach Todd Monken want to do offensively, much like the lightbulb clicked once Wyatt Teller had a change of scenery from Buffalo to Cleveland. Heading into camp, I get that Johnson has a starting role locked up, but I won’t know what to expect from him until we’re a couple of games into the season. Barry Shuck’s write-up on everything to know about Jenkins is here . Final Roster Odds: 100% 8. Teven Jenkins – Competing OG Height: 6-6 | Weight: 321 lbs | Age: 28 Experience: 6 years | College: Oklahoma State Last year, the Browns signed Teven Jenkins to a cheap deal after he was coming off some injuries from his time with the Chicago Bears. Jenkins made 4 starts with the Browns and saw action in a few other games due to injuries across the line, and the former second-round pick did an adequate job. If Jenkins starts at right guard, he would be the only returning player starting on the offensive line this year. He has the potential to be a slightly above average pass and run blocker, a degree of consistency in both aspects of his game that others on the line might lack (i.e. they might excel in pass blocking, but struggle against the run). Even if Jenkins does not start, he’d be the team’s top option as a backup, which puts his roster odds at a high percentage. Final Roster Odds: 90% 9. Parker Brailsford – Rookie C Height: 6-2 | Weight: 290 lbs | Age: 22 Experience: Rookie | College: Alabama If I called Dawand Jones one of the top players to watch in Browns camp this offseason, then Parker Brailsford is right up there with him. As a fifth-round pick in this year’s draft, it’s natural to think that Brailsford won’t be ready to win the starting center job from day one. However, if he thrives in camp, then I’m sure the coaching staff would love to stick him at center and make E. Jenkins happy by putting him at right guard. Dane Brugler had Brailsford as the 7th-ranked center in this year’s draft class: Overall, Brailsford will only appeal to certain teams, because of his frame, but he is light on his feet, tough as nails and can handle everything from a mental standpoint. He has the potential to be a starter for a scheme living in an outside-zone world. Brugler mentions how Brailsford would only appeal to certain teams, and DBN’s Matthew Wilson wrote about why Cleveland is definitely one of those teams , calling him “a slightly smaller version of Tyler Linderbaum ” (who was the Ravens’ center under Todd Monken ). Here is Shuck’s profile on Brailsford’s background . Final Roster Odds: 100% 10. Luke Wypler – Backup C Height: 6-3 | Weight: 303 lbs | Age: 25 Experience: 3 years | College: Ohio State Maybe it’s too soon to write off Luke Wypler , who was a 6th round pick in 2023 by the Browns out of Ohio State. However, when Cleveland goes out and drafts a potential replacement center (Brailsford) and signs a guy (E. Jenkins) who started at center last year, Wypler immediately falls to third on the depth chart in my opinion, fighting for a roster spot. Wypler missed all of 2024 with an ankle injury, but started 5 games last year. He was carted off in the season finale with a knee injury, but is good-to-go for camp. Even though my mental perception is down on Wypler, the center position is one that is up for grabs. Entering his fourth year, maybe Wypler can build off his experience from a year ago. Monken has indicated previously that he’d prefer to have E. Jenkins at guard, so if that holds true, then it could be a competition between Brailsford and Wypler. If Brailsford isn’t quick to pick things up, maybe Wypler provides a more stable presence initially. Final Roster Odds: 60% 11. Zak Zinter – Backup OG Height: 6-6 | Weight: 310 lbs | Age: 25 Experience: 3 years | College: Michigan The final of the top contenders on the interior of the offensive line (besides KT Leveston and Dawand Jones potentially, which we mentioned in our tackle piece) is Zak Zinter . Unfortunately for Zinter, despite being a third-round pick a few seasons ago, his ceiling to compete for in camp is to hang on to a reserve role. After starting 3 games as a rookie, he only played in 5 games last year and did not start any of them despite the team’s injury woes across the line. Lance Reisland thinks the broken tibia and fibula he suffered with Michigan against Ohio State has hurt the short-area burst he used to have: For me, Zak Zinter is not about effort or talent, it is about health. The film shows it. His lateral movement, his ability to redirect, and that short-area burst have not been the same since the injury against Ohio State. #Browns — Lance Reisland (Coach Riz) (@LanceReisland) March 29, 2026 Final Roster Odds: 60% Next up, we’ll look at the remaining players competing for backup spots in camp on the offensive line.

title: NFL contracts: Denzel Ward’s contract extension tops the top 10 cornerback deals
summary: In the era of sports news where the biggest reporters all get their information from and have to give credit to the agents, the first reports on deals are often not the real story. The structure of a contract, as noted in our piece on DT Vita Vea, is often setup to make the agents […]
full_text: SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 2: Denzel Ward #21 of the Cleveland Browns participates during a Pro Bowl team practice during the NFL Pro Bowl Games at Moscone Center South on February 2, 2026 in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the era of sports news where the biggest reporters all get their information from and have to give credit to the agents, the first reports on deals are often not the real story. The structure of a contract, as noted in our piece on DT Vita Vea , is often setup to make the agents look good and make the player feel good about how much money they are getting, even if they are unlikely to see all of it. While we wait for the details on the two-year contract extension CB Denzel Ward signed with the Cleveland Browns, it is notable that both Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport both noted that Ward’s deal “makes him the highest-paid DB in NFL history for the second time in his career.” The only difference between those parts of the reports is that Schefter’s includes the hyphen and Rapoport’s does not. Given that Ward’s extension is reportedly for two years and $62.2 million, his yearly average on the extension would just barely clear the deal signed by CB Trent McDuffie this offseason. On his previous deal, Ward’s yearly average was $20.1 million, which at the time was the highest in the NFL. Adding the extension to his contract, instead of a new deal, jumps the total value of the contract well over $160 million for seven years. While we wait for the details to confirm the above reports, the Top 10 cornerback contracts , based on annual value, before Ward’s extension, were as follows: Rams Trent McDuffie – $31 million Colts Sauce Gardner – $30.1 Texans Derek Stingley Jr. – $30 Panthers Jaycee Horn – $25 Steelers Jalen Ramsey – $24.1 Broncos Patrick Surtain II – $24 Cowboys DaRon Bland – $22.5 Falcons AJ Terrell – $20.5 Browns Denzel Ward – $20.1 Ravens Marlon Humphrey – $19.5 Once all the contract details are released, we will be able to see in what ways Ward is “the highest paid DB in NFL history for the second time in his career,” as well as all the salary cap implications.

summary: Stop us if you have heard it before: The Cleveland Browns have a lot of young players and a lot of good young players with upside on their roster. We know many of you have heard it before because we’ve covered it in a myriad of ways: For lifelong Cleveland fans, the hyperbole is a […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 03: Carson Schwesinger #49 of the Cleveland Browns walks off the field after the Cleveland Browns OTA Offseason Workouts at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 03, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Stop us if you have heard it before: The Cleveland Browns have a lot of young players and a lot of good young players with upside on their roster. We know many of you have heard it before because we’ve covered it in a myriad of ways: 54 players on the Browns roster are 25 years old or younger GM Andrew Berry took the fast path to a young roster the last two years ESPN’s survey of coaches, scouts, and execs points to Cleveland having a talented young roster Browns under-25 roster ranked in the Top 5 For lifelong Cleveland fans, the hyperbole is a little overwhelming. Yes, the 2025 NFL draft class performed very well , and the 2026 draft class has been graded very highly , but the latter is fully unproven, and the former must be consistent before it can be fully trusted. LB Carson Schwesinger , the NFL’s reigning Defensive Rookie of the Year , may be the best player on the Browns roster and the one you’d want to build your franchise around . He’s also the lone Cleveland under-25 player to make The NFL Network’s “All-NFL team” of young players : A former walk-on at UCLA, Schwesinger has routinely overcome long odds to find success on the gridiron. He arrived in Cleveland without much of a national reputation but quickly won the hearts of Browns fans with his relentless motor, which saw him tally 156 tackles (11 for loss), nine QB hits, 2.5 sacks and two interceptions in 16 games. Schwesinger proved himself as a versatile, athletic, three-down linebacker capable of leading a defense by example, then earned a permanent place in Browns lore with his performance in a Week 17 win over the rival Steelers, a 13-6 triumph that leaned heavily on Cleveland’s defense and required Schwesinger to play through an obvious injury before calling it a season shortly after the victory. When it came time to choose a Defensive Rookie of the Year, debate was minimal: Schwesinger took home the award with 80 percent of first-place votes, capping a fantastic rookie season with some hardware for his trophy case. Now, with DE Myles Garrett playing for the Los Angeles Rams, Schwesinger has a chance to take another step forward as the leader of Cleveland’s defense. TE Harold Fannin Jr. , DT Mason Graham , and RB Quinshon Judkins would be the next players that would have been considered for this list. A small or cheap item can have a regal name attached that does not fit the size or stature of the actual product. For years, the “Great Lakes Classic” preseason matchup between the Cleveland Browns and Detroit Lions fit the “big name, small game” typology. “The Battle for the Barge,” as fans would call the GLC, was regularly played between two teams who were only “Classic” in that they have both been around a long time, both were founded in Ohio (the Lions were originally the Portsmouth Spartans), and both have been classically bad since the Browns returned in 1999. Detroit has seen a strong turnaround since 2022, with four straight winning records and two playoff appearances, while Cleveland has made the playoffs twice since 2020 but has seen four losing seasons in that timeframe as well. According to Joel Walkowski, author of the book “Honolulu Blues: How The Detroit Lions Saved My Life,” fans of the Browns and Lions are 1a and 1b in having “the worst go of it of any franchise,” similar to the NBA’s GOAT debate between Michael Jordan and LeBron James: “I exist on this planet to make the argument that the Lions fans have the WORST go of it of any franchise…” “I gotta give a hat tip to the Cleveland Browns. A look at the historical numbers between each team: Record: CLE – 567-560-14, DET – 615-717-34 Winning %: CLE – 50.3%, DET – 46% Championships: CLE – 8, DET – 4 Maybe Walkowski is on to something, big picture and in the long-term. For the more recent history, the Browns have been far more downtrodden and have had an organization that has made mind-numbing decision after mind-numbing decision. Then again, Detroit and Cleveland are also the only two teams since the strike-shortened season of 1982 to have winless seasons, so both fan bases have gone through a lot. Overall, which fan base do you think has it worse? title: Should the Browns have trade interest in Vita Vea? A complicated answer
summary: Any type of big-money negotiations is tough. Neither side wants to budge, and neither wants to leave money on the table. A little give here, a concession here, until the deal is done – or both sides step away. Cleveland Browns fans have seen it play out time and time again. For the most part, […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - JUNE 16: Tampa Bay Buccaneers Defensive Lineman Vita Vea (50) watches the action on the field during the Tampa Bay Buccaneers Mini Camp on June 16, 2026 at the AdventHealth Training Center in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Any type of big-money negotiations is tough. Neither side wants to budge, and neither wants to leave money on the table. A little give here, a concession here, until the deal is done – or both sides step away. Cleveland Browns fans have seen it play out time and time again. For the most part, NFL contracts are handled by attorneys who are called sports agents. And they should be. Each NFL club has a lawyer who draws up the agreements, so it’s only fitting that on the other side, a licensed, fully-schooled law school graduate should be looking it over for his client. RELATED: DT DEPTH CHART AND EXPECTATIONS Back in the day, Green Bay Packers head coach Vince Lombardi traded anybody away who had an agent. He dealt with all contracts and wanted it one-on-one. Even though Lombardi wasn’t the owner of the Packers, he acted like it and was the team’s GM. Former Cleveland Browns Paul Brown was the same way. He always owned a small percentage of the Browns, but in every aspect, it was his decisions. There is a little trick that sports agents do these days, called “back loading.” What this is, the agent will get his client signed for, say, $60 million on a four-year deal. There is a signing bonus, workout incentives, plus other bonuses, and of course, the obligatory guarantee. The athlete gets paid $9 million the first year, $12 million in the second season, $14 million in Year 3, and then $25 million in the final year. Except the player rarely gets the $25 million. In reality, it is just a three-year deal. The team is cool with paying those first three years, but there is no way they want to allow the athlete to cash out in the final year of the deal. The agent knows this. So, what the sports agency does is add a huge amount to the end of the deal to make the signing seem huge, so that they can say, “Look what our agency got for (fill in the blank).” What sounds better? A three-year agreement for $35 million or a four-year contract for a whopping $60 million? That is what Tampa Bay Buccaneers DT Vita Vea is experiencing right now. He is at the end of his four-year $71 million deal he signed back in 2023. His cap hit this year will be $22.19 million. This is his contract year, and the team is balking at it. Negotiations have been ongoing since the end of the 2025 season, and here it is time for training camp, and his deal remains the same. Vea (6’-4”, 347 pounds) has now requested a trade. Dexter Lawrence (traded this offseason) and Vea are the two best defensive tackles in the game. Vea has been very durable over his eight-year career, including 17 starts last year, and is an excellent run stopper. He is one of those defensive tackles that has a rare gift of getting into the offensive backfield and causing disruption. Most DTs just plug a gap and dare offensive guards to move them, but both Lawrence and Vea are also pass rushers. Vea has 35 career sacks. His sack numbers in the past four years are 4.5, 7.0, 5.5, and 6.5. He has 79 QB hits, 9 batted passes, 30 hurries, 42 knockdowns, and 112 pressures. That is his pass rush. For run stoppage, Vea has 256 total tackles, 21 missed tackles, 48 tackles for loss, 3 fumble recoveries, and 3 forced fumbles. Should the Browns reach out for Vea? DBN’s Thomas Moore recently wrote a great article on how the Browns remain in the hunt for another good pass rusher to pair with the new guy, DE Jared Verse. It’s true. Out of all the transactions GM Andrew Berry has made this offseason, there still remains only one pass rusher. The DT room currently consists of Mason Graham and Maliek Collins as starters, newly-signed Kalia Davis, the so-far disappointing Mike Hall as primary backups, plus Adin Huntington, Sam Kamara, and veteran Elijah Chapman. Here’s the rub. Hall was selected in Round 2. If he had come along like the franchise assumed he would, this would not be a conversation. In all fairness, this is probably the training camp that Hall either shows out or gets out. But Berry did attempt to pair first-and second-round draft picks on the interior. Collins has been added to the active/PUP list , so there’s no telling if he will begin the season here or if his issues will be resolved before Week 1. Every NFL club needs four guys for the defensive tackle position, and then rotates them in and out. Obviously, the two starters get more snaps per game, but the two backups will have plenty of reps as well. It is a well-known fact that Berry has attempted to improve the interior of the defensive line. After failed signings from guys like Dalvin Tomlinson, he has drafted Hall in the second round and Graham in Round 1 last year. Vea was taken #12 overall in the 2018 NFL draft and has a Super Bowl ring, plus owns two pieces of Pro Bowl hardware. Yes, he is age 31, so there’s that. But for the next three years, paired with one of the NFL’s promising rookies, Graham , this would completely end the inability to stop the run. Lawrence recently went from the New York Football Giants to the Cincinnati Bengals after requesting a trade and was signed to a one-year $28 million deal. Cincy gave up its first-round draft pick in this year’s draft in the deal. So, what would it take to get Vea in-house? How about second and fifth-round draft picks? The team has extra picks all over the place after the Myles Garret trade . Marinate on that a bit. Last year’s first-round draft pick Mason Graham and another first-round draft pick, Vita Vea, are lining up in the middle of the defensive line for the next three years. Then Collins and a fourth guy who shows out in training camp to rotate in. If Moore’s assessment is correct and Cleveland is still in need of a pass rusher, here he is. Now keep in mind that a trade request is also a negotiation tactic. But many players who ask to be traded actually do get shipped off. Should Berry make the call? Buccaneers veteran players are scheduled to report to training camp on Tuesday, as are the Browns. What say you? Should the Browns trade for Vea and extend his contract or just go with the young guys they have? Share your thoughts in the comment section below Join the conversation! title: Cowboys news: Notes from the opening training camp press conference
summary: Is a big trade coming for the Dallas Cowboys? Jerry Jones says he’s working on it – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram The Dallas Cowboys sound like they’re working behind the scenes on making the team better. Less than 10 minutes later, Jones was asked about his urgency to win compared to trusting the process […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Oxnard, CA, USA; Dallas Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer (left), executive vice president Stephen Jones (center) and owner Jerry Jones at training camp opening press conference at River Ridge Playing Fields. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Is a big trade coming for the Dallas Cowboys? Jerry Jones says he’s working on it – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram The Dallas Cowboys sound like they’re working behind the scenes on making the team better. Less than 10 minutes later, Jones was asked about his urgency to win compared to trusting the process of having a lot of change on the defensive side of the ball, and he answered with a major headline that will dominate the early news cycles of the team’s training camp. “Candidly, I’d be very interested to give up future to add substantive to where we are today,” Jones said. “Would I invest something substantive to get the right kind of deal to improve us opening day? I would. I feel that good about this team this year.” Jones hasn’t been a stranger to big trades in the past 18 months. The team has acquired wide receiver George Pickens, defensive tackle Quinnen Williams and defensive tackle Kenny Clark in megadeals since the start of the 2025 calendar year, and he is making it publicly known that he is open to continuing that trend. He also made it known that the phone lines are actively being worked. “Yesterday, I talked about a situation with another team, another owner,” Jones said. “Yesterday.” Speaking with a group of reporters after the press conference, Jones was asked if the conversation he had with the mystery owner was heading in the right direction. “No, I wouldn’t classify it like that,” he said. “It was a very legitimate discussion, but I wouldn’t give it a direction.” While the team and the player(s) at the core of the discussion remain unknown, Jones was asked directly about Las Vegas Raiders defensive end Maxx Crosby a few moments later. The Cowboys were known to be deep in the mix for the five-time Pro Bowler when he was shopped by the Raiders this offseason, but after the deal with the Baltimore Ravens fell through due to a failed physical, his market cooled. However, Jones made sure to emphasize that the Cowboys still remained interested even after news around the injury arose prior to the draft. Jerry Jones confident Cowboys can compete for a Super Bowl in 2026 – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com The optimism for Jerry Jones seems as high as ever about his 2026 squad. From a media perspective, the term “quiet offseason” has been used plenty recently, with quiet being relative to the noise around ongoing contract negotiations when the Cowboys arrive on the west coast. For Cowboys owner/GM Jerry Jones, the past few months have been far from quiet in his world. “I like the idea that the word is that we have had a quiet offseason, relative to dare I say off the field noise or chatter,” Jones said. “I like that, that hasn’t been the case. We’ve had a lot going on. We’ve had to really scramble a lot, the kind of stuff that you don’t see. But that should be that way, it’s supposed to be hard… We even did more than I could have anticipated when we started. I personally like the fact that the perception is that it’s been a quiet, non-confrontational offseason. That’s good.” That doesn’t mean Dallas will be out of headlines or not engaging in contract negotiations while in Oxnard. Jones mentioned several times that he’d be willing to trade high-level draft capital to supplement his roster , and COO/co-owner Stephen Jones said Dallas was “absolutely” willing to engage in extension talks with Pro Bowl defensive tackle Quinnen Williams. A lot of the work during the offseason has gone towards rebuilding the defense, which was one of the worst units in franchise history last season and allowed over 30 points per game. With a new defensive coordinator in Christian Parker, the potential to have as many as seven new starters and a new defensive coaching staff, Dallas will need to the find the balance between integrating all the new elements of the team and competing right away. “We don’t have any alternative,” Jones said. “We made that bed when we brought in new scheme, new coaches, new players. We’re going with new right there. I’ve bought into that, that’s going to happen, we’re here. Now, in dealing with it, we’ve got to start out here right now doing as best we can and bringing that thing to opening day.” Stephen Jones: Cowboys interested in Quinnen Williams extension – RJ Ochoa, Blogging the Boys The Cowboys getting a contract extension done with Quinnen Williams would be a huge boost this offseason. The Dallas Cowboys held court on Tuesday for their press conference to start training camp in Oxnard, and as they did matters are officially underway. The opening presser is a tradition for the team at training camp, and to a lesser degree so is an extension for one of the team’s players while the team is in California. Everyone being together in a tighter compound just seems to be a recipe for deals to get done, and the subject of a particular one coming together came up. Stephen Jones noted that the Cowboys have held discussions with Quinnen Williams’ agent about the process of a hypothetical extension. He noted before he said that the team is quite invested in Williams which is the case as they executed a trade deadline deal to acquire him last season. On some level this gives Williams a bit of leverage. His representation knows that the Cowboys traded what they did for him so they are pot committed on some level. It doesn’t help that the defensive tackle market is on the rise at the moment, consider that about an hour before Stephen said this that the Philadelphia Eagles gave Jalen Carter a four-year, $152M extension . That is the new going rate. Training camp has just begun so perhaps a deal will come together. Williams is the only player of note who the Cowboys have to work with on something like this at the moment, keep in mind that George Pickens is playing on the franchise tag and as we are past the July 15th the team and he can literally not negotiate a new deal until the season is over. Credit Jerry Jones and George Pickens for the rare quiet Dallas Cowboys offseason – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News For better or worse, give a pat on the back to Jerry Jones and George Pickens for keeping things amicable this training camp. Cowboys wide receiver George Pickens traveled with the team Monday to California. Pickens said at mandatory minicamp — when he showed up for that, too — that he planned to participate in training camp despite receiving the franchise tag . He explicitly said he would not do a hold in and go to practice but not participate. As of Tuesday afternoon, there’s been no indication that Pickens plans to change his mind. That one-year, $27.3 million deal without the potential for an extension appears good enough for him. It’s not out of the question things could’ve been different, even if it was always unlikely. This is the same Pickens, after all, who was traded from Pittsburgh shortly after former Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin declared that he needed to grow up. This is the same Pickens who was prolific last season in a breakout year , finishing with career highs in every major receiving category, despite being fined multiple times for being late to meetings or for missing the team bus on the way to the road game against the Las Vegas Raiders. Despite that reputation, the Cowboys, led by head coach Brian Schottenheimer, have preached Pickens’ love for the sport and for how things went on the field last year with the Cowboys. Ultimately, Pickens proved them right with how he handled the franchise tag. For what it’s worth: Jones appreciates it. “The way we have worked this out is the way it fit. I’m proud that he will work it that way. I’m proud that he will,” Jones replied after the first Pickens question, which was…
