title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 47
summary: It is Day 47 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: WEST HAVEN, CT - NOVEMBER 11: Jack Gregory #81 of the New York Giants in action against the Dallas Cowboys during an NFL game November 11, 1973 at the Yale Bowl in West Haven, Connecticut. Gregory played for the Giants from 1972-78. (Photo by Focus on Sport/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is Day 47 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. It’s Day 47 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff when we revisit an early-season NFC East road win from a Cowboys team trying to defend its first Super Bowl title. Dallas went to Yankee Stadium in Week 2 of the 1972 season and faced the New York Giants. In a 14-game season, division wins carried extra weight, and this one mattered because New York would go on to finish 8-6 and stay in the playoff conversation late into the year. Sunday, September 24, 1972 — 1:00 p.m. ET Yankee Stadium, Bronx, New York Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 23, New York Giants 14 Walt Garrison opened the scoring with a one-yard touchdown in the first quarter, giving Dallas a 7-0 lead. Toni Fritsch then drilled a 54-yard field goal in the second quarter to make it 10-0, a huge kick in an era when long field goals were far less routine than they are today. New York answered before halftime when Norm Snead hit Rich Houston for a 55-yard touchdown, cutting Dallas’ lead to 10-7. That made the second half less comfortable than the Cowboys would have wanted, but it also turned the game into the kind of road test championship-caliber teams have to pass. Dallas was not blowing the Giants away, it was having to manage the game, protect the ball, and find enough offense to keep the lead. Fritsch added another field goal in the third quarter, this one from 13 yards, then made an eight-yard field goal in the fourth to push Dallas ahead 16-7. The Giants still had one big punch left. Snead and Houston connected again, this time on a massive 94-yard touchdown, suddenly trimming the Cowboys’ lead to 16-14 and putting real pressure on Dallas late. That is where the Cowboys answered like a veteran team. Craig Morton led the response, and Lance Alworth finished it with a three-yard touchdown catch in the fourth quarter. That score pushed Dallas back ahead by nine, and the Cowboys closed out the 23-14 win. It was not flashy, but it was efficient, composed, and exactly the kind of road division victory that helps shape a playoff season. This game belongs on the countdown because it reflects the 1972 Cowboys perfectly. They were no longer the dominant 1971 championship version, especially with Roger Staubach injured before the season, but they were still tough, resourceful, and dangerous. Dallas would finish 10-4, take the NFC wild card, beat San Francisco in a famous divisional comeback, and then fall to Washington in the NFC Championship Game. This win over the Giants was one of the early building blocks in that run. #Cowboys vs #Giants 1972 Week 2 Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 23, New York Giants 14 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/5DYIOLqcku — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) July 27, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game The division race stayed meaningful all year. Washington won the NFC East at 11-3, Dallas finished second at 10-4, and the Giants finished third at 8-6. title: Cowboys 2026 roster rundown: WR Denzel Mims
summary: It wasn’t that long ago that Denzel Mims was a more highly-regarded WR prospect than George Pickens. Their careers have gone very different directions, with Pickens playing 2026 on the franchise tag and Mims coming off a two-year stint in the UFL. While likely not to the same degree, can the Cowboys help Mims’ career […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - APRIL 19: Denzel Mims #11 of St. Louis BattleHawks warms up prior to the game against the Arlington Renegades at Choctaw Stadium on April 19, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Jack Gorman/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images It wasn’t that long ago that Denzel Mims was a more highly-regarded WR prospect than George Pickens. Their careers have gone very different directions, with Pickens playing 2026 on the franchise tag and Mims coming off a two-year stint in the UFL. While likely not to the same degree, can the Cowboys help Mims’ career as they did Pickens’ last year? Background Years in NFL: 4* Acquired by: Free agency (2026) Mims was a second-round pick by the Jets in 2020, part of a loaded WR class that included CeeDee Lamb, Justin Jefferson, Brandon Aiyuk, Jerry Jeudy, and several others who’ve found steady, contributing roles in the NFL. But on top of entering the league during COVID, which that entire class had to overcome, Mims also missed most of his rookie training camp to injury. He didn’t play until Week 7, but still had what ended up being his most productive season with 23 catches for 357 yards in nine games. In Mims’ second season, the Jets went from offensive-minded head coach Adam Gase to Robert Saleh, who brought in Matt LaFleur as a new offensive coordinator. This regime change, plus his own issues, hurt Mims’ development and footing with the team. He went from eight starts as a rookie to just three in 2021. Mims requested a trade ahead of the 2022 seasons but was denied, and again was limited to a minor role in the WR rotation. The Jets did finally trade him away in the 2023 offseason to the Lions, but he was waived/injured by Detroit midway through the preseason. He spent about two months on the Steelers’ practice squad but didn’t make it to their training camp the following year. The Jaguars gave him a look during their camp in 2024, but released him before final cuts. Without an NFL job, Mims started working in the UFL. He spent 2025 with the St. Louis Battlehawks and this past spring with the Dallas Renegades. He only had 11 catches for 110 yards over those two UFL seasons. Still, someone in the Cowboys’ scouting department must have kept tabs on Mims, and he signed with Dallas in mid-June. Contract Status Years Left: 1 2026 Cap Hit: $1.15 million As the veteran minimum is based on accrued seasons, and not just when you got drafted, Mims’ salary is a little lower than what most 2020 draft picks would be making. But even a fifth- or sixth-year player would only get $1.22 million, so it’s a nominal difference in the grand scheme. 2026 Projections Role: Backup WR Roster Chance: 10% After that damning background section, you may be struggling with why Mims is even here. While Dallas has dabbled with spring league talents before, they’ve generally been league leaders. KaVontae Turpin was the USFL MVP before Dallas signed him, and Brandon Aubrey was its scoring leader. So for Mims, who flamed out of the NFL and then couldn’t even shine in the minors, this opportunity is rather surprising for the now 28-year-old. Between the pandemic, injuries, and three years with the Jets, Mims didn’t get an ideal start to his professional career. His primary QBs during that run were Sam Darnold, who was still looking like a bust in 2020, and then two years of Zach Wilson. Mims certainly didn’t help the situation, but a late second-round pick is often more of a dependent than a catalyst. Someone in the Cowboys organization must feel that Mims has unrealized potential. If nothing else, he’s still 6’3” and known for being a dangerous redzone target. Last year, Dallas’ offense had no problem getting close to paydirt but struggled at times to finish the job. If Mims can show there’s an NFL player in that big body, perhaps that redzone threat gives him an edge over some of the WR competition. Still, there’s a lot of competition for the bottom of the depth chart. We’ve been through it several times already: three assured spots for Lamb, Pickens, and Flournoy, then a likely fourth for Turpin. Mims isn’t even the front-runner among the other veterans vying for work: Jonathan Mingo or Marquez Valdes-Scantling is right now. Then you have all of the young prospects: Anthony Smith, Traeshon Holden, Jordan Hudson, and others. Mims has to be shockingly good to beat out the experienced guys and the youth, especially if Dallas only keeps one more WR on the roster. All that said, Mims isn’t here because he won a raffle or a reality show. Someone decided that this 28-year-old backup from the UFL was worth one of Dallas’ 91 spots for training camp. Will Mims make that person look really smart, or will this be the last gasp of his NFL dream? summary: The Dallas Cowboys appear to have some things that they need to figure out. As the team arrived in Oxnard, California for training camp on Monday, one of the early headlines to emerge involved Tyler Smith and that he did not know what position he was going to play. Given that he is the best […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys appear to have some things that they need to figure out. As the team arrived in Oxnard, California for training camp on Monday, one of the early headlines to emerge involved Tyler Smith and that he did not know what position he was going to play . Given that he is the best interior lineman in the NFL, that raised a few eyebrows. Things happen in the NFL, though. Sometimes you have to move players around and it is possible that it works best for the team to play Smith at left tackle as opposed to left guard. The purpose of training camp is to mine answers like that out. It seems that another question to work on is where another Tyler is going to play. No, not Tyler Guyton, although if Smith is at left tackle then Guyton is going to have to figure something else out. Brian Schottenheimer said during the team’s introductory press conference on Tuesday that Smith would get work at tackle and that Tyler Booker would get work at center. Hmm. That’s interesting. Schotty also noted that Terence Steele could be moved around. This is purely me speculating, but maybe the Cowboys are considering some sort of offensive line like: LT: Tyler Smith LG: T.J. Bass C: Tyler Booker RG: Cooper Beebe RT: Tyler Guyton That is just one possible hypothetical. Obviously Terence Steele is a factor, too. The point is the Cowboys are clearly dedicated to fielding their best five and that there are a number of possible amalgamations on the path there. What should the offensive line look like in your opinion?

full_text: DETROIT, MI - DECEMBER 04: Quinnen Williams #92 of the Dallas Cowboys runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on December 4, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys held court on Tuesday for their press conference to start training camp in Oxnard, and as they did matters are officially underway. The opening presser is a tradition for the team at training camp, and to a lesser degree so is an extension for one of the team’s players while the team is in California. Everyone being together in a tighter compound just seems to be a recipe for deals to get done, and the subject of a particular one coming together came up. Stephen Jones noted that the Cowboys have held discussions with Quinnen Williams’ agent about the process of a hypothetical extension. He noted before he said that the team is quite invested in Williams which is the case as they executed a trade deadline deal to acquire him last season. On some level this gives Williams a bit of leverage. His representation knows that the Cowboys traded what they did for him so they are pot committed on some level. It doesn’t help that the defensive tackle market is on the rise at the moment, consider that about an hour before Stephen said this that the Philadelphia Eagles gave Jalen Carter a four-year, $152M extension . That is the new going rate. Training camp has just begun so perhaps a deal will come together. Williams is the only player of note who the Cowboys have to work with on something like this at the moment, keep in mind that George Pickens is playing on the franchise tag and as we are past the July 15th the team and he can literally not negotiate a new deal until the season is over. Would you pay Quinnen Williams the new going rate? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Jerry Jones says Cowboys did not walk away from Maxx Crosby idea
summary: The Dallas Cowboys held their annual press conference to start training camp on Tuesday, and the idea of the offseason being free of drama came up a lot at the beginning. Jerry Jones noted that he liked that perception and then matters turned to what lies ahead instead of what is in the rearview mirror. […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - NOVEMBER 06: Maxx Crosby #98 of the Las Vegas Raiders stands on the field during the coin toss prior to an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field At Mile High on November 06, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys held their annual press conference to start training camp on Tuesday, and the idea of the offseason being free of drama came up a lot at the beginning. Jerry Jones noted that he liked that perception and then matters turned to what lies ahead instead of what is in the rearview mirror. In a very non-Jerry way, the team’s owner, president, and general manager was expressing such confidence in the group set to start out in Oxnard by saying that he would be willing to risk future assets in the name of helping them. Obviously that is a hint that Jones could orchestrate a trade to help the Cowboys. In fact, he said that he specifically spoke to an NFL team about “something” on Monday. It is worth noting that on Monday it was reported that Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea requested a trade. That could just be coincidence, though. As this conversation was going on, Jerry was asked why he and the team moved on from the Maxx Crosby situation after Crosby’s trade from the Las Vegas Raiders to the Baltimore Ravens fell through. He thought long and hard and then was pretty pointed. “ We didn’t. We did not walk away. “ Everyone involved suddenly recognized that the conversation could be viewed as tampering as Crosby is currently a member of a different NFL team, so matters turned hypothetical. Still though, Jerry clearly made it known that they did not walk away from a Maxx Crosby deal. Should the Cowboys pursue Maxx Crosby? Again? What do you think? Let us know.
author: RJ Ochoa

title: Will McClay reveals the truth behind the Cowboys roster decisions
summary: The perception of the Dallas Cowboys front office among the fanbase is often filled with tension, frustration, and misunderstanding. Fans feel they know exactly what the team needs to do to win, yet the front office consistently moves in a different direction. Recently, Dallas Cowboys Vice President of Player Personnel Will McClay appeared as a […]
full_text: Aug 20, 2022; Inglewood, California, USA; Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones (left) talks with vice president of player personnel Will McClay before the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images The perception of the Dallas Cowboys front office among the fanbase is often filled with tension, frustration, and misunderstanding. Fans feel they know exactly what the team needs to do to win, yet the front office consistently moves in a different direction. Recently, Dallas Cowboys Vice President of Player Personnel Will McClay appeared as a guest on the Doin’ Alright podcast with Voch Lombardi and Bryan Broaddus. This interview provided a rare window into the mind of the man building the roster. They asked questions that are right on the pulse of the fanbase, but McClay’s answers weren’t what people might expect. For fans looking for confirmation of some prior theories, his responses instead painted a different picture, but one we should all take a close look at. Here are five key reveals that everyone should take notice of. Why aren’t the Cowboys spending money in free agency? Broaddus was very blunt with his questioning, sugarcoating nothing. He said that sometimes the fanbase wants to scream at the Cowboys because they do not think the front office does enough in free agency. He asked for some type of explanation about why the team refuses to spend money on outside talent. McClay responded by saying he understands it is a business and that everyone thinks they know what is going on, but added that he does not tell others how to run their checkbook. He continued with a subtle dig at armchair GMs, stating there are all of these self-proclaimed capologists who think they can find easy solutions, but everyone’s way of managing a roster is different. Interestingly, he did not go into any specific details about why the Cowboys are so free agency averse, other than they can’t have the best at every position and have to make tradeoffs accordingly. It might also suggest that this is a strategic philosophy he wants to keep close to his vest. We have written ad nauseum explaining that heavy spending in free agency is a fool’s game . McClay seems perfectly content with letting others believe that overspending in March is the way. What is the real truth on the T.J. Watt vs. Taco Charlton ordeal? McClay has already corrected Broaddus on this specific topic in the past, but Broaddus is relentless. He believes in his heart that McClay was secretly fighting to draft T.J. Watt over Taco Charlton back in 2017, and that he simply fell on the sword for the Dallas draft team because that’s just the kind of guy he is. Broaddus used this interview as another chance to get him to come clean on what really happened. McClay took the opportunity to explain his actual evaluation from that draft. He explained that he liked Watt for his high-energy, and he was highly impressed by how well Watt performed in drills and his ability to get to the quarterback in college. However, he admitted he was put off by what he perceived as stiffness in Watt’s movement at the time, which created some doubt that this style was sustainable at the NFL level. When Broaddus countered by saying Watt seemed like his kind of player, McClay quickly responded with a definitive no. He explained that they took Charlton over Watt because they put grades on those players and that is simply how things stacked up on their board. His stiffness and scheme fit were factors in the grade. While he admitted in hindsight that he was wrong and will learn from it, he 100% owns that decision. Any alternative narrative about him being overridden continues to have very little support. Why do the Cowboys struggle in the middle rounds of the draft? He was asked about why the Cowboys struggle in the middle rounds of the draft despite knocking them out of the park in early rounds. They wanted to know what McClay’s explanation was for this drop-off in success. McClay quickly reminded them that a lot of NFL teams do not even get it right in the first and second rounds. He stated that “our blessing is our curse,” indicating that the massive success the team has enjoyed early in drafts has created unreasonably high expectations for the later rounds. He pointed out that historical data shows the success rate of later picks is naturally much lower across the league, hinting that this perception of Dallas being bad late in the draft is being overstated by fans. He also noted that certain positions, like offensive linemen, have completely different development windows. Expecting a mid-to-late round guy to step in and immediately contribute is not always fair to the player’s developmental path. Do media narratives bother him and make his job harder? Broaddus asked if there are things the media says that bother him, and if those reports ultimately make his job harder. McClay quickly responded with a definitive yes. He stated that they are in a business of secrecy and they ideally do not want to let other teams know what they are doing. He provided an example of when they bring a free agent into the building. The moment everyone finds out about it, it compromises their leverage, whereas he would prefer to have some alone time with the player before other teams start calling the agent’s phone. He also stated that young players are human beings with emotions who are constantly attached to their phones. These players get a regular dose of media scrutiny, creating outside noise that upper management and the coaching staff have to actively work around. Would McClay be better served if he ran his own team? Broaddus cringingly stated that he wants to see McClay run his own team, insisting that if he were a traditional general manager elsewhere, he would do it the right way. That’s obviously not in the best interest of the Cowboys if you are a fan of McClay, but we understand what Broaddus was getting at with this question. He believes in his heart that if McClay ran his own team, he would be even better than Los Angeles Rams general manager Les Snead. That’s high praise. McClay was appreciative of the high compliment but then turned around and interjected that the Cowboys are one of the few teams you have to worry about in the league. That is what he truly believes, and he believes it because of the way the staff works together within the organization. This is an important distinction. He does not feel this is a work environment where he is being strong-armed or overridden in roster decision-making by ownership. He made it clear that what they are doing in Dallas is exactly what he wants in a player personnel role. McClay stated that “you are only as good as the people you are surrounded by,” concluding with how badly he wants to win a Super Bowl for the Cowboys. He believes if you win in Dallas, “that is the golden ticket,” and “doing everything within his power to achieve that is of paramount importance” to him. This interview with McClay serves as a reminder that NFL front offices operate in a different world than the average observer. While fans rely on rumors, media narratives, and retrospective analysis, McClay and the rest of the Cowboys’ front office are managing the complicated business of winning football games. The belief that the front office is fractured by internal power struggles is false according to McClay. McClay is exactly where he wants to be, running the department the way he chooses, and owning both the hits and the misses.

The Dallas Cowboys are about to begin work out in Oxnard, California and when they do everyone will be out on the field working on getting better. Seriously. Literally everyone. From time to time there are players who are placed on unique lists and given particular designations relative to the Cowboys roster. This is to allow for injury situations and things of the like. The Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list is a space where they are often held to start training camp, and we are accustomed to the Cowboys (like most teams) having a player or two there. Not this year! Starting off on the right foot: the Cowboys aren't expected to add any player on the roster to PUP or NFI, per source. They expect to have everyone available to practice tomorrow. It isn’t a big deal. But the Cowboys are extremely healthy which is another point of excitement for all of the activity that is set to unfold. It feels incredible. Right?!

title: Dallas Cowboys 2026 Opponent Preview: Green Bay Packers
summary: With training camp here, the excitement for football season is about to ramp up to a fever pitch. For the Dallas Cowboys, it’s been an offseason where more noise has come from their roster moves, free agent acquisitions, and draft picks than any off the field drama, which is a welcome change for a team […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - JANUARY 14: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers looks to pass during the second quarter against the Dallas Cowboys in the NFC Wild Card Playoff game at AT&T Stadium on January 14, 2024 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Richard Rodriguez/Getty Images) | Getty Images With training camp here, the excitement for football season is about to ramp up to a fever pitch. For the Dallas Cowboys, it’s been an offseason where more noise has come from their roster moves, free agent acquisitions, and draft picks than any off the field drama, which is a welcome change for a team that will begin the regular season 973 days removed from their last playoff game appearance. That playoff game was the now-infamous 48-32 home loss to the Green Bay Packers. The Cowboys and Packers have met just once since that January game in AT&T Stadium, and it was memorable for a whole other host of reasons, ending in a 40-40 tie on Sunday Night Football last season in week four. The Cowboys and Packers will meet again on Sunday night primetime this season, at Lambeau Field, this time in week six. As we continue our season preview series, Dallas’ division rivals are now all behind us, and our focus will shift to some of the potential toughest games on the schedule against either other rivals or expected playoff contenders at large. Also for the second year in a row, the Cowboys and Packers early season meeting will be marked by a trade between the two sides involving a pass rusher. Last season, it was Kenny Clark coming over to the Cowboys from the Packers (plus some draft picks) in exchange for Micah Parsons, and this year the Cowboys acquired Rashan Gary after seven seasons with the green and gold. With Parsons still rehabbing from a week 15 ACL tear last season against the Broncos, the Cowboys may not be playing against their own former pass rush star this time around. The Packers scored 40 points on the Matt Eberflus defense in 2025; this game will be a very important early comparison point to just how much of a difference new defensive coordinator Christian Parker is making. Another theme both of these teams will have going into 2026 is the expectation for their all-important QB/HC pairing to prove they are the right men for the jobs. The Packers will go into year four of Jordan Love as the starting quarterback and year eight for Matt LaFleur having lost in the Wild Card round the last two postseasons. For the Cowboys, it will be just year two of Brian Schottenheimer but year 11 for Dak Prescott. There was a point when Love was an up-and-coming quarterback and Prescott was in the midst of the three straight 12 win seasons under Mike McCarthy, and both were seen as potentially battling for supremacy at the position in the NFC, but so far it still hasn’t manifested for either. Love hasn’t dominated the NFC North, he has a career record of 9-8 against the Lions, Bears, and Vikings, but could also be looking to capitalize on the Lions seemingly hitting a downturn under Dan Campbell with Jared Goff and the Vikings bringing in Kyler Murray, leaving the Bears with Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams as their biggest rival. Packers Key Free Agent Signings/Departures * SIGNED IN FREE AGENCY QB Tyrod Taylor OL Darian Kinnard (Re-signed) CB Benjamin St-Juste DL Javon Hargrave * DEPARTED IN FREE AGENCY QB Malik Willis WR Romeo Doubs LB Quay Walker C Elgton Jenkins EDGE Kingsley Enagbare LT Rasheed Walker CB Nate Hobbs RB Emanuel Wilson SAF Zayne Anderson For a team without a first-round pick due to the Micah Parsons trade last offseason, the Packers have a potentially worrying list of departures compared to a short list of acquisitions in free agency this year. Doubs, Walker, and Jenkins are among the most significant contributors to leave the team, while Javon Hargrave coming over from the Vikings is their biggest outside name brought in – partially because it weakens a division rival and strengthens a position where the Packers previously had Kenny Clark as a mainstay. One of the things the Packers are banking on to finally take the next step is something very similar to the Cowboys – continuity at wide receiver. Christian Watson, Matthew Golden, and Jayden Reed are all returning, and Doubs is the only significant loss. The Cowboys will be particularly happy to not see Doubs this season as he had three touchdowns on six catches against them in that overtime tie last season. Reed is going into year four, Golden year two, and Watson year five, which the Packers will be hoping is the right formula along with Josh Jacobs in year three as the starting running back to have consistency both through the air and on the ground offensively. Defensively, the Packers have struggled to hold up against more physical teams in their most decisive games in the front seven, and appear to be taking a new approach still with familiar names throughout to the point of attack on defense going into 2026. Walker and Enagbare are significant losses at linebacker and defensive end respectively, but Devonte Wyatt, Lukas Van Ness, Edgerrin Cooper, and the addition of Hargrave along with rookie draft pick Chris McClellan on the interior give the Packers the talent to compete on this side of the ball while they work on reintroducing Parsons back to the lineup deeper into the regular season. This brings us to the rest of the Packers draft class, where four of their six total picks went to defense as well. Packers 2026 Draft Class Round 2, Pick 20 (52 Overall): CB Brandon Cisse Round 3, Pick 13 (77 Overall): DT Chris McClellan Round 4, Pick 20 (120 Overall): EDGE Dani Dennis-Sutton Round 5, Pick 13 (153 Overall): C Jager Burton Round 6, Pick 20 (2o1 Overall): CB Domani Jackson Round 6, Pick 35 (216 Overall): K Trey Smack When it comes to the draft in recent history, the Packers have been known to target very specific, certain archetypes of prospects, and find a way to get them at high value. Brandon Cisse may have been outside the radar of top cornerback talent in this class, but an athletic profile featuring a 93rd percentile vertical jump result and 91st in the broad jump along with being a strong run support secondary player make him an intriguing pick at 77th overall. While Cisse does not necessarily impress as a physical specimen, the Packers next pick of Chris McClellan at DT makes up for it. With plus hand size and arm length, and flashes as both a pass rusher and run defender, Green Bay is hoping this is their next long-term solution on the defensive interior. The Packers double-dipped on the defensive line with their next pick, getting another plus athlete with an untapped high ceiling but perhaps lower-than-ideal floor in Dennis Sutton out of Penn State. The Packers’ one pick on offense went to the offensive line with Jager Burton, who could slide in to the center spot vacated by Elgton Jenkins in free agency, or either guard spot. Packers 2026 Coaching Changes * New to staff this season: Wide Receivers Noah Pauley Defensive Coordinator Jonathan Gannon Secondary/Pass Game Coordinator Bobby Babich Cornerbacks Daniel Bullocks Linebackers Sam Siefkes Special Teams Coordinator Cam Achord Head coach Matt LaFleur has retained a very impressive amount of continuity on his offensive coaching staff, but the one new position coach in Noah Pauley comes at an interesting spot considering what we said about the Packers developing their wide receiver corps. The much bigger change comes on defense, where LaFleur will have the fourth new defensive coordinator over his tenure in Jonathan Gannon. The former Cardinals head coach brings a dynamic the Packers have not had in this position under their offensive play-calling head coach. The Gannon style of defense when playing well can be adept at forcing teams to take the long way downfield, limiting big plays well and relying on the front to shut down the run. It will be very interesting to see how this stacks up with LaFleur’s ability to control games with balance in…

title: 8 Detroit Lions thoughts prior to training camp
summary: Detroit Lions training camp officially kicks off on Wednesday morning with the first practice of the season. But before we dig into our training camp coverage, I wanted to offer eight overall thoughts I have on the team as they enter the preseason. These are not necessarily thoughts on what will happen in training camp, […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MI - AUGUST 08: A general view of the Detroit Lions training camp graphics and logo is seen on a tent during the Detroit Lions Training Camp afternoon practice session on August 8, 2022 at the the Detroit Lions Training Facility in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Detroit Lions training camp officially kicks off on Wednesday morning with the first practice of the season. But before we dig into our training camp coverage, I wanted to offer eight overall thoughts I have on the team as they enter the preseason. These are not necessarily thoughts on what will happen in training camp, but overall wide-ranging, lingering thoughts about the team as a whole. 1. Derrick Barnes may be the most important player on defense Don’t confuse “important” with best or even most impactful. Obviously, Aidan Hutchinson may be the most impactful, and Jack Campbell has an argument for best. But if the Lions’ defense is going to succeed in 2026, they need Barnes to live up to the contract he signed last offseason. With no Alex Anzalone anymore, Barnes is currently expected to not only be a full-time starter, but likely expand his role beyond the niche SAM position he held last year. Even with the team moving to more nickel sets, Barnes will be on the field 80-90% of the time, and if Detroit is going to keep their linebacking corps a strength, Barnes will have to improve as a coverage linebacker and pass rusher—two things he was just okay at last year. 2. Ennis Rakestraw has a very real chance to win the starting CB2 job The loss of Terrion Arnold is a massive disappointment, as he was one of the most likely candidates for a Year 3 breakout. But Rakestraw was drafted just 37 picks later, and Detroit still has a ton of hope in him. Injuries derailed his first two seasons, but it’s easy to forget he was in line to be a starter in his rookie season before an injury during warmups sidelined him. In the spring, we saw Rakestraw mix in with the first-team defense, and I don’t expect that to change in the upcoming month. While Rock Ya-Sin is certainly the more trusted option right now, Rakestraw has a higher ceiling, and I expect Detroit to fully explore that. 3. I’m not giving up on Levi Onwuzurike Call me naive or a hopeless optimist, but I still think Levi Onwuzurike can be a difference-maker on this team. I can’t shake his 2024 season, where he produced 13 quarterback hits and 45 pressures—ranking seventh and 15th among interior defenders that year, respectively (although he played a lot on the edge, too). His back injury has been in the rear-view mirror for a full two years now, and he’s over a year removed from ACL surgery. Injury will still obviously remain a concern, and he’s already 28 years old, but Onwuzurike has a relentless attitude and a chip on his shoulder. And with Detroit clearly looking to improve their pass rush this year, I think Onwuzurike will be a key part of that plan. 4. The Lions defense may look more different than expected All offseason, I was expecting Detroit to make a little tweak here, a little tweak there on defense. However, as we get deeper and deeper into the offseason, more hints arise that this could be a lot more different than last year. It starts with the defensive front. Detroit’s roster moves tell a very interesting story. They let DJ Reader and Roy Lopez walk in free agency, and the one player they signed to replace them at nose tackle— Jay Tufele—was released on the eve of training camp . Only Chris Smith and UDFA Aidan Keanaaina remain among nose tackle depth. Detroit also invested in two Day 3 defensive linemen in the draft who are both better pass rushers than run defenders, and Tyleik Williams came into camp 50 pounds lighter. All of this points to a more dynamic, athletic, and pass rush-leaning defensive line. That’s a significant departure from “stop the run, earn the right to pass rush.” That may still be the mantra, but it’s clear Detroit is now willing to sacrifice some run-stopping ability to get to the passer. Beyond that, it’s clear based on Detroit’s lack of Anzalone replacement—and Kelvin Sheppard’s own words—that the team is planning on playing more nickel going forward. I do like Sheppard’s willingness to change—stubbornness was always Aaron Glenn’s biggest weakness—but I do wonder about this strategy a little. Detroit’s defense really fell apart at the end of last year when their run defense dropped off a cliff. And by personnel, they look a little worse off in that department. 5. I don’t know if Giovanni Manu can win a roster spot I came to this epiphany during this week’s Lions training camp preview PODcast. While I’m later on this than others, I just don’t see a case in which keeping Manu around makes any sense. There’s obviously no path for Manu to ever win a starting job, with Penei Sewell and Blake Miller holding down those roles for hopefully the next decade or so. Manu is also very unlikely to win the OT3 job this year, as the Lions invested in Larry Borom with a $5 million contract that is essentially fully guaranteed. The question is whether Manu can warrant keeping an OT4 or figure out another position he can backup. But is that even worth it at this point? He has just one more year left on his rookie contract beyond this season, so any financial benefit is pretty much null and void. I do believe Manu still has development within him, and he may be a good reserve one day for one team. However, with Detroit’s offensive line depth improved everywhere and Manu’s contract coming to an end relatively soon, I believe his runway in Detroit has come to an end. 6. I’m still holding out hope for another cornerback While I expect Rakestraw and Ya-Sin to battle it out for the starting cornerback job opposite D.J. Reed, I wish there was a third contender in the mix. For me, it’s less about finding someone better than those two to start and more about getting a player they can rely on as a primary backup. Detroit could still field an okay defense if Reed and Ya-Sin are the starters. My confidence completely sinks if an injury hits one of those players—or, god forbid, both. Cornerback tends to be one of the most injured positions with the speed and change of direction they play with, so the Lions going into this season with almost zero experience among their depth is highly concerning to me. 7. The Lions offensive line will go through growing pains, but end up significantly better than 2025 The Lions made it clear that offensive line improvement was one of the primary goals. They moved on from Taylor Decker and Graham Glasgow, and invested in Cade Mays as their new center and first-round pick Blake Miller to be their tackle of the future. But we must remember that offensive line chemistry takes time to build. And the reality of the situation is that there isn’t a single player on this Lions offensive line who will be working alongside the same person they played with in 2025. Penei Sewell’s move to left tackle means new chemistry with the left guard. The left guard starter will have a new left tackle and center to play between. And right guard Tate Ratledge will no longer have the benefit of Sewell alongside his right shoulder. There had to be a youth movement and some change along the offensive line after the golden years of 2023 and 2024, but that will not come without some early hardships. Just don’t panic when it doesn’t look perfect in September, but the potential payoff in November and December should be huge. 8. The Lions’ 2026 season will sink or swim with the 2025 draft class The reality of this offseason is that the Lions lost more talent than they added, but that had to be the case. This team is fully committed to the draft-and-development strategy, and that’s going to leave you short-handed in offseason resources. With the 2024 class looking like a pretty massive disappointment, the pressure is on the 2025 draft class…

title: Adam Schefter hints Lions RB Jahmyr Gibbs extension could be coming soon
summary: It’s been eerily quiet when it comes to a potential contract extension for Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs, but ESPN’s Adam Schefter suggested the silence could break very soon. In an interview with local Detroit sports reporter Brad Galli, Schefter said there’s buzz about a Gibbs extension coming down the pike in the next […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MICHIGAN - JUNE 17: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions works out at mandatory minicamp at Detroit Lions Meijer Performance Center on June 17, 2026 in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s been eerily quiet when it comes to a potential contract extension for Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs, but ESPN’s Adam Schefter suggested the silence could break very soon. In an interview with local Detroit sports reporter Brad Galli, Schefter said there’s buzz about a Gibbs extension coming down the pike in the next couple weeks —with not as much known about a potential Sam LaPorta extension. “I think the Gibbs thing could be relatively quick, whatever that is,” Scheter told Galli. “And, LaPorta, I haven’t heard as much on, but I think they’ll be moving in the running back market in the coming week plus.” Lions general manager Brad Holmes has been very proactive when it comes to signing Detroit’s young, core players. We’ve already seen eight of his draft picks—Penei Sewell, Alim McNeill, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Derrick Barnes, Aidan Hutchinson, Jameson Williams, Kerby Joseph, and Jack Campbell—receiving significant extensions, and those deals were typically done well before their rookie deals expired. Gibbs has two years remaining on his rookie contract after the Lions exercised his fifth-year option earlier this offseason. But despite that extra cushion, Holmes has expressed publicly an interest in signing Gibbs to a long-term deal—along with Campbell (who got his extension already), LaPorta, and Brian Branch. Gibbs is the most logical player to be next in line for his extension. LaPorta and Branch are returning from injury, while Gibbs is coming off another fantastic season. He has now found the end zone at least 10 times in three consecutive seasons, and in the last two seasons alone, Gibbs has 2,635 rushing yards, 29 rushing touchdowns, 1,133 receiving yards, and nine receiving touchdowns. It’s unclear how much Gibbs is set to make on a new contract, but this offseason saw a few big-time running backs set the market. Devon Achane got a four-year, $64 million extension ($16 million per year) and Breece Hall got three years, $43.5 million ($14.5M/year). The top of the market still belongs to Saquon Barkley (two years, $41.2M — $20.6M per year) and Christian McCaffrey (two years, $38M — $19M per year). In the meantime, Lions veterans reported to Allen Park on Tuesday for the start of training camp. We’ll see if Gibbs takes the field with a new deal or not on Wednesday.

title: Detroit Lions place 2 on NFI, release NT Jay Tufele
summary: The Detroit Lions open their 2026 training camp on Wednesday, and on Tuesday, their veterans reported to the team’s Allen Park training facility. As players rejoin the team, it’s common for the team to make a few last-minute transactions in preparation for camp. Earlier in the week, we saw the Lions place three players on […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - DECEMBER 22: Guard Christian Mahogany #73 of the Detroit Lions stands on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Chicago Bears, at Soldier Field on December 22, 2024 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions open their 2026 training camp on Wednesday, and on Tuesday, their veterans reported to the team’s Allen Park training facility. As players rejoin the team, it’s common for the team to make a few last-minute transactions in preparation for camp. Earlier in the week, we saw the Lions place three players on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list , and on Tuesday, they placed Christian Mahogany on the Non-Football Injury (NFI) list, Christian Izien on the Non-Football Illness (NFI) list, and released veteran nose tackle Jay Tufele. If you’re not familiar with the difference between the lists, which list a player lands on is based on where they were injured and the type of injury. If a player was hurt while participating in an activity directly related to the NFL (games, practices, workouts, etc.), they land on the PUP list. If a player was injured in a non-NFL activity (which can include private workouts or in their personal life), they land on the NFI (injury) list. If a player is dealing with an illness (which can range from having the flu or Mononucleosis—like Mahogany had as a rookie—or even more serious illnesses), they land in the NFI (illness) category. These lists also have some similarities as well. Like with the PUP list, placing a player on either NFI list at this stage does not require them to miss any games. They are restricted from practicing while on the injury lists, but players are also eligible to be removed from any of these lists at any time if a team believes a player is healthy enough to begin practicing. However, if a player remains on any of the lists through roster cutdowns, they will be forced to miss the first four games of the regular season. Mahogany returns to Detroit this season expecting to work to retain his starting left guard job, so any absence will certainly hinder his ability to compete for that role. While he is out, look for either veteran Ben Bartch, second-year lineman Miles Frazier, or recently traded-for Juice Scruggs to try to seize the opportunity in front of them. Izien joined the Lions this offseason and was working with the starting safeties in the spring as he was trying to acclimate to the Lions’ scheme quickly, as he was also expected to compete for a starting role with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph on the PUP list. While Izien misses time, Thomas Harper and Avonte Maddox, along with veteran Chuck Clark, should have great opportunities to get into the starting rotation at practice. Ideally, we will get an update on the statuses of the injured players on Wednesday at coach Dan Campbell’s press conference ahead of the Lions’ first training camp practice.

title: 20 Detroit Lions on the defensive roster bubble entering training camp
summary: On Monday, we examined the Detroit Lions’ roster bubble on offense. With so much talent on that side of the ball, we only found 15 players we believed were entering training camp on the bubble, and we were probably a little generous with some roster long-shots. The outlook on defense is much more up for […]
full_text: Detroit Lions edge Ahmed Hassanein(99) during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 29, 2026. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images On Monday, we examined the Detroit Lions’ roster bubble on offense . With so much talent on that side of the ball, we only found 15 players we believed were entering training camp on the bubble, and we were probably a little generous with some roster long-shots. The outlook on defense is much more up for grabs. With a lot of roster turnover from last year—plus a lot of rotational roles available—we have the Lions starting training camp with 20 players on the roster bubble. So before camp officially kicks off on Wednesday, the Pride of Detroit staff made their predictions for all 20 players. Below is a chart of all of our picks. A discussion on each position follows underneath that. View Link Defensive end : Assumed in: Aidan Hutchinson, DJ Wonnum, Derrick Moore Payton Turner: 6 “IN” votes Ahmed Hassanein: 3 votes Anthony Lucas: 0 votes As is typically the case, we’re giving the slight edge to the veteran player over the young, developmental option. Payton Turner is a former first-round pick who just hasn’t been able to stay healthy, earning himself a reputation much like Marcus Davenport. He didn’t play at all last year with a rib injury, so expectations should be relatively low, but the potential is high. Hassanein also didn’t play last year. That was the combination of a pectoral injury and the rest of the season spent on the practice squad. He’s already endeared himself to Lions fans with his infectious attitude and relentless drive, but he’s still very new to the game, and now he’ll have to endure a role change from the rush edge position to the big end position. That’s a tough ask for a young player, so he’ll face an uphill battle this camp. Defensive tackle: Assumed in: Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams, Levi Onwuzurike Tyler Lacy: 11 “IN” votes Skyle Gill-Howard: 9 votes Jay Tufele: 6 votes Mekhi Wingo: 3 votes Chris Smith: 1 vote Tyre West: 0 votes Aidan Keanaaina: 0 votes This is a tough group to judge, because there are so many different roles within the defensive line. Tyler Lacy (11 votes) and Tyre West (0) may be fighting for the same big end role (with Hassanein). Jay Tufele (9 votes) and Aidan Keanaaina (0) are likely battling for a reserve nose tackle. Skyler Gill-Howard (9 votes) and Mekhi Wingo (3) are both pass-rushing three-techs. But there’s no guarantee the Lions keep one of each of those reserve positions on the 53-man roster. That makes for some messy predictions, but it’s interesting to see that Lacy is the only unanimous in. I suppose that’s because he stuck around after playing 10 games with the team last year. Linebacker: Assumed in: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, Jimmy Rolder Trevor Nowaske: 9 “IN” votes Damone Clark: 8 votes Erick Hunter: 1 vote NOTE: These votes were made before the Lions signed veteran linebacker Troy Reeder on Monday . One of the bigger challenges of predicting the linebacker room is projecting the amount they’ll keep. They’ve previously liked rostering at least six linebackers, but with more nickel formations in this defense’s future, it’s possible they only keep five. The top four seem fairly settled, but there’s a pretty fierce competition brewing for that fifth spot. Nowaske brings some SAM reserve skills. Damone Clark is well experienced both on defense and special teams. And newly signed Troy Reeder is a former special teams captain with a long history of beating the odds. Cornerback: Assumed in: DJ Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Ennis Rakestraw, Roger McCreary, Keith Abney Khalil Dorsey: 10 “IN” votes Nick Whiteside: 1 vote Unless the Lions end up adding a cornerback—which many, myself included, think they should following Terrion Arnold’s waiving—this room is oddly straightforward. It seems quite likely the Lions will have two starters out of Reed, Ya-Sin, and Rakestraw, while McCreary and Abney will fight for the nickel role—although both players have the flexibility to provide depth on the outside. From there, it’s a matter of what you want in a CB6. Dorsey is the heavy favorite given his value as a special teamer. However, Whiteside has shown brief flashes of solid cornerback play, and Detroit may want to see his development through. Safety Assumed in: Kerby Joseph, Christian Izien Assumed out: Brian Branch ( PUP ) Avonte Maddox: 11 “IN” votes Thomas Harper: 11 votes Chuck Clark: 11 votes Dan Jackson: 0 votes Loren Strickland: 0 votes As of right now, POD is unanimous in how they believe the safety room will play out. But that is assuming that Kerby Joseph will eventually come off the PUP list and be ready for the regular season. As of now, that’s a pretty big assumption to make, but we’ll hopefully get some clarity later this week. The rest of the room is filled with a nice mix of youth (Izien, Harper) and veterans (Maddox, Clark). And Detroit may have enough special teams experience out of Izien (440 snaps) and Harper (312) to make it very hard for Jackson or Strickland to work their way out of the basement.

title: Discussion: Where will the Detroit Lions’ defense rank in 2026?
summary: On Sunday, we discussed the potential of the 2026 Detroit Lions offense. Almost everyone agrees that it will be a top-10 unit in the NFL this season, and per the poll we ran on this site, 90 percent of our audience believes the Lions will have a top-five offense. I’m guessing Lions fans will be […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 20: Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard of the Detroit Lions while playing the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Ford Field on October 20, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday, we discussed the potential of the 2026 Detroit Lions offense. Almost everyone agrees that it will be a top-10 unit in the NFL this season, and per the poll we ran on this site, 90 percent of our audience believes the Lions will have a top-five offense . I’m guessing Lions fans will be a little less optimistic about the other side of the ball. The Lions defense has been an issue for most years under Dan Campbell. While they’ve been able to add some blue chip players like Aidan Hutchinson, Jack Campbell, Kerby Joseph, and Brian Branch, the unit hasn’t been able to put together a full season of strong play. Sometimes, it’s been injuries. Other times, it feels like Detroit is being overcoached. Certainly the lack of a pass rush has been culpable at times. Regardless of the reasoning, the defense has regularly let the Lions down. But could 2026 bring some extra hope? Detroit finally invested in their defensive line, and the players along that front are entering training camp healthier than ever. Additionally, Detroit has fortified their depth at linebacker and safety. And young players like Tyleik Williams, Jack Campbell, and Ennis Rakestraw could elevate their games and jump in their development. That said, there are huge questions about health and starters in the secondary, and Detroit still needs to show they can account and adjust to the losses of DJ Reader, Roy Lopez, Al-Quadin Muhammad, Alex Anzalone, and Amik Robertson. And defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard has a lot to prove in his second season at that position. So today’s Question of the Day is: Where will the Lions’ defense rank in 2026? My answer: First, let’s go back and look at last year’s rankings by several metrics: 5.4 yards per play — 18th 24.3 points per game — 22nd 7.3 yards per pass attempt — 24th 92.5 passer rating — 19th 4.4 yards per carry — 24th 9th in DVOA 15th in EPA per play 11th in success rate In general, this was an average-to-below-average defense. They graded out a little better in advanced statistics—likely because Detroit allowed a high amount of explosive plays that skewed some of the other basic statistics. But despite their surprisingly high DVOA ranking, no one would mistake the 2025 Lions as a top-10 defense. That said, I do think it’s fair to call them average. At times, they were a very good defense, particularly on early downs. What killed them were those explosive plays. They allowed a total of 68 plays of 20+ yards, which was sixth-most in the NFL. Bump that up to 30+ yard plays and Detroit jumps to FIRST, with a league-leading 34 explosives allowed. Point being, if Detroit can manage the frequency of those back-breaking plays, they become a much better defense instantly. Like cutting pop out of your diet, it’s a quick way to trim fat. But that’s a lot easier said than done, and a very easy argument could be made that Detroit’s defensive roster is worse than it was last year. I’m hopeful that Detroit can find a steady—but unspectacular—pairing at safety while Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch recover from injury. I like the overall outlook of the defensive front. I believe Jack Campbell will continue to grow and get better. But I don’t have confidence in anyone else in the linebacker room. The depth at cornerback is perilously thin. And Sheppard still has to prove he can provide logical, effective game plans each week. All of that is to say that I’m not sure expectations should be much higher or lower than last year. If things break the right way (e.g., youth development, injury luck), Detroit’s defense could certainly crack the top-10. For the first two months of last year, Detroit’s defense was playing at a top-10 level. But once the depth got tested, the Lions played some better offenses, and some of Sheppard’s techniques got figured out, the Lions slid quickly. So I’m going to put the Lions right around average in their defense this year with the potential to slide into either the top-10 or bottom-10, but not much beyond that. What are your thoughts? title: Packers add 5 more to injury list, including Micah Parsons
summary: The Green Bay Packers placed six players on injury lists on Monday: running back Chris Brooks (non-football injury list), tight end Tucker Kraft (physically unable to perform), tight end Luke Musgrave (PUP), left guard Aaron Banks (PUP), defensive lineman Javon Hargrave (PUP) and cornerback Kamal Hadden (PUP). On Tuesday, the team added five more players […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - DECEMBER 14: Micah Parsons #1 of the Green Bay Packers defends during the third quarter against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on December 14, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers placed six players on injury lists on Monday : running back Chris Brooks (non-football injury list), tight end Tucker Kraft (physically unable to perform), tight end Luke Musgrave (PUP), left guard Aaron Banks (PUP), defensive lineman Javon Hargrave (PUP) and cornerback Kamal Hadden (PUP). On Tuesday, the team added five more players to the list, including two we expected — edge rusher Micah Parsons (PUP, torn ACL) and defensive lineman Jordon Riley (PUP, torn Achilles). The other three players were surprises: tackle Brant Banks (PUP), defensive lineman Nazir Stackhouse (PUP) and long snapper Matt Orzech (PUP). Notably, Orzech is the only long snapper on the team, meaning that the Packers will presumably be without one until he returns or another player is signed. Green Bay officially starts training camp practices on Wednesday, so keep an eye out for some potential action there. As a reminder, the PUP list doesn’t come with any timeline designation. A player can be placed on the PUP list upon reporting to camp but can be taken off as early as the first practice. The same is true for NFI players, which currently only applies to Chris Brooks. The good news here: right tackle Zach Tom and defensive lineman Devonte Wyatt are full go for training camp. It’s a bit of a surprise that Hadden isn’t ready to return to the field yet, considering that he said his recovery was going to be a four- to five-month process back in January. It was already assumed that Kraft was going to miss the first week or two of camp, so there’s no major worry there. Parsons will miss at least the first four weeks of the regular season (as the team has stated he’s starting the 2026 campaign on the regular-season PUP list), and Riley is unlikely to contribute in 2026. So far, we have no word on the injuries to Musgrave, Banks, the other Banks, Hargrave, Stackhouse or Orzech. We’ll probably get more answers on that front on Wednesday.

title: Packers sign tight end Thomas Yassmin, designate him as international exemption
summary: When it was reported earlier on Tuesday that international kicker Lenny Krieg was signed by the Green Bay Packers, but that Krieg wasn’t designated as the Packers’ international exemption player moving forward, it raised some eyebrows. That role, apparently, was going to go to tight end Thomas Yassmin following the release of edge rusher Dante […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - DECEMBER 02: Thomas Yassmin #87 of the Utah Utes runs with the ball during the fourth quarter of the PAC-12 Championship football game against the USC Trojans at Allegiant Stadium on December 02, 2022 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The Utah Utes won 47-24. (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images When it was reported earlier on Tuesday that i nternational kicker Lenny Krieg was signed by the Green Bay Packers , but that Krieg wasn’t designated as the Packers’ international exemption player moving forward, it raised some eyebrows. That role, apparently, was going to go to tight end Thomas Yassmin following the release of edge rusher Dante Barnett, who previously served as the Packers’ exemption player. In total, here were the moves that the Packers made on Tuesday, following a nine-man workout on Monday : Signed K Lenny Krieg Signed TE Thomas Yassmin (international exemption) Waived EDGE Dante Barnett Waived K Lucas Havrisik Below is the blurb we wrote about Yassmin yesterday: Yassmin is a former rugby player who is eligible to be designated as an international exemption player (currently a spot taken by edge rusher Dante Barnett). Yassmin transitioned to football in South Wales before joining Utah’s football team. After six years of college football, he got his NFL start with the Denver Broncos and was also a member of the Los Angeles Chargers in 2025. He was drafted in the CFL’s global draft as the 14th overall pick in the 2024 class, becoming the second tight end off the board (five of the first nine picks were kickers or punters, for perspective). When the Broncos signed Yassmin, he received $47,000 in guarantees. For reference, the Packers signed R.J. Maryland to $15,000 in guaranteed money this offseason. Yassmin’s initial signing cost dwarfs more than half of Green Bay’s 2026 UDFA signings. Between being let go by the Broncos and signing with the Chargers, Yassmin also worked out with the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2025. Yassmin was waived by Los Angeles in May. Notably, the Packers worked out three tight ends (and four running backs) on Monday out of the nine players they brought in. Green Bay placed both Tucker Kraft and Luke Musgrave on the physically unable to perform list to start training camp . On paper, the following tight ends are healthy at the start of camp, following the addition of Yassmin: Josh Whyle Luke Lachey (signed post-draft this offseason) Messiah Swinson Drake Dabney R.J. Maryland (UDFA rookie) Thomas Yassmin For what it’s worth, the Packers can add the international exemption status to Krieg in the future if they would like to. This is to say that if the team wanted to move on from Yassmin once Kraft and/or Musgrave get healthy, Krieg can slide into the international exemption slot and free up another roster spot for an American player.

title: Packers make kicker swap, signing Lenny Krieg and releasing Lucas Havrisik
summary: Let’s add some more intrigue to the Green Bay Packers’ kicking situation this summer. A few months after drafting Trey Smack in the 6th round of the 2026 NFL Draft and releasing veteran Brandon McManus, the Packers are making another swap in the specialist room. After working out German kicker Lenny Krieg on Monday, the […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - AUGUST 8: Lenny Krieg #46 of the Atlanta Falcons warms up on the sideline during the first half of the NFL Preseason 2025 game between Detroit Lions and Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on August 8, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s add some more intrigue to the Green Bay Packers’ kicking situation this summer. A few months after drafting Trey Smack in the 6th round of the 2026 NFL Draft and releasing veteran Brandon McManus, the Packers are making another swap in the specialist room. After working out German kicker Lenny Krieg on Monday, the team is signing him to the 90-man roster, as first reported by Bill Huber of SI. This move puts Krieg into the summer competition along with Smack, moving forward with a pair of youngsters with no NFL experience. That competition remains a two-man fight, however. Lucas Havrisik will not be part of the battle, as Tom Silverstein reports that the team has waived him in order to make room for Krieg on the roster. Havrisik was a great story and set a Packers franchise record with a 61-yard field goal last season, but he was unable to hold onto the kicking job despite McManus’ ongoing injury issues around midseason. A major benefit to the Packers in the long term is the fact that Krieg could qualify for an International Player Pathway exemption due to his being from Germany. The Berlin native picked up football a few years ago after playing soccer in his youth, and if the Packers designate him as their IPP player, he would qualify for a bonus 91st roster spot this offseason and an extra practice squad spot should the team elect to sign him to that part of the roster during the regular season. That could allow the team to keep Krieg in the organization on the practice squad without taking up a normal spot, should they keep Smack on the 53-man roster as their #1 kicker after training camp. Krieg could then develop while providing some injury insurance for Smack at the same time. Still, this sets up to be a real competition between the two players once practices begin on Wednesday. Currently, the Packers have applied their IPP designation to Dante Barnett, an edge rusher from England. However, the team can change which player receives that designation in the future. Thus, if Barnett does not end up making the team or the practice squad in the regular season, the team could shift the IPP status to Krieg at a later date.

In truth, we’ve really only had one significant moment with the Packers’ new president, and it happened yesterday. Yes, in his still-short career as the Packers’ head man, this is pretty much the only significant public thing he’s done so far. And more or less, he seemed to hit the right notes. But what else do you expect him to say? It’s the most public event, sure, but in a lot of ways, the shareholders meeting is about the easiest job on Policy’s calendar. You show up, say “we believe in Brian Gutekunst and Matt LaFleur,” tell everyone you’re trying to win a championship, promise to never sell the naming rights to Lambeau Field or move the team (neither of which was ever going to happen, anyway), and then go home. The real job of presidenting (presiding? being the president?) is everything that happens when Policy isn’t talking to the public. It’s one thing to have happy talk about the future of the team and what comes next for the Packers. It’s another thing to actually ensure the future is bright, and we won’t know for months or years what Policy is actually doing on that front. full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - JUNE 11: Daniel Jones #17 and Anthony Richardson Sr. #5 of the Indianapolis Colts participate in minicamp at Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center on June 11, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images On training camp eve, Indianapolis Colts general manager Chris Ballard indicated that the club currently intends to keep all three quarterbacks: Daniel Jones, Anthony Richardson, and Riley Leonard. While Richardson’s earlier offseason trade request still stands, the Colts have appreciated the ongoing positional competition between Leonard and him behind Jones, with Richardson consistently being a high quality teammate—and don’t plan to ‘give him away’ by any means (via WISH-TV): #Colts general manager Chris Ballard said the intention is to keep all three quarterbacks: Daniel Jones, Anthony Richardson, and Riley Leonard. Ballard on if Richardson's trade request is still on the table: "It is, but… we're not just giving him away." pic.twitter.com/KJNeDxTOx9 — WISH-TV News (@WISHNews8) July 28, 2026 Perhaps it’s purely trade posturing, but Ballard insinuated that he believes Richardson still has a bright future in this league—although he stopped short of saying it will continue to be with the Colts. It’s worth noting that Richardson is in the last year of his Colts rookie contract, and Indy would save $5.385M if traded this season. With Jones limited, the Colts had been splitting offseason reps between Richardson and Leonard with the first-team offense. It’ll be interesting to see who primarily receives the backup quarterback reps behind Jones now or whether it’ll continue to be a split throughout training camp and preseason until the QB2 victor emerges. At any rate, it seems as though if the Colts get meaningful trade return value for Richardson, they may move him. Otherwise, given that Jones is coming off a torn Achilles and has had some durability concerns throughout his career—dating even back to his New York Giants days, it may be more prudent to keep him around for additional quarterback depth, with Leonard only having one career start to his name.

full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - JUNE 11: Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce (14) watches a drill during the Indianapolis Colts Minicamp on June 11, 2026 at the Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images According to their longtime general manager Chris Ballard, Indianapolis Colts starting wide receiver Alec Pierce, who was recently placed on PUP, is ‘a week or so away’ from returning (via Fox59/CBS4’s Mike Chappell): Alec Pierce. Week or so away with ankle rehab. https://t.co/0lEVU4BU2O — Mike Chappell (@mchappell51) July 28, 2026 The lucratively re-signed lead wideout underwent minor cleanup surgery on his injured ankle earlier this offseason, and the expectation was that he’d be back some time during the back half of Colts training camp. Colts training camp officially kicks off tomorrow and concludes on Thursday, August 20th, so that would put him right in line with that updated recovery timeline—which is encouraging news. That being said, the Colts may initially take it a bit easy initially on Pierce during his eventual training camp return, gradually ramping him up and seeing how his surgically cleaned up ankle responds. The Colts reached a contract extension with Pierce on a once historic 4-year, $116 million deal right when free agency formally kicked off in early March. He’s coming off a breakout career year in which he recorded 47 receptions for 1,003 total receiving yards and 6 touchdown receptions during 15 games (14 starts). His 21.3 yards per reception average led the league for a consecutive year among qualifying wideouts. His return will obviously be a big one for the Colts receiving corps as their lead wideout and one of the offense’s best playmakers collectively.

title: Colts are taking major gambles heading into the season (part 2)
summary: Daniel Jones will be back on the field for the Indianapolis Colts sooner than expected. The highly anticipated news came down that Jones will be a full participant in training camp. Fans can rejoice. That is a big piece of the puzzle, but the Colts are still risking their entire season. Jones needs someone to […]
full_text: Jun 10, 2026; Indianapolis, IN, USA; Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Ashton Dulin (16), Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Coleman Owen (9) and Indianapolis Colts safety Daniel Scott (32) participates in a drill during minicamp at Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center. Mandatory Credit: Robert Goddin-Imagn Images | Robert Goddin-Imagn Images Daniel Jones will be back on the field for the Indianapolis Colts sooner than expected. The highly anticipated news came down that Jones will be a full participant in training camp. Fans can rejoice. That is a big piece of the puzzle, but the Colts are still risking their entire season. Jones needs someone to throw it to, and currently, the options are sparse. Alec Pierce is starting camp on the PUP list, which isn’t a surprise. Just because no one was caught off guard, it doesn’t mean it isn’t something to stir slight concern, though. Heck, even if he was full go from the start, are you ranking this receiving corps as one of the tops in the league? I know we all bleed blue here, but if you think that, you might have lost a little too much blue blood because you aren’t thinking straight. I’ll take Pierce on my team for sure, but stacked against Justin Jefferson or Ja’Marr Chase, he falls short. Worse yet is the drop-off behind him. Josh Downs will still do his thing, but that number two on the outside is missing. Ashton Dulin is slated for that role currently. If the Colts don’t nab a veteran soon, it will be sink or swim, and I am not prepared to see a ton of swimming. There continues to be a lot of smoke around Keenan Allen and even some mentions of Deebo Samuel. Neither of those men will save the day, but that is the current reality. It’s best to pile on as many sandbags as possible, even if it won’t keep all the water out. The Colts must bring in a veteran wideout who can be a threat to soften the opposing defense. There are weapons on offense, but more is needed. Peyton Manning and Philip Rivers thrived because they could get the ball out immediately. Their running backs and receivers made quick work of things to give them a target. If Daniel Jones has to sit back in the pocket, waiting for separation, he is exposed to another injury. Alec Pierce should be back for the regular season. Then again, he might not be. Regardless, he can’t do it alone. If the Colts fail to bring in another established receiver, they are facing a gamble they might not recover from.
