title: Colts futures watch: Which player bets are worth considering?
summary: Odds courtesy of FanDuel, please gamble responsibly After looking at the Colts’ team futures, the player markets are a little more interesting. The team lines are mostly priced around Indianapolis being what it has been for years: average, competitive, but not fully trustworthy. The player markets give a little more room to find value, especially […]
full_text: Odds courtesy of FanDuel , please gamble responsibly After looking at the Colts’ team futures, the player markets are a little more interesting. The team lines are mostly priced around Indianapolis being what it has been for years: average, competitive, but not fully trustworthy. The player markets give a little more room to find value, especially if you believe the Colts’ offense can take a step forward and some of their young players are ready for bigger roles. The four futures worth looking at are Jonathan Taylor over 1,225.5 rushing yards , Tyler Warren over 750.5 receiving yards , CJ Allen for Defensive Rookie of the Year at +1800 , and Daniel Jones for Comeback Player of the Year at +1700 . There is some logic behind all four, but the value is not equal. Jonathan Taylor over 1,225.5 rushing yards: -110 This number looks tempting at first because Taylor rushed for more than 1,500 yards last season, but it is not quite that simple. The Colts have already talked about wanting to lighten his workload Taylor is still the centerpiece of the offense, but Indianapolis has every reason to be careful with him early in the season and against weaker opponents. They need him fresh for the biggest games, not overloaded in September. There is also the durability factor. Last season was only the second time in Taylor’s career that he played all 17 games, so this line appears to already account for some missed time or reduced usage. If Taylor plays 17 games again and remains the clear lead back, he can fly over this number. If he misses even one or two games, or if the Colts are serious about shaving down his touches, the path gets much tighter. The line is well priced. I actually lean slightly under, not because Taylor is declining, but because the number assumes a lot has to go right from a workload and health standpoint. There is not enough value either way. Verdict: Slight lean under, but no strong play. Tyler Warren over 750.5 receiving yards: -110 This is my favorite player future on the board. Warren cleared 800 receiving yards last season and should be even more involved in the offense now, especially with Michael Pittman Jr. gone. The Colts need reliable targets, and Warren has the kind of skill set that should make him a major part of the passing game regardless of who is playing quarterback. That is what makes this over appealing. It is not just about Warren being talented, but rather it’s about role, opportunity and offensive need. He can work the middle of the field, create mismatches, help on third down, and become the kind of security blanket quarterbacks lean on over a full season. Even if Daniel Jones misses time, Warren should still have enough volume to push for this number. There is also a realistic ceiling beyond the line. This is not just a bet on Warren barely getting to 760 yards. He has a legitimate chance to push toward 1,000 if the passing game is functional and the Colts build the offense around their best young weapon. At -110, this is the cleanest value. Verdict: Best bet. Over 750.5 receiving yards is worth playing. CJ Allen Defensive Rookie of the Year: +1800 If you want a longshot, this is the one. Allen should play right away, and he should play a lot. That is the first thing you need with any rookie award bet. Talent is important, but opportunity matters more. Allen enters a defense where he can immediately become one of the central pieces, and coming from Georgia should help make the transition more manageable. His path is not easy because Defensive Rookie of the Year often favors edge rushers, corners with interception production, or players who create splash plays. Off-ball linebackers need volume, tackles, impact moments and team relevance to stay in the conversation. Allen will need to be visible early, not just solid. Still, at nearly 20-1, the value is strong. He could be asked to do a lot right away, and if he becomes the immediate star of the Colts’ rookie class while helping stabilize the middle of the defense, the case can build quickly. This is not the safest bet, but it is a good longshot. Verdict: Worth a shot at +1800. Daniel Jones Comeback Player of the Year: +1700 On paper, this makes sense. Jones is coming off an Achilles injury, he is expected to start, and if the Colts make the playoffs with him playing well, the narrative is obvious. Former Giants quarterback revives his career in Indianapolis, stabilizes a franchise that has been searching for answers, and leads a playoff push. That is exactly the kind of story that can win this award. The issue is the competition. Patrick Mahomes being the favorite makes this much harder to like. If Mahomes plays most of the season and returns to his usual level, it is hard to imagine voters ignoring that narrative. Jones would likely need not just a solid season, but a very good one, plus a Colts playoff berth, plus enough national attention to overcome bigger-name candidates. At +1700, the number is not ridiculous, but I do not see enough value. Jones can be a worthwhile bet in team markets because competent quarterback play may be enough to lift the Colts. For an individual award, the bar is higher. Verdict: Makes sense logically, but I would avoid it. Final verdict The best Colts player future is Tyler Warren over 750.5 receiving yards . The role should be there, the talent is obvious, and the number feels very reachable with real upside beyond it. CJ Allen for Defensive Rookie of the Year at +1800 is the best longshot because he should play immediately and could become a major part of the defense fast. Jonathan Taylor’s rushing total is well priced, but the workload concerns make the over harder to trust. Daniel Jones for Comeback Player of the Year has a clean narrative, though the award race may be too difficult with bigger names in the mix. Best play: Tyler Warren over 750.5 receiving yards. Best longshot: CJ Allen Defensive Rookie of the Year at +1800.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Should the Jaguars Be in Play for Vita Vea?
summary: On the eve of Tampa Bay Buccaneers veterans reporting to training camp on Tuesday, one of the most dominant interior defensive linemen in the NFL made his situation very clear. Two-time Pro Bowl nose tackle Vita Vea formally requested a trade Monday after extension negotiations with the Buccaneers reached an impasse, with his agent Collin […]
full_text: On the eve of Tampa Bay Buccaneers veterans reporting to training camp on Tuesday, one of the most dominant interior defensive linemen in the NFL made his situation very clear. Two-time Pro Bowl nose tackle Vita Vea formally requested a trade Monday after extension negotiations with the Buccaneers reached an impasse, with his agent Collin Roberts confirming the move to multiple outlets. The 6-foot-4, 347-pound former first-round selection is entering the final year of the four-year, $71 million extension he signed in 2022, due a $17 million base salary in 2026 with none of it guaranteed. Despite the trade request, Vea, reportedly, intends to report when veterans are due in camp. A Pass Rush Fix? For fans closely following Jacksonville’s pass rush, the news is worth sitting with. The Jaguars ranked 27th in sacks in 2025, and while injuries to Travon Walker and Arik Armstead clearly accounted for a significant portion of that shortfall, the nose tackle position was a persistent problem that no amount of edge production could fully compensate for. Davon Hamilton, Jacksonville’s primary interior presence at the position, is a dominant presence in the run game. However, he generated just 11 quarterback pressures for the entire 2025 regular season. Vea, playing all 17 games for Tampa Bay, produced 51 pressures, a number that would have led every defensive tackle on the Jaguars’ roster, with Armstead’s 48 ranking second on the team. According to Pro Football Focus, Vea’s 77.0 pass rush grade ranked 12th among all interior defensive linemen in the league, including nose tackles and three-technique defensive tackles. Meanwhile, his overall defensive grade placed him 20th among 134 qualified players at the position. Even in run defense, his 62.5 PFF grade edges out Hamilton’s 61.1. Put plainly, acquiring Vea would represent a meaningful upgrade over what Jacksonville currently deploys at the position, addressing one of the most glaring structural weaknesses in Anthony Campanile’s defensive front in a single move. Teams I think should seriously be in on Vita Vea: – Bills (idk if they have the space though) – Chargers – Packers – Jags – Bears — JP Acosta (@acosta32_jp) July 27, 2026 A Cost Must Be Paid The cost, however, will be the conversation stopper for many. Most evaluators around the league have framed any Vea trade discussion as beginning in the range of a player and a second-round pick, with some suggesting a first-round selection is not entirely out of the question, depending on the market that develops. ESPN’s Benjamin Solak noted that Vea is one of only two players in the NFL to produce 50 or more pressures from the nose tackle position over the last three combined seasons, and the other player on that list was Dexter Lawrence, who was ultimately traded to the Cincinnati Bengals for the tenth overall pick in this year’s draft. Vea is likely a step below Lawrence’s trade value, but the range being discussed is somewhat similar, and it would require genuine organizational commitment for any team to engage seriously. I could see an eventual trade taking place anywhere from a player (Davon Hamilton), plus a 2027 third round pick being a reasonably fair offer. However, an eventual landing point on the draft compensation could be anywhere from a player plus a third to a first without a player from a competing team (IE: a projected late 2027 first). The Money Must Make Sense Jacksonville’s leverage in this conversation is an interesting one, also. Vea has, reportedly, preferred a move to a California market or to the Las Vegas Raiders following any trade, which would position him closer to his roots. While Florida is neither of those destinations, it does carry one significant financial advantage that no California team can offer: zero state income tax. On a salary of $17 million or more, the difference between playing in Florida and playing in California represents a meaningful real dollar figure that a general manager like James Gladstone is perfectly capable of putting in front of a player during negotiations. While Vea doesn’t have a no-trade clause in his contract, he would need to sign off on any extension, as he’s currently on the final year of his contract, making $17 million in 2026. Whether that pitch is compelling enough to move Vea’s preferred destination list is an open question, but it is a card Jacksonville holds that California franchises can’t match. And with Vea currently playing right down the road in Tampa, a short relocation, while remaining in sunny Florida could still be an appealing package. Similar Path to a Trade? The Jaguars have already shown a willingness to use preseason opponents as trade partners. In 2025, Jacksonville and New Orleans completed the Luke Fortner-for-Khalen Saunders swap shortly after the two teams met in the preseason. Being around another team’s coaches and front office gives both sides a unique opportunity to evaluate players, discuss roster needs, and naturally begin trade conversations. The circumstances with Vita Vea are somewhat similar on paper: Tampa Bay and Jacksonville are scheduled for a joint practice on Aug. 25 before their preseason, Week 3 finale on Aug. 28. Liam Coen has strong relationships within the Buccaneers organization from his time there, which could make communication easier if Tampa Bay becomes serious about moving Vea. If Vea’s reported trade request remains unresolved into training camp, the joint practices could become a logical point for discussions. If Vita is still available, don’t be surprised if those conversations happen behind the scenes. Whether a deal gets done is another story, but the setting has already proven to be fertile ground for James Gladstone and the Jaguars’ front office. Chances of a move materializing The realistic assessment is that this deal likely does not happen and that Tampa and Vita eventually come to terms. Live games and deadlines often have a way of curing prior disagreements, in matters of money. For Jacksonville, James Gladstone has clearly operated with a clear long-term capital strategy throughout his tenure. Surrendering meaningful draft assets for a 31-year-old nose tackle, entering a contract year, who would then require a significant extension to justify the trade runs somewhat counter to the organizational approach he has established. The Buccaneers are also under no obligation to move Vea at all and may ultimately determine that absorbing the tension is preferable to reshaping their defensive line ahead of what is a pivotal season for head coach Todd Bowles. But could it happen? A phone call costs nothing. And for a Jacksonville defense that generated just 11 nose tackle pressures all season while watching the pass rush struggle through injuries and depth issues, the gap between what Davon Hamilton provides and what Vita Vea provides is significant enough that Gladstone would be doing his job simply by picking up the phone and finding out the exact number it would take to keep one of the NFL’s best interior defenders in the state of Florida. What are your thoughts on a trade for Vita Vea, BigCatCountry? Too rich a cost for this 2026 Jaguars team? Or a worthwhile investment in shoring up one of Jacksonville’s primary 2025 defensive areas of opportunity? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

title: Chiefs Market Movers: Bulls and Bears at start of training camp
summary: Kansas City Chiefs training camp has arrived. It’s like waking up from a long summer nap, feeling optimistic about the upcoming season, and hoping not to hear any bad news that happened when you weren’t paying attention. Unfortunately, we just learned about the very serious situation at the Bieniemy household that will likely keep offensive […]
full_text: ST JOSEPH, MISSOURI - JULY 26: Peter Woods #99 walks toward the practice field during Kansas City Chiefs Training Camp at Missouri Western State University on July 25, 2026 in St Joseph, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs training camp has arrived. It’s like waking up from a long summer nap, feeling optimistic about the upcoming season, and hoping not to hear any bad news that happened when you weren’t paying attention. Unfortunately, we just learned about the very serious situation at the Bieniemy household that will likely keep offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy away from St. Joe for the foreseeable future. Our hearts go out to his family, and we can only hope for their healing. While the team forges ahead and training camp practices begin in earnest, it felt like a good time to identify some Chiefs who might be trending in one direction or another. It’s fair to say that this Chiefs roster should be better than the last, but also has more questions that need answered. The focus will be on the youth— the team seems to be counting on improvement in-house and a boost from the rookie class. Based on what we’ve heard so far, here are some potential trends to watch when you get to St. Joe. If you can’t make it (or even if you can), be sure to watch for updates from new AP “Chief,” Ron Kopp, Jr. Bulls Defensive Lineman Peter Woods: Our own Brandon Kiley wrote about the Chiefs’ plan to build a deeper, more productive defensive line. It’s a formula we’ve been talking about, and offseason reports seem to indicate they are on the right track. The strategy requires versatile young linemen with the ability to play all three downs, and enough depth that they don’t all have to. So far, Peter Woods is drawing rave reviews from the coaching staff for his football IQ and a little bit of bend. Given the relative weakness on the edge, Woods may have the opportunity to play inside and out, in the mold of Chris Jones. The second first-round pick this year is off to a great start, reporting to camp at a comfortable weight — heavier than last season at Clemson. The Chiefs’ offensive line: Maybe I’m reading too much into this, but given the Chiefs already have the league’s best interior offensive line, some recent news makes me bullish on the unit as a whole. First, Josh Simmons shows up all offseason looking lean and mean. Then, the Chiefs felt comfortable enough to trade Wanya Morris to the Atlanta Falcons — likely because of the development of Esa Pole, Kahlil Benson and maybe Chu Godrick too? Pay attention to the actions of the front office this offseason, not their words. The only real investments in the offense were to the coaching staff and run game. The team is leaning into the big uglies this year. There are only two real questions to answer in camp. 1. Who is the starter at right tackle? 2. Is there finally enough depth to make it through a full season? The other rookies— Cyrus Allen, Xavier Nwankpa, Jadon Canaday : Training camp starts with quarterbacks and rookies, and there were a few guys who seemed to get a head start on the camp competition. Allen might be competing for the No. 4 wide receiver job— but he’s already building chemistry with Mahomes and showing the types of skills that translate. Nwampka and Canaday have opportunities to impress on special teams and in a young defensive back room with uncertain depth. Running back Kenneth Walker III: There is now another Super Bowl MVP on the Chiefs roster, and he should be a massive part of the offense this season. Walker seems to be starting off on a good foot, with the respect of Mahomes and the coaching staff. We’ve long wondered what it would be like to see Mahomes play with a great running game; is this the year? Given the investment in Walker, and the lack of investment elsewhere on the offense— it had better be. Count me in for a 1,500 yd, 10-touchdown season for Kansas City’s new bellcow. Bears Cornerback Mansoor Delane, Tight end John Michael Gyllenborg and Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott: The Chiefs’ top 2026 draft pick and the first two players on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list; there’s some significant talent here waiting to get healthy. Delane and Norman-Lott are each critically important to Spagnolo’s defensive reboot. Each will be given every opportunity to ease into the preseason. But if either is expected to miss significant time when the games start counting, a roster move and a veteran replacement could be necessary. As for Gyllenborg, he’s a hometown kid with a real shot at making the roster in a thin position group, but his knee injury could cost him his rookie season. Training camp is the time to get healthy and to learn the playbook, so let’s hope that these guys can still do that. Defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah: If it’s ever going to happen, it has to be this preseason. He’s still young enough to turn his career around, but a breakout season feels very unlikely. Let’s hope for some excitement for FAU in St. Joe. Wide receivers Nikko Remigio and Jalen Royals: Yes, the wide receiver room should be wide open . There are questions about the health and decision-making of Rashee Rice. There are some (not me) who doubt Xavier Worthy will live up to his ability. There are also 13 guys competing for the jobs after Rice, Worthy and Tyquan Thornton. Among those are Remigio, a previous camp “darling” who became a productive return man, and Royals, who was once a promising draft pick, but never found a role in 2025. This year’s training camp wide receiver battle is likely to be all about a couple of rookies from Cincinnati that were built for St. Joe. Can Remigio or Royals create some buzz? Or will they fade into the hall of “what could have been had they been given more chances? “ Value (sleeper) pick Cornerback Kader Kohou: After missing the entire 2025 NFL season, many have forgotten about Kader Kohou. Prior to the injury, he was an impressive slot corner with physicality, the ability to blitz, and a nose for the football. He’ll have real competition for the job with the Chiefs from Chris Roland-Wallace and the aforementioned Canaday. But we shouldn’t be shocked if Kohou slides in as the starter and doesn’t give the job back anytime soon.
author: Matt Stagner

title: Chiefs’ rookie E.J. Smith has different path to NFL than his father did
summary: Kansas City Chiefs’ rookie running back E.J. Smith had imagined the moment before. But when he finally came down the hill at Missouri Western State University and onto the Chiefs’ training camp practice fields, the journey required to get there made the moment mean something more. “It was a dream come true,” Smith said Monday […]
full_text: ST JOSEPH, MISSOURI - JULY 25: Running back EJ Smith #35 walks toward the practice field during Kansas City Chiefs Training Camp at Missouri Western State University on July 25, 2026 in St Joseph, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs’ rookie running back E.J. Smith had imagined the moment before. But when he finally came down the hill at Missouri Western State University and onto the Chiefs’ training camp practice fields, the journey required to get there made the moment mean something more. “It was a dream come true,” Smith said Monday following practice. “It was a long road to get here, but I’m very grateful for the opportunity. Just through all the obstacles that made me become the person who I am today in order to prepare me for this opportunity.” Smith knows better than most what an uncomplicated path to the NFL can look like. His father, Emmitt Smith, starred at Florida, where he rushed for more than 1,300 yards as a freshman and went on to a dominant three-year college career totaling 3,928 rushing yards. He earned All-American honors and SEC Player of the Year before the Dallas Cowboys selected him with the 17th overall pick of the 1990 NFL Draft. The rest became NFL history: three Super Bowl championships, a league MVP award, eight Pro Bowls, the NFL’s all-time rushing record and eventually a gold jacket in Canton. E.J.’s road to an NFL training camp looked nothing like it. “Y’all know who my dad is,” Smith said. “He was a first-rounder. I’m an undrafted guy, so my path is already different from his.” E.J. grew up with one of the most recognizable surnames a running back could carry. His father didn’t simply play the same position — he became the standard by which generations of running backs have been measured. But Emmitt’s message to his son wasn’t to follow him. It was to find his own way. “Just as a kid, my dad always told me, you know, build my own legacy,” E.J. recalled. “It’s my life, and so making the best out of it.” That philosophy would become increasingly important as E.J.’s football career unfolded. His college journey stretched across six seasons, beginning at Stanford before finishing at Texas A&M. Instead of the steady climb toward the NFL that his father experienced, E.J.’s career repeatedly stopped and restarted. Smith said Monday that he endured approximately four injuries during his college career. One of the most significant came at Stanford in 2022, just as it appeared he was beginning to emerge. Smith opened the season with a career-high 118 rushing yards against Colgate and had 206 rushing yards and three touchdowns through Stanford’s first two games. Then his season was over. Rather than view those setbacks as something that derailed his path, Smith now sees them as part of what made reaching Kansas City possible. “I wouldn’t say it changed it,” Smith said when asked how the injuries affected his NFL journey. “I feel like it molded the person who I am today. “I went through about four injuries throughout my whole college career. And so it just made me show more perseverance, made me more resilient, and it prepared me for this moment, for this opportunity.” That opportunity was never guaranteed. Smith finished his college career at Texas A&M without the résumé that once made his father a first-round selection. When the 2026 NFL Draft ended, Smith’s name had not been called. His father’s NFL journey began with the Cowboys trading into the first round to select him. His began with a phone call after the draft. On the other end was a familiar voice. Chiefs running backs coach DeMarco Murray had recruited Smith coming out of high school. Years later, Murray was offering him an opportunity to continue his career in Kansas City. “Coach DeMarco called me right after the draft,” Smith recalled. “It was awesome to hear him. He recruited me out of high school, and so just hearing his voice, talking to him, knowing that he’s going to be my running back coach, I was really excited for the opportunity.” The Chiefs officially list Smith as an undrafted rookie entering his first NFL season. That designation might represent another stark contrast with his father’s journey, but it also places E.J. exactly where his father’s advice prepared him to be: building something of his own. For Smith, making an NFL roster now requires embracing more than carrying the football. As an undrafted rookie, every practice rep matters. So does every special-teams assignment, block and opportunity to demonstrate that he can contribute somewhere. Smith believes versatility and effort can separate him. “They love hard workers here,” he said. “Guys that grind, hustle every play, show great effort. And so I believe that I’m that guy. Wherever they need me to be utilized, I’m there and I’m ready for it.” “A lot of people didn’t think I would be here today,” Smith continued. “Just through the amount of injuries I went through in college and everything of that nature. And so just being out here, being able to practice with these guys and getting better every day, it’s a blessing for sure.” E.J. Smith isn’t trying to recreate his father’s road. He couldn’t if he wanted to. One arrived as a first-round pick with expectations of becoming a franchise running back. The other arrived undrafted, fighting for every rep and searching for any role that could keep his NFL opportunity alive. Two running backs. One family. Two very different roads to the NFL. And after everything it took E.J. Smith to reach the bottom of that hill in St. Joe, he’s finally getting the chance to build the legacy his father always told him should be his own.
author: Maurice Elston

title: Chiefs Mailbag: Answering position questions ahead of training camp
summary: Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions. The team’s quarterbacks, rookies and select veterans have already arrived at training camp at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph and have multiple practices under their belt. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 2: Jaylon Moore #77 of the Kansas City Chiefs blocks during an NFL football game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on November 2, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions. The team’s quarterbacks, rookies and select veterans have already arrived at training camp at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph and have multiple practices under their belt. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds ahead of full squad workouts beginning on Wednesday. Andyreidsmustache_ asks: Although there’s supposedly no battle for right tackle, just how much of an eye is there from the coaching perspective is being placed in it? I get the sense it’s more open than we’re being lead to believe, and for an all-world QB coming off a major surgery, it’s even more important that the entire line is as tight as possible. Truthfully, we know very little about the team’s feelings at right tackle — the only offensive line position without a clear starter. Because the position went unaddressed both in the draft and free agency, we can infer that the team believes the solution is in-house. Veteran Jaylon Moore and second-year man Esa Pole were floated throughout the offseason as the main options for the job. I suspect the Chiefs will begin full-squad workouts on Wednesday with the decision roughly made in the coaches’ minds. It would actually be somewhat unlike head coach Andy Reid and offensive line coach Andy Heck to have a true competition still unfolding at such an important position. If Moore and Pole are splitting first-team work in camp, that really shouldn’t inspire confidence. If we see reports that the Chiefs are bringing in a free agent for competition, that will also speak loudly. My guess is that Moore will get most of the first team reps with Pole sprinkling into both tackle spots for a swing role. TheSovereign1587 asks: Mahomes, Mahomes, Mahomes. Is quarterback Patrick Mahomes truly cleared for full activity? Can he physically handle that? Will he avoid the almost obvious move of putting him on the Physically-Unable-to-Perform (PUP) list to miss the first 4 weeks going into the early bye and play week 6? The PUP list is no longer an option because Mahomes has taken part in practices. Part of why you see most players with any lingering injury worse than a hangnail placed on PUP is that teams want the protection against an unexpected setback in injury recovery. Avoiding the PUP list does not guarantee Mahomes will play in Week 1, but it would be a significant upset if he does not. All indications are the Chiefs have been cautious with his rehab and gone through the proper channels to clear him for practice. Perhaps there will be some unexpected rest days at camp (likely stacked with already scheduled off days). His preseason action will probably be minimal, if it happens at all. Gameplans may keep him in the pocket much more than we are used to. It is unrealistic to expect to have everything we are accustomed to, especially early in the season. But whatever he can or cannot do at this point appears set to be worked out on the field — and not the training room. RoyalsFanBill asks: Who is going to be the blocking TE? I’m still worried about the tight end room in general. Reid also did not sound optimistic on the status of undrafted rookie John Michael Gyllenborg — who was placed on the PUP list to start camp. Offseason reports from beat writers about the in-house options were not encouraging, but the Chiefs seem intent on letting things play out in camp. One player to watch seems to be second-year man Trey Watson — who split his college days between Fresno State and Texas A&M. Watson has been the only tight end working in the rookie portion of camp, and he has reportedly gotten in a lot of work ahead of the veterans reporting. Want to give a shout out to Tight Tre Watson. Only TE to participate in the rookie ramp up period, has run A LOT of reps. pic.twitter.com/vElFtq2nhK — Harold R. Kuntz (@HaroldRKuntz3) July 26, 2026 There’s also a legitimate chance the Chiefs’ best blocking tight end in 2026 isn’t on the roster yet. If the Chiefs were wanting to add an option as a pass catcher, I think they would have done that by now. However, general manager Brett Veach is always on the lookout near cut-down day for players who may be available from other teams’ rosters. It won’t be surprising if he looks for a blocking option late in camp. The team will also have its earliest waivers priority in a generation to start the season, meaning it could take several more days than we are accustomed to for the effective “final” roster to be known. california chief asks: Who is replacing linebacker Leo Chenel..?? Chenal appears to have made a difficult free agency decision for the Chiefs by offering exceptional value in a limited role. Kansas City appears to have decided that they are simply not going to find a player with his unique fit. Nominally, second-year man Cooper McDonald is expected to take over Chenal’s role in the base defense. McDonald saw extended action on defense in the Chiefs’ final two games last season after Chenal had been lost to injury. Quietly, the team appeared to have moved another second-year player, Ethan Downs, from defensive end to linebacker. Presumably, the idea was to see if he could offer some of Chenal’s versatility. Downs left the first practice of the early portion of training camp on Saturday with an apparent injury, and Matt Derrick of Chiefs Digest has since reported that he tore his ACL . The Chiefs toyed with deploying Chenal more as a designated pass rusher in previous camps. If the Chiefs want the most out of second-round pick R Mason Thomas, he will need to at least get some work as a standing pass rush linebacker. Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! We will be back to our weekly schedule ahead of the Chiefs’ preseason opener against the Los Angeles Rams on August 15. Keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.
author: Jared Sapp

title: Can Chiefs safety Jaden Hicks take a step forward in 2026?
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs will kick off training camp this week, and with it a new season! Chiefs’ safety Jaden Hicks will enter his third camp with Kansas City, playing under the radar of the coaching staff so far in his career. Through his first three seasons, Hicks has been a role player, often used […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - OCTOBER 27: Jaden Hicks #21 of the Kansas City Chiefs defends in coverage during an NFL football game against the Washington Commanders at Arrowhead Stadium on October 27, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs will kick off training camp this week, and with it a new season! Chiefs’ safety Jaden Hicks will enter his third camp with Kansas City, playing under the radar of the coaching staff so far in his career. Through his first three seasons, Hicks has been a role player, often used in Nickel situations and as a box safety against teams using heavier personnel. He has shown flashes, but so far they have been inconsistent. Hicks will likely start camp in competition with Chammari Conner for the Chiefs’ starting strong safety, but he should look to see his role grow, especially with his versatility and how much defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo tends to line up his safeties all across the field. Hicks has the skill set to be a tremendous “big Nickel” and should be a playmaker for the Chiefs’ defense in 2026. A look at the film Playing as a traditional strong safety, Hicks is at his best when he can get rolling downhill quickly and make a play on the ball. With good size and length, he has the physicality needed to compete with tight ends and contest catches when the ball is thrown in his direction. Good play recognition and break on the ball by Hicks to break up the intended pass. Dissects the pattern and times it perfectly. pic.twitter.com/Elw1tUL9eQ — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) July 23, 2026 On the snap, Hicks quickly reads the out route from the tight end and bursts toward the flat. As the tight end prepares to catch the pass, Hicks makes a great play to knock his hands down, runs through contact, and forces an incomplete pass. Hicks is at his best when defending the flats and other areas around the line of scrimmage. Hicks plays his best when he can make a quick decision and get rolling downhill. pic.twitter.com/vPzl5KUJf7 — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) July 23, 2026 Playing from a deep position, Hicks does a great job of reading the tight end’s quick route to the flat and times his route perfectly. The tight end makes the catch, but Hicks makes a perfect form tackle and drops him behind the sticks. Hicks is a natural downhill thumper, and this helps him against plays designed to go to the flats, but he shows this skill set best when he can line up in the box and make plays on ball carriers. The motion pulls Hicks away from the run, but he recovers and gets downhill quickly to keep Lawrence out of the end zone. pic.twitter.com/5v8pQrGs4D — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) July 23, 2026 On the goal line, Hicks is lined up in the box, and a pre-snap motion moves him with the play. The quarterback shows the ball to the motion player, but quickly pulls it. Hicks is initially out of position due to the motion, but he quickly recovers and takes aim at the quarterback. With a good angle, he delivers a big hit as the quarterback attempts to go for the pile on. The hit is enough to keep him short of the end zone and displays Hicks’ natural ability to play in the box. In Spagnuolo’s defense, Hicks will always have a role as the box safety or big Nickel, but if he can continue to improve, he should see more consistent snaps as a true strong safety. Where to improve While Hicks is a good man-to-man defender and a good downhill safety, he still has room to improve in zone coverage and when defending passes downfield. A larger defensive back, Hicks can struggle at times with lateral quickness and the ability to recover downfield. Hicks drifts a bit too far inside, and this gives the TE all the separation he needs to work his route back to the inside. pic.twitter.com/GOzNyF2kUC — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) July 23, 2026 Hicks is playing shallow in a hybrid box look on the snap. Recognizing a pass, he keys in on the tight end and begins to drop into coverage. The tight end initially heads outside, but quickly plants his foot and breaks to the inside. Hicks is caught off guard by the quick break, and transitions too slowly to catch up to the tight end. The quarterback throws a good ball, and it is a decent pickup for the offense. Hicks’ lack of quickness when transitioning in coverage has limited him, and his overall lack of chase-down speed does limit him in pass coverage, which has so far in his career kept him plugged in as the team’s box safety on regular downs. Hicks could be close to breaking through as the team’s full-time starting strong safety, but during training camp and preseason, he must hone his downfield coverage skills and show improvement in route recognition. The bottom line While his physical traits help him to play well in the flats and around the line of scrimmage, they also hurt Hicks’ game when he is asked to cover against long patterns downfield or play tight man coverage. Hicks will be 24 by the time the 2026 season kicks off, and in Year 3, he is no longer a spring chicken by NFL standards. He is still at an age where adding athleticism is possible, but for Hicks to progress in his career, the key will be to hone his fundamentals and continue to put himself in good spots against the downfield passing game. The Chiefs need a good season from Hicks, and a good season would help him solidify himself as the team’s everyday starting safety.
author: Caleb James

title: Andrew Armstrong working to factor into the Chiefs’ receiving corps
summary: Before the NFL season kicks off, we will see the annual training camp and preseason slate. This is the time when every fan base has at least one previously unknown player who suddenly finds himself a local celebrity. One Kansas City Chiefs player who may win the hearts of the fans over the next few […]
full_text: ST JOSEPH, MISSOURI - JULY 25: Andrew Armstrong #85 walks toward the practice field during Kansas City Chiefs Training Camp at Missouri Western State University on July 25, 2026 in St Joseph, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Before the NFL season kicks off, we will see the annual training camp and preseason slate. This is the time when every fan base has at least one previously unknown player who suddenly finds himself a local celebrity. One Kansas City Chiefs player who may win the hearts of the fans over the next few weeks at Missouri Western State University in St. Joe is wide receiver Andrew Armstrong. Standing 6 feet 4 inches tall, Armstrong has taken a long road to keeping his NFL dreams alive. As a no-star recruit in 2019 out of Bishop Dunne Catholic School in Dallas, Texas, Armstrong committed to nearby Texas A&M – Commerce (now East Texas A&M). However, he did not get on the field his first season at the Championship Subdivision and redshirted. He would have to wait an extra year to get onto the field, as the program’s 2020 season was canceled completely due to the COVID pandemic. After easing into action in 2021, Armstrong broke out in 2022 with 62 catches for 1,020 yards and 13 touchdowns. That season earned him a transfer to Arkansas. In two seasons as a Razorback, Armstrong totaled 134 catches for 1,904 yards while finding the end zone six times. Armstrong was not selected in the 2025 draft, and he failed to make the Miami Dolphins roster (or even practice squad) after catching on as an undrafted free agent. After a short stint on the Detroit Lions ’ practice squad, Armstrong signed a Reserve/Future contract with Kansas City during the first week of January. Speaking at the conclusion of the rookie portion of Chiefs’ training camp, Armstrong detailed his journey through the 2025 season. “I started undrafted,” he recalled. “I ended up going to Miami. It didn’t work as much there. I ended up getting cut. After I got cut, I was off a team for literally 15 weeks… Just working out. A lot of people ask me if I was working out. I know the type of player I am. I know that type of area that I want to get to in life and on the field as well.” “I had a workout with the Chiefs. I got signed in January, and then I’m here now. I’m ready to show what I can do.” Though Armstrong is a Texas native, he has strong family ties to Kansas City. He also appreciates the environment head coach Andy Reid and wide receivers coach Chad O’Shea foster. “It’s been great,” Armstrong remarked. “My dad lives in Kansas City, Missouri. My brothers, my aunts, my cousins — everybody is from here. Just coming back to here has been amazing. Coach Reid, teammates, the receiver room, Coach O’Shea — it’s just been great all around.” When beat reporters have been around the team, O’Shea has been noticed working with Armstrong more deliberately than many players on reserve/future contract players often see. The wideout knows the value of the coach’s attention. Andrew Armstrong talks about Chiefs New WR Coach Chad O’Shea and his coaching style 🎙️ “I love Coach O’Shea. [He’s] the type of Coach that is going to be really hard on me, and that’s the type of coach I love to play for.” 🔥 🎥 | Chiefs on YT pic.twitter.com/MFsai0ifjE — Daily Chiefs (@Daily_Chiefs_) July 27, 2026 “I love Coach O’Shea,” said Armstrong. “He’s going to be hard on me. That’s the type of coach I love to play for. A coach that’s really going to get on you, really going to tell you what you need to do [and] the small details — that’s exactly what O’Shea does. When I get that coaching from him, I love it. That’s the type of way I want to get coached.” The Chiefs face questions about the wide receiver depth chart. Armstrong, however, values the environment he has found in Kansas City more than seeing the team as a more direct path to catch on the roster. “It wasn’t too much of knowing the best way to earn a roster spot,” he explained. “It’s just coming in to work and knowing that nothing is given to anybody. I knew I was going to have to come in here and do the best that I can, be the best type of player I can on and off the field. In the training room, inside of the locker room, [they’re] great teammates. It’s just little things like that that help me come in here and fight for a spot.” A pair of extra practices to work directly with quarterback Patrick Mahomes before the full squad reports to St. Joe this week has also been valuable. “It’s been great,” Armstrong noted of catching from the face of football. “Just working in the summer, before the summer in OTAs and things like that, it was great just catching the ball from him…Being here and being able to catch with him and earn that chemistry with him, it’s been great. It’s been fun.” As a soon-to-be 26-year-old yet to play a regular-season NFL snap, Armstrong faces long odds to make the roster. He wants to prove to his coaches how hard he will work for any opportunity. “Whatever I can do to help the team,” he stated of his ambitions. “Wherever it is. If it’s on offense, special teams, if they need a safety. Wherever they need to put me, I’m just here to work and be the best player that I can be.”
author: Jared Sapp

title: 48 Days, 48 tackles by George Karlaftis for the Chiefs last season
summary: We are 48 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 48 jersey will be worn by linebacker Cole Christiansen in Chiefs training camp, and he has worn it since he joined Kansas City before the 2022 season. The uniform has […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 21: (NEW YORK DAILIES OUT) Russell Wilson #3 of the New York Giants in action against George Karlaftis #56 of the Kansas City Chiefs at MetLife Stadium on September 21, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The Chiefs defeated the Giants 22-9. (Photo by Jim McIsaac/Getty Images) | Getty Images We are 48 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 48 jersey will be worn by linebacker Cole Christiansen in Chiefs training camp, and he has worn it since he joined Kansas City before the 2022 season. The uniform has an underrated group of all-time Chiefs to have worn it: The memorable No. 48s in franchise history Todd McNair (1989 – 1993, 1996) Duane Wood (1960 – 1964) Nate Allen (1971 – 1974) James Hadnot (1980 – 1983) After the Chiefs drafted McNair in the eighth round of the 1989 draft, he carved out a receiving-first role out of the backfield when the Chiefs ran the West Coast offense. Over six years with the Chiefs, McNair caught 186 passes , gained 1,856 yards and caught six touchdowns while rushing just 128 times for 667 yards and another three scores. In a late-season, 24-21 win over the San Diego Chargers in 1990, McNair gained a career-high 111 receiving yards on three catches, one gaining 65 yards and another being a 40-yard touchdown catch late in the first half. 48: The number of combined tackles by George Karlaftis last season The leading tackler among the Chiefs’ defensive linemen in 2025 was Karlaftis, who finished (48) with the 11th-most combined tackles among all NFL defensive ends, according to Pro Football Reference . It speaks to how active Karlaftis is on all downs, even as he played through a broken hand for a portion of last year. His 23 quarterback hits, which ranked 18th among all NFL defenders, are also a strong indicator of how consistently Karlaftis makes his presence felt. Kansas City just needs those hits to result in more sacks in 2026, which could be aided by effective pass rush from teammates like Chris Jones and rookie R Mason Thomas.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Chiefs News: Rookie running back has standout pass-catching routine
summary: The latest There’s one thing Kansas City Chiefs fans can feel certain about the 2026 offense: running back Kenneth Walker will be a large, pivotal factor in its success. That said, there’s a lot to learn about the backs behind him on the depth chart. Veteran running back Emari Demercado projects to fill the third-down […]
full_text: ST JOSEPH, MISSOURI - JULY 26: Emmett Johnson #10 participates during Kansas City Chiefs Training Camp at Missouri Western State University on July 25, 2026 in St Joseph, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest There’s one thing Kansas City Chiefs fans can feel certain about the 2026 offense: running back Kenneth Walker will be a large, pivotal factor in its success. That said, there’s a lot to learn about the backs behind him on the depth chart. Veteran running back Emari Demercado projects to fill the third-down back role, but could rookie running back Emmett Johnson challenge him for those pass-down snaps? Emmett Johnson’s pass-catching prowess and 6 things that stood out in Kansas City Chiefs’ head start to 2026 training camp | A to Z Sports That third area stood out the most. Johnson has proven to be a natural catcher of the football. It’s through hard work, as he was seen on the JUGS machine before and after practice. He told reporters he gets 200 catches in per day, and prides himself on catching the ball well. He sees it as his path to contribute quickest in the NFL. All-Under-25 team: Drake Maye, Abdul Carter among NFL’s ascending young players entering 2026 season | NFL.com Pos. OT J. Simmons KC | Age 23 He was remarkably solid in his first few games as a pro, seemingly answering Kansas City’s persistent question at left tackle. But after Simmons missed four games because of a “family matter,” a wrist injury ultimately ended his rookie season after just eight contests. The health issues will remain a concern, especially when considering the patellar tendon injury that tanked his draft stock, but if Simmons stays active, he’ll own a place on this team at this time next year, too — and the Chiefs will be glad they took a risk on him with the 32nd pick two Aprils ago. Joe Bleymaier to help lead Chiefs offense while Eric Bieniemy is away | KMBC 9 During Bieniemy’s absence, pass game coordinator Joe Bleymaier will help oversee the offense, and offensive line coach Andy Heck will continue to lead the run game. “So, we’ll be able to keep it moving here. But the most important thing is that EB has an opportunity to spend some time there and take care of that business,” Reid said. Bleymaier has been with the Chiefs since 2016, beginning as an offensive quality control coach. He later served as pass game analyst and assistant quarterbacks coach from 2018 to 2020, and as wide receivers coach from 2021 to 2022. The 1 UDFA with Best Chance to Make the Roster in Every NFL Team’s Training Camp | Bleacher Report Kansas City Chiefs: S Xavier Nwankpa “Nwankpa is routinely in the right place,” Harms said. “As such, he can wear a multitude of hats for a defense. He excels as a box safety, reading out plays and triggering downhill to make big hits. The defensive back reads the quarterbacks eyes and locates the football at a high level, adding to his impact as a read-and-react defender, particularly in the run game. He’s a well-equipped tackler and understands leverage.” The Kansas City Chiefs have two more Bearcat pass catchers that are turning eyes | FanSided Chiefs digest writer Matt Derrick has been at almost every Chiefs practice and camp available to the media and has noted that “He’s looked the same in every practice. I have not seen him have a bad practice yet.” Derrick also said that he had a few catches from Mahomes in a 7-on-7 period and that he continues to be impressed with him. There haven’t been much camp news surrounding Jeff Caldwell, but his NFL Combine athleticism score of 99 keeps fans excited for what is it come of the 6-foot-5 receiver. Around the NFL Two-time Pro Bowl DT Vita Vea requests trade from Buccaneers | ESPN Vea was a hold-in at the team’s mandatory minicamp last month because of his contract situation. Coach Todd Bowles said he wasn’t concerned at that time, calling it “part of the business.” Vea, 31, is entering the final year of a four-year, $71 million contract. He is set to earn $17 million this season, but none of it is guaranteed. He also is set to earn a per-game roster bonus that is capped at $1 million total. Commanders fire TE coach Ben Steele following DWI arrest in Virginia | Yahoo! Sports In the announcement, the Commanders said they would share no further information. But The Athletic’s Nicki Jhabvala reported that Steele was arrested on suspicion of driving while intoxicated on June 7 in Loudoun County, Virginia. Additionally, Steele was charged with obstruction/resisting an officer without force for refusing to take a blood/breath test on the scene, according to court records (via ESPN’s John Keim). Jamal Adams joins the Vikings | Pro Football Talk Adams spent three years with the Jets, making it to two Pro Bowls and finishing 2018 as a second-team All-Pro and 2019 as a first-team All-Pro. He was traded to the Seahawks in 2020, qualifying for a third Pro Bowl and finishing on the All-Pro second team. The next year, he signed a four-year, $70 million extension that made him the highest-paid safety in NFL history. He stayed with the Seahawks through 2023. In 2024, he played for the Titans and Lions. After switching last year from safety to linebacker, Adams appeared in 17 games with four starts for the Raiders. ‘Madden NFL 27’ 99 Club Revealed: Josh Allen, Matthew Stafford, Myles Garrett Headline 6-player class | NFL.com The cover athlete for Madden NFL 24 , Allen returns for his second straight 99 Club appearance following a debut in the group in last year’s title. Allen finished third in MVP voting last season after posting 3,668 passing yards and 25 touchdowns along with 579 yards and 14 more TDs on the ground. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride 10 Biggest Chiefs Questions: Can Mahomes play with fewer scrambles? Mahomes has long helped this issue with his legs. If that’s off the table, how will the Chiefs be able to compensate for that? The offense will need receivers to step up in these situations to help Mahomes out. I’m skeptical. The Chiefs will likely struggle to move the chains on third-and-long if Mahomes has to stay within the pocket, but having a stronger run game can mitigate how many of those situations you’re put in. title: Could Beaux Limmer make a return to the starting lineup?
summary: One training camp battle for the Los Angeles Rams that is under the radar is at center. Could Beaux Limmer potentially unseat Coleman Shelton in the starting lineup? Rookies rarely crack the rotation under Sean McVay. Limmer started 16 games in his first year including two playoff contests. He did not make a single start […]
full_text: WOODLAND HILLS, CALIFORNIA - JUNE 3: Beaux Limmer #50 of the Los Angeles Rams walks off the field during an OTA offseason workout on June 3, 2025 in Woodland Hills, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images One training camp battle for the Los Angeles Rams that is under the radar is at center. Could Beaux Limmer potentially unseat Coleman Shelton in the starting lineup? Rookies rarely crack the rotation under Sean McVay. Limmer started 16 games in his first year including two playoff contests. He did not make a single start during his sophomore campaign. That’s because the Rams watched the 2024 season end at the hands of Limmer in a missed blocking assignment that allowed Jalen Carter to wreck a red zone possession in the NFC divisional round. LA responded by signing Coleman Shelton in free agency. Shelton may not be a Pro Bowl caliber player in terms of performance; however, he excels in the key area that Limmer lacked: communication. Player Season Label Overall Pass Block Run Block Coleman Shelton 2025 Highest season 70.9 53.1 77.2 Coleman Shelton 2022 Lowest non-2019 season 58.0 71.3 55.4 Beaux Limmer 2024 2024 season 55.5 40.2 65.4 Source: Pro Football Focus (PFF) Premium Stats. It seems fair to expect that Limmer has made progress in this area after spending a year behind Shelton and more time in McVay’s offense. If he can take strides in signal calling at the line, his play as a rookie wasn’t disqualifying and he would still have starting potential. Life in the NFL usually comes down to the business side of things. Limmer is a former sixth-round pick that is cost-controlled through 2027. Shelton’s 2025 free agent deal expires at the conclusion of the season. He’ll be age 32, and it would be tough to renew the financial commitment to a player whose best days are likely behind him. Similar to how the Rams found lost money in replacing long-term starter Rob Havenstein with Warren McClendon a year ago, starting Limmer could favor LA in both the short and long terms. Shelton is unlikely to return in 2027. Limmer could help thread the needle in a volatile period where the other four starters—McClendon, Kevin Dotson, Steve Avila, and Alaric Jackson—may all need new contracts soon. At some point the Rams will need to build an offensive line succession plan. They could take a step towards future-proofing the front by starting Limmer over Shelton.

title: Which QB will finally topple Norm Van Brocklin’s record?
summary: Heading into the 2026 season, Los Angeles Rams legend Norm Van Brocklin’s single-game passing record has stood for almost 75 years. With all the changes made to benefit the passing game over the years, it’s truly astonishing that Van Brocklin’s mark of 554 yards has stood for this long. That said, which quarterback is most […]
full_text: Football: Los Angeles Rams QB Norm Van Brocklin (11) in action vs Detroit Lions. Los Angeles, CA 10/31/1954 CREDIT: Mark Kauffman (Photo by Mark Kauffman /Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) (Set Number: X1953 TK1 R4 F5 ) Heading into the 2026 season, Los Angeles Rams legend Norm Van Brocklin’s single-game passing record has stood for almost 75 years. With all the changes made to benefit the passing game over the years, it’s truly astonishing that Van Brocklin’s mark of 554 yards has stood for this long. That said, which quarterback is most likely to break it this season? Having a 500-yard passing game is a crowning achievement for single callers. Including the playoffs, there have only been 27 such games in NFL history, with Ben Roethlisberger, Tom Brady and Drew Brees the only QBs to have thrown for over 500 yards multiple times. Kirk Cousins is the most recent to have done so, throwing for 509 yards in a 2024 win over the Buccaneers. Without further ado, let’s take a look at the top candidates to topple Van Brocklin’s record in 2026. Matthew Stafford Let’s start with the option closest to home. Stafford once threw for 520 yards as a member of the Lions in the 2011 regular season finale against the Packers at Lambeau Field. Unfortunately, it came in a losing effort, as the quarterback on the opposite sideline, Matt Flynn, threw for 480 yards and six touchdowns in a 45-41 Green Bay win. Stafford seems like an easy choice given that he’s already a member of the 500 Club and has one of the league’s most explosive offenses at his disposal. However, he’s thrown for at least 450 yards with the Rams once , which came against the Seahawks late last season. It’s unlikely that he’ll break the record, as he plays in a more balanced offense that doesn’t ask him to pass a ludicrous amount. Never say never, though, considering he plays against the Cardinals twice a year. Joe Burrow Out of anyone on this list, Burrow is the most likely to break it. He has the fourth-most passing yards in a game with 525, which came in a masterclass performance versus the rival Ravens in 2021. The 41-21 win helped Cincinnati secure the AFC North and make a surprise run to that year’s Super Bowl. With 525 passing yards, @Bengals Joe Burrow finished 30 yards shy of breaking Norm Van Brocklin's @NFL record for a single-game. He is the 1st player to pass for 900 yards vs a single team in a season, breaking the record previously shared by Joe Montana and Dan Marino. pic.twitter.com/6ePZK1jcfr — ESPN Insights (@ESPNInsights) December 26, 2021 With Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins in tow, he’ll undoubtedly have another crack to try and break it. Cincy is certainly a pass-happy team, which helps his chances. Dak Prescott Similar to the Bengals, America’s Team (barf) loves to air it out, boosting Prescott’s stats significantly. The Cowboys’ quarterback threw for 502 yards and four touchdowns in a 49-38 win over the upstart Browns. Dallas fell behind 41-14 before scoring 24 unanswered to close the gap to three points. Prescott’s efforts were wasted as Cleveland scored a late touchdown to put the game away. At least Prescott’s stats looked wonderful in the box score, and that’s all that really matters in Big D, right? Dak Prescott passed for 502 yards in today's game – most of his career and the second-most in a single game in team history. He is only the second quarterback (Tony Romo – 506 vs. Denver, 2013) to pass for 500 yards in a single game in franchise history. — Dallas Cowboys Public Relations (@DallasCowboysPR) October 4, 2020 Joking aside, the Cowboys boast one of the best wide receiver duos in the NFL with All-Pros CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. So even when Dallas inevitably disappoints per usual, they have an exciting trio to watch, making Prescott a dark-horse to surpass Van Brocklin. Jared Goff I know, I know, this is a controversial pick. But hear me out first! Goff had his 500-yard game in a Rams uniform, and like most of the quarterbacks on this list, it came in a losing effort. He had 517 yards in a 55-40 loss to the Bucs in Week 4 of the 2019 campaign. That was the good, as he turned the ball over four times, one of which was returned for the deciding touchdown. Regardless of that bad game, Goff has been remarkably efficient with the Lions. He even came close to becoming the fourth QB with multiple 500-yard games in December 2024, falling six yards shy against the Bills in Detroit’s 48-42 loss. So why does Goff have a chance this season? The Lions are playing a last place schedule and are set to face cupcakes in the Jets, Dolphins, Cardinals and Titans this season. Expect offensive dominance in those matchups, if not the possibility of an NFL record.

title: Alex Cook may not be ‘just another camp body’
summary: The L.A. Rams signed free agent safety Alex Cook to their roster on Monday and he may be more than just a camp body. […]
full_text: BIRMINGHAM, ALABAMA - MAY 17: Alex Cook #30 of the Birmingham Stallions reacts during the first quarter against the Columbus Aviators at Protective Stadium on May 17, 2026 in Birmingham, Alabama. (Photo by Stew Milne/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images The L.A. Rams signed free agent safety Alex Cook to their roster on Monday and he may be more than just a camp body. There is some serious history here between Cook and several members of the Rams organization, and you have to assume there were many conversations before GM Les Snead approached Cook’s representatives. This past season, Cook played for the Birmingham Stallions of the UFL. Here is how Bianca Gamez summed up Cook’s year with the Stallions: The 6’, 195-lbs defensive back completed a breakout spring season as a dynamic defensive anchor for the Stallions, finishing the UFL regular season with 45 total tackles (27 solo), 6 pass breakups, 1.0 tackle for loss, 1 interception and 1 fumble recovery. His standard-setting campaign was highlighted by big plays, including a spectacular, one-handed interception that he returned for a 70 yards for a pick-six touchdown against the Gamblers on June 6. He added a 73-yard scoop-and-score on a backwards lateral he knocked out in Week 10 against the Columbus Aviators. Prior to that, Cook was teammates with Harrison Mevis, Trent McDuffie, and Puka Nacua at the University of Washington, where they were all coached by current Rams pass game coordinator and defensive backs coach Jimmy Lake . View this post on Instagram How he got here During his time at Washington, Cook was a wide receiver during his freshman year before converting to safety. He didn’t see much playing time until his junior year, when he accumulated 32 tackles in 11 games. As a senior, Cook was one of the best players on the 11-2 Huskies team. He had a team-high 82 tackles (3.5 for loss) and was named to the All-PAC-12 Second Team. His 56 solo tackles ranked sixth in the conference. After going undrafted in the 2023 draft, Cook signed as an undrafted free agent with the New York Giants. He missed making the final roster but was added to their practice squad. In October of that year, the Carolina Panthers poached Cook from the Giants’ practice squad and added him to their 53-man roster. He saw action in 10 games and started 2 of them. He was active on special teams as well. During the 2024 preseason , Cook was waived by the Panthers and re-signed to the practice squad. He was released from the team in December. Three weeks later , he was signed to the Giants’ practice squad. Obviously, the Giants thought he was worth keeping around. In January of 2025 , Cook signed a reserve/future contract with the Chicago Bears. He was waived by the Bears seven months later. Can he make the roster? At the moment, the Rams have Cook listed fourth on the strong safety depth chart, right behind Nate Valcarcel. But the way the Rams treat their defensive backs as interchangeable pieces, maybe he wouldn’t be looked at as strictly a safety. After the top five of Kam Curl, Kamren Kinchens, Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson and Quentin Lake, the depth is somewhat sketchy. Could there be a spot for Alex Cook? We’ll see.

title: Fernando Mendoza Rose Bowl versus Alabama, Part XIV of Las Vegas Raiders’ Mendoza Mania
summary: It’s Bowl Season in Silver and Black Pride’s Mendoza Mania series, as we’ll be taking a look at the first of three Fernando Mendoza College Football Playoff games from last season. This one wasn’t much of a contest as Indiana took down Alabama 38-3 in the Rose Bowl. The Hoosiers didn’t need a heroic performance […]
full_text: PASADENA, CALIFORNIA - JANUARY 01: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Indiana Hoosiers celebrates after defeating the Alabama Crimson Tide 38-3 in the College Football Playoff Quarterfinal at Rose Bowl Stadium on January 01, 2026 in Pasadena, California. (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s Bowl Season in Silver and Black Pride’s Mendoza Mania series , as we’ll be taking a look at the first of three Fernando Mendoza College Football Playoff games from last season. This one wasn’t much of a contest as Indiana took down Alabama 38-3 in the Rose Bowl. The Hoosiers didn’t need a heroic performance from the No. 1 pick of the 2026 NFL draft. Instead, the Las Vegas Raiders’ new quarterback put together an efficient outing, completing 14 of 16 passes (87.5%) for 192 yards and three touchdowns with no interceptions. Diving deeper, he was also credited with three “big-time throws” from Pro Football Focus to earn an elite 92.9 passing grade, his highest mark as a passer for the season. Additionally, Mendoza had a handful of impressive runs against the Crimson Tide, recording 38 rushing yards on five attempts when removing sacks from the stat line. Among those were a couple of third-down conversions that give us a starting point for this breakdown. Good play call from Bama to take away the short routes on 3rd & 3, but Fernando Mendoza uses his legs to pick up the 1st anyway #Raiders pic.twitter.com/ZUAQyAtgU1 — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 21, 2026 This first play has to be frustrating for Alabama’s defensive coordinator because it’s a great design and call; the Heisman Trophy winner just makes a play with his legs to pick up the first down anyway. Pre-snap, Bama shows a double-mug look with seven defenders on the line of scrimmage to force the offense to account for a blitz and make the quarterback think he has to get the ball out quickly. However, it’s a simulated pressure where the four defenders in two-point stances on the line drop in coverage while the right defensive end pinches into the B-gap and the nickelback blitzes off the edge for a four-man rush with Cover 2 behind it. The four backers who dropped in coverage are all in perfect spots to take away Indiana’s quick game concept. Starting at the top of the screen: the flat defender (No. 8) is in the passing lane against the short route by the single receiver, the middle hook (No. 18) takes away the sit route from Omar Cooper Jr. while the curl-to-flat defender (No. 10) also steps into that window on his way to pickup the short curl from the tight end, and the other flat defender (No. 1) has the other short out taken care of. Maybe Mendoza can squeeze the ball into the tight end before No. 10 can get there, and it looks like he considers it by rearing back to throw. However, that’s a risky decision since the defender’s momentum is taking him into the passing lane for a potential PBU or even a pick-six. So, Mendoza wisely pulls the ball down and starts to scramble. The quarterback’s subpar change of direction skills do show up, as he takes a couple of gather steps around the 40-yard-line to pivot up the field. But once he gets north and south, his ability to read blocks and find rushing lanes comes into play. Mendoza eventually locates an opening and dives forward to pick up the first down, keeping the drive alive. Good play call from Bama to take away the short routes on 3rd & 3, but Fernando Mendoza uses his legs to pick up the 1st anyway #Raiders pic.twitter.com/ZUAQyAtgU1 — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 21, 2026 This next clip is pretty similar to the last one; it’s just a different pre-snap look and a designed quarterback run on third and three. Granted, this is an RPO, as all the receivers are running routes instead of run blocking. The decision for the quarterback likely comes down to two factors: how many defenders are in the box, and what the right (from the defense’s perspective) edge defender does. So, with Alabama in a six-man box and the edge (who it looks like Mendoza is reading) dropping into coverage, the correct read is for the quarterback to keep the ball and run. He starts to press toward the wide side of the field since the interior gaps/lanes are pretty congested with the defensive line slating and getting penetration. However, with his eyes on the other side of the field, Mendoza is late to see the SAM linebacker blitzing off the other edge. Also, since the right tackle has to pass off the defensive end and make sure the guard has control of the end, the linebacker penetrates the backfield unblocked. Luckily, Mendoza recognizes the blitz before it’s too late and pivots toward cutting upfield. That action also sets up the other linebacker and helps make the running back/lead blocker’s block easier, allowing the running back to seal the backer outside. But what makes this run really impressive is how the quarterback navigates the traffic in the backfield and squeezes through a very narrow rushing lane (see the end zone view above) to move the sticks on third down, again. That’s the result of impressive vision and a good job of setting up a second-level defender. 3rd and long facing Cover 0, Fernando Mendoza puts it up in the end zone for Charlie Becker to go up and get it #Raiders pic.twitter.com/TIN4F4deil — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 21, 2026 We’re moving on to the passing game but sticking with third-down situations, as the No. 1 pick was money on money downs against the Tide. Something he does well when throwing into the end zone is putting the ball up high but still in a spot where the receiver can get to it. Typically, that’s to beat tight coverage. While that’s not the case here since Charlie Becker has plenty of separation on the post route, Mendoza is facing some pressure in the pocket with the Cover 0 call from Alabama and the running back holding on for dear life against the blitzing linebacker. So, the quarterback does have to put some air on the pass to prevent the ball from getting tipped at the line of scrimmage. That makes the catch more difficult for Becker, but the trajectory is still well within his reach to turn third down into a touchdown. Even if the defensive back had tight coverage or undercut the route, this still would be six points with where the ball was placed. 3rd and 1, nice ball from Fernando Mendoza for 6 #Raiders pic.twitter.com/P89hokPvJq — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 21, 2026 Rinse and repeat, as this is a pretty similar rep to the one we just dove into. It’s third down again; it’s just third and short this time. Indiana appears to be expecting Cover 0 or at least a blitz from Alabama by using heavy personnel with the extra offensive lineman in the game at tight end while dialing up a pass with max protection and a two-man route. The offense doesn’t get the exact look they were expecting from the defense with just a five-man rush where one line of scrimmage linebacker drops into coverage and one off-ball linebacker blitzes off the edge, but the Hoosiers still have the upper hand with the play call. The Tide are in quarters, which essentially turns into Cover 0 without the blitz since the extra offensive lineman—who is ineligible because linemen can’t report as eligible in college and the outside receiver covers him up—can account for the extra pass-rusher. Also, especially with the running back and other/eligible tight end on the same side of the formation as the receivers, there is no eligible receiver on the ride side (offense’s perspective) of the field. However, Bama has three defenders in coverage on that side, all of whom end up covering nothing but grass. On top of that, the back and eligible tight end are involved in the pass protection call, forcing the strong safety (No. 18) to bracket the slot receiver with the nickel corner. All of that sets up for a one-on-one matchup with Elijah Sarratt against a corner with no safety help at the bottom of the screen. Mendoza immediately takes his eyes to that. Once he sees…

title: Klint Kubiak provides updates on Maxx Crosby’s, Jermod McCoy’s status for Las Vegas Raiders 1st training camp practice
summary: Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp is finally here, as the team’s veterans reported to camp on Tuesday, Aug. 28. One of the biggest questions from the Raiders’ OTAs and minicamp sessions is centered around the health and availability of defensive end Maxx Crosby and cornerback Jermod McCoy. Head coach Klint Kubiak provided updates on Crosby’s […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JUNE 09: Maxx Crosby #98 of the Las Vegas Raiders stretches during mandatory minicamp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on June 09, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Louis Grasse/Getty Images) | Getty Images Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp is finally here, as the team’s veterans reported to camp on Tuesday, Aug. 28. One of the biggest questions from the Raiders’ OTAs and minicamp sessions is centered around the health and availability of defensive end Maxx Crosby and cornerback Jermod McCoy. Head coach Klint Kubiak provided updates on Crosby’s and McCoy’s statuses, stating that “everyone’s going to be practicing [on Wednesday].” “The plan is to get [McCoy] reps early and see how he responds in his recovery,” Kubiak explained. “It’s a moving target with him. He’s a guy that worked extremely hard and has been dedicated to the program that we’ve put in front of him. But Jermod hasn’t played football in a year and we’re aware of that. But he’s ready to practice [on Wednesday], and we’re also going to be really smart with him and develop him the right way.” On Crosby: “[Crosby is] going to get all of the reps [on Wednesday] with the ones,” the coach continued. “He’s ready to go; he’s ready to practice. As practice unfolds and we’re watching our players, it’s always a moving target. But as of right now, [Wednesday] is a pretty short workday, an hour and 30 minutes. So, we’re expecting him to be ready to take all of those reps.” What’s interesting about Kubiak’s response is that he was asked if Crosby was going to be a full participant in practice, which Kubiak didn’t directly answer and instead pointed out that the first practice is a shorter session and described the situation as a “moving target”. So, whether or not that means Crosby will still be limited during training camp remains to be seen. The five-time Pro Bowl defensive end is recovering from offseason surgery to repair a torn meniscus in his knee, which infamously led to the Raiders putting him on injured reserve at the end of last season and a botched offseason trade with the Baltimore Ravens. McCoy, a rookie fourth-round pick, missed all of last season at Tennessee after suffering a torn ACL in January of 2025 and slid in the draft due to concerns over the knee. Both players were present but either limited or non-participants during OTAs and minicamp practices. Meanwhile, free agent linebacker Nakobe Dean’s status is also up in the air heading into training camp after he missed several spring practices. Dean wasn’t brought up specifically in Kubiak’s press conference, but the assumption is that he’ll be on the field on Wednesday too, with the coach stating that everyone is available for the team’s first session of the summer.
