title: Las Vegas Raiders Summer Scouting: TE Rankings
summary: I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. Brock Bowers remains an elite […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - JANUARY 09: Jamari Johnson #9 of the Oregon Ducks catches a pass for a two-point conversion against D'Angelo Ponds #5 of the Indiana Hoosiers during the third quarter in the 2025 College Football Playoff Semifinal at the Chick-fil-A Peach Bowl at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on January 09, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Jonathan Bachman/Getty Images) | Getty Images I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. Brock Bowers remains an elite tight end, and arguably the best in the NFL, but the Raiders do have some questions behind Bowers after the 2026 season. Former 2nd rounder Michael Mayer is sent to be a free agent, and with a good season he should be looking at a decent contract as a TE2, blocking specialist. Additionally, Ian Thomas is set to be a free agent and Las Vegas also has former UDFA Carter Runyon, who’s flashed, but it’s likely even with retaining Mayer the Raiders should add another TE. These rankings are extremely early, and they will evolve over not only the summer but the next 8-10 months throughout the season, and into draft season. Some lists will feature 10, 15, 20, or more ranked prospects but I’ll include others on the list below to note. Jamari Johnson, Oregon – 6’5/260, R-So Johnson was a key focal point of the Ducks offense last year with 32 receptions, 510 yards, and 3 TD after coming over from Louisville. He’s better than Kenyon Sadiq, and in my opinion has a chance to be a better prospect than Bowers. Johnson has absurd movement skills, he’s shown exceptional length, fires off the ball, and Johnson also shows a ton of quickness and movement in his route running. Johnson has fluid hips, he makes his cuts well, and Johnson shows an innate ability to adjust to the ball in the air and come down with tough catches. Where he makes a ton of impact is as a run blocker, where Johnson uses his length and athleticism with good technique, and a ton of lower body power to get off the line of scrimmage and into space. Johnson will need to continue his play as the starter at TE, instead of the supplementary piece, but he has the core traits, athleticism, and technique to be a top 10 pick. Peter Clarke, Temple – 6’6/270, Sr Pete Clarke exploded onto the scene in 2025 with 30 receptions, 483 yards, and 6 TD for Temple. He had the chance to transfer to multiple P4 programs but chose to remain at Temple. He has exceptional size, power, and length, and he’s also relatively new to football after playing at the NFL Academy in London before landing with Temple. Clarke has good movement off the line of scrimmage, his initial quickness is elite, and likely the best in the class where Clarke blocks like an offensive tackle. He has an innate ability to seal the corner, walls off defenders, finishes blocks, and drives his full body through the rep. Clarke’s natural movement excells in the run game, but he can also work as a functional pass protector as well. As a route runner Clark moves well for his size, he sinks his hips, has good initial quickness out of his breaks, and Clarke also does a good job to adjust to the ball in the air, work in YAC situations, and all around can be a very high end TE in the NFL. Chris Corbo, Georgia Tech – 6’5/246, Sr Corbo is someone to know, and I may be a bit high on his ranking but I have faith. The former Dartmouth standout had 32 receptions, 315 yards, and 7 TD in 2024 then 45/516/4 in 2025. He has great size, incredible length, and he moves well for someone at his size as well. Corbo fires off the line of scrimmage, has a quick second step, and his explosiveness out of cuts is also exceptional which is where Corbo wins. He’s a high end route runner who uses his lower body agility, football IQ, and ability to diagnose coverages/leverage to his advantage. Corbo does a good job coming back tot he ball, has strong hands, and he can win majority of contested catches with good YAC skills as well. Corbo wins a ton in the run game, often off his athleticism but advanced technique, though there’s a question mark on his power profile. Corbo is someone to watch, and he has a chance to be a longtime NFL player, and may project best as an elite TE2. DJ Vonnahme, Iowa – 6’5/240, R-Jr Vonnahme is a former QB, but his ceiling as a TE is truly incredible. A year after logging 29 receptions, 434 yards, and 3 TD, Vonnahme is a high end athlete, has elite physicality to pair with his explosiveness, and he shows advanced receiving skills for his limited experience at the position. Vonnahme does struggle with drops, he’s an average contested catch receiver, and he’ll need to improve as a blocker which is a given due to his limited experience. Vonnahme is a good route runner, who shows flashes of high end traits, and he wins largely off his athletic ability. The Iowa TE does a great job controlling his body, has good movement skills, and he’s powerful while also having top end speed at the position. He may be a 2028 option but Vonnahme has a chance as a first rounder in 2027. Trey’Dez Green, LSU – 6’7/245, R-Jr When you talk about athletes, there’s really no one better than Green. The 6’7, 240 TE wins mainly off his athletic profile, with inconsistencies in his route running, receiving, and he’s an adequate blocker. Green has the size, length, and athleticism to be a top TE in both college and the NFL, but he’ll need to get better in the small technique fashions. Green is likely a big slot, or H-Back TE in the NFL, as he’s an average blocker who doesn’t show a ton of immediate movement, and defenders do get up under his pads easy which pushes him out. As a receiver, he’s fluid, a decent route runner with flashes, and there’s also moments in the YAC game as well. After 33 receptions, 433 yards, and 7 TD, Green is looking for a consistent season to build on, and pivot his name higher. Ben Brahmer, Penn State – 6’7/255, R-Jr Brahmer transferred to Penn State from Iowa State, and there’s a lot of potential in his game. A big player, Brahmer has been a dominant blocker at the Big 12 level, and needs to show so again in the Big 10. He has above average movement skills, but needs to be more consistent as a receiver with flashes of being an above average route runner, though there’s also come questions in his hands which have been up and down. Brahmer is coming off his best sesaon, where he showed a good ability to work the intermediate range, and his natural athleticism shows he has the potential to be a good receiver in the NFL. Andrew Rappleyea, Penn State – 6’4/251, Sr Likely more of a 2028 candidate, but Rappleyea projects to start for Penn State with Brahmer and he has incredible athleticism. He’s played just 17 games in his career, with 13 coming in 2025 where he logged 20 receptions, 190 yards, and 3 touchdowns. Brady Foley, Louisville – 6’6/260, Sr Dorian Thomas, Cal – 6’4/240, Jr Thomas has bounced around in his career, he transferred to New Mexico in 2025 after spending 2024 at Arizona, before now landing at Cal. Thomas is an incredible athlete, he shows an elite blend of lower body agility, with good hips, ankles, and explosiveness off the line of scrimmage. Thomas does an incredible job after the catch, with good initial movement skills, and natural hip/ankle flexibility that allow him to maneuver past defenders. Additionally, Thomas did show a good ability to snag the ball in tough situations, he attacks out of his frame, and he’ll track the ball as well. Thomas’ biggest concern is as a blocker, where he’s undersized with average length, but does have some flashes using his athleticism to his advantage and can seal outside as a blocker. Thomas only has one real year of production in 2025 with 56 receptions, 560 yards, and four touchdowns but he joins a high octane Cal offense. Lawson…

title: Las Vegas Raiders 2026 Special Teams Wildcards
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are set to start training camp within the next month, and as they gear up for an interesting 2026 season, a few players and/or position groups can really make or break the season. The Raiders added a plethora of talent over the last off-season, with the Raiders likely to only return […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Place kicker Matt Gay #7 of the Indianapolis Colts warms up before the preseason game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 22, 2024 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Mowry/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are set to start training camp within the next month, and as they gear up for an interesting 2026 season, a few players and/or position groups can really make or break the season. The Raiders added a plethora of talent over the last off-season, with the Raiders likely to only return starters at left & right tackle, tight end, runningback, and one wide receiver on offense. Defensively, they likely return 3 starers on the defensive line, one at safety, one at corner, and none at linebacker. Needless, to say the Raiders are turning over the roster with talent, and for a roster that has been void of young talent in previous years, that was crucial. Additionally, they see three or four of their special teams playmakers likely change hands with Daniel Carlson and Jacob Bobenmoyer out, while new kick and punt returners should take the helm as well. I already broke down the defense, and that article may be live when you are reading this, and if not it will be soon. I’ve also already broke down the offense. The Kicker The Raiders parted ways with Daniel Carlson after 8 seasons, and Carlson saw his FG rate fall steadily since 2020 going from 94.3% to 81.5% in 2025. Additionally, his abilities to hit from 50+ also fell down the board competing just 5 of 8 in 2025 after 8 of 11 in 2024, and 11 of 13 in 2022. The Raiders bring in two options, with veteran Matt Gay looking to rebound his career under DeCamillis, and rookie Kansei Matsuzawa dubbed the “Tokyo Toe, and Special-K”. Gay converted 17 of his 23 attempts (74%) in 2025 though he was 4/4 in 2 games with the 49ers. He’s struggled to regain his form from 2021-2022 where he 2as a Pro Bowler converting 60/64 field goals including 12/14 from 50+. Those two seasons came under new Raiders special teams coordinator, Joe DeCamillis. As for Matsuzawa, the 2025 consensus All-American went 39/45 in his Hawaii career and another 72/72 on his PAT’s. Matsuzawa is relatively new to kicking, having only done so for 5 years now, and he’s not been tested from 50+ routinely which will be a big test in the NFL. Matsuzawa has the leg, and he’s shown elite accuracy, but also kicking in the NFL comes with it’s own challenges. The Raiders have seen their ability, and confidence, to hit field goals dip the last two seasons which has impacted not just their scores, record, but also playcalling. Las Vegas needs to be consistent at kicker to help ease pressure on the offense, and open up Klint Kubiak’s playbook. Dareke Young Dareke Young comes to Las Vegas following Klint Kubiak, and there’s a plethora of jobs for him to take on in Las Vegas. The 6’2, 230 receiver has just 72 receiving yards in his career, but he may have a chance to take the “X” role for Klint Kubiak if he can stay consistent which has a chance to lead to 400-600 yards. Additionally, Young’s best impact comes on special teams. He’s been a proven gunner with a career 24 tackles and 3 FF including 2 FR, and 4 tackles in the playoffs. Young can provide as a kick returner with 322 yards on 10 attempts in 2025, and he may take that role as well. He’ll impact the Raiders on special teams, but his ability to become a dynamic, or higher end, kick returner could prove pivotal for the Raiders special teams that has lacked juice on kick returns. Tommy Eichenberg, Segun Olubi, & Cody Lindenberg Similar to Young, Olubi, Eichenberg and Lindenberg may see big roles for the Raiders defense in reserve linebacker roles or sub packages. That said, all three are special teams standouts. Olubi has a career 4 blocked punts and kicks, with a special teams TD, 2 FF, 3 FR, and 34 tackles. Additionally, Olubi has just a 4.7% missed tackle rate on special teams in his career. Lindenberg and Eichenberg combined for 34 special teams tackles, and a FF in 2025 and the two of them can be focal points of the teams unit again in 2026. The Raiders special teams ranked exceptionally low in 2025, at one point being on a historically bad trajectory. Despite that, there was some standouts and if the Raiders depth linebackers can combine to be high end playmakers again on special teams, while forcing turnovers, blocked kicks, and possible touchdowns they are in a way better spot to change the game. Joe DeCamillis Similar to the other two iterations of this, the Raiders unit can only go as far as their play caller and head man will let them. DeCamillis has preached versatility, aggression, and fundamentals on special teams his whole career and that should remain the same mentality in Las Vegas. His units have ranked inside the top 15 for most of his NFL career, including from 2015-2022 ranking top 6 in 5 of those seasons, though he also ranked in the bottom 5 in two of them as well. DeCamillis saw a ton of improvements on his units kick returns last season with the South Carolina Gamecocks. The Raiders had a lot of inconsistences in their units the last few seasons, and at worst DeCamillis should improve them to league average at worst.

title: Las Vegas Raiders: The 5-1-5 Defense & Treydan Stukes
summary: Previously, an article was published outlining what to really expect from the Rob Leonard defense, over the next week or two, I’m going to outline a few specific concepts that I believe Leonard will run, and thus what to expect from these units. The first of these, is the 5-1-5 defense, which at it’s core […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS , NV - DECEMBER 7: Maxx Crosby (98) of the Las Vegas Raiders hangs his head after a first down by RJ Harvey (12) of the Denver Broncos during the third quarter of the Broncos' 24-17 win at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, Nevada on Sunday, December 7, 2025. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images Previously, an article was published outlining what to really expect from the Rob Leonard defense, over the next week or two, I’m going to outline a few specific concepts that I believe Leonard will run, and thus what to expect from these units. The first of these, is the 5-1-5 defense, which at it’s core is a 3-4 defense with some core adaptations. The defense originally was developed by Wink Martindale, and then adopted heavily by Brian Flores, before both Mike MacDonald & Jesse Minter adopted the unit. If you didn’t see the trend, Raiders DC Rob Leonard has worked under MacDonald & Flores, while also working for Patrick Graham who dabbled with the 5-1-5 defense, but lacked the personnel to do so. * If you want a quick prediction what I think the defense looks like, scroll to the bottom * / The core of the defense is to build the defense around a hybrid front that can work against the run & the pass, with core of the unit surrounding hybrid DE/DT’s on the interior defensive line and hybrid DE/OLB types on EDGE. Additionally, the defense has some core principles which are largely in line with what Raiders DC Rob Leonard wants to run which are aggression, attack, pursuit, and communication. The defense can often be classified as a 3-4 defense, largely because of the way the EDGE & LB are positioned, though a core part of the linebackers are often their existence as a box safety. An additional core part of this defense comes at linebacker, with run defense linebackers, who can also provide production in the pass rush department. As for the secondary, the scheme lives off versatile defenders in the secondary, and a bandit (which I touch on later). Below is a standard picture, via “That Franchise Guy” on YouTube showing the Vikings iteration of the 5-1-5 look: The Vikings traditionally run the defense with 3 safeties, as Josh Metellus plays their “bandit safety” role, and while the Raiders don’t have an identical player to Metellus there’s a few players on the roster with those capabilities to play a nickel defender, slot corner, free safety, and box linebacker role. The defense lives in a zone where at it’s core 4 defensive backs are on the field, though most often it’s 5 with one charted as an inside linebacker which is something I’d expect to see a bit of this season for the Raiders. Unlike the Vikings, the Raiders main defense will not be the 5-1-3 “penny” defense, largely with their backend personnel and the Raiders having two good linebackers in Quay Walker and Nakobe Dean who signed large contracts this off-season. Despite that, it’s likely a unit that will be ran heavily this year, and one if done well can see a ton of success. The 5-1-3 defense also adds a strong layer of versatility, something again that has been a priority for Rob Leonard. Unlike the Vikings, the Raiders will not live out of the 5-1-3, but they will run the defense with the ability to rotate into other coverages such as a traditional 3-4, a 4-3, and even a 3-3 defense with a variety of rotations during pre and post snap. Another core aspect of the defense comes with the ability to rotate the defensive backs, which Rob Leonard has stated will happen. The unit has the ability to rotate their strong safety into the bandit role, or into the nickel, while their free safety can also swap with the bandit and strong safety. When it comes to Cover-3, you’ll see the boundary corners flip into the back third coverages, the free safety often rotates up to cover one flat along with the strong safety, and your bandit safety plays a hybrid deep middle and mid coverage. Defensive Line: As mentioned, the 5-1 defense has a core philosophy that surrounds athletic versatile DT/DE hybrids, which despite lacking some talent on their interior defensive line, the Raiders do fit that mold. For a full breakdown of how their DL will operate, you can check out an article from April where I broke down the unit . The traditional “defensive tackle” is going to be a primary 2, 3, and 4i defensive tackle while your “defensive end” traditionally lines up at the 4 & 5 technique (don’t read too much into this please). A true traditional EDGE rusher will likely be aligned at the 9 or 7 technique, with some time at 6 and 5 technique as well dependent on the system. Lastly, a “nose tackle” is usually lining at the 0, 1, or 2i technique. If you want to sum it up in one sentence “The IDL is a traditional 3-4, focusing on taking gaps, and attacking the front while the EDGE rushers collapse the pocket horizontally” In terms of a 5-1-5 front, a true NT will be on the field often aligned at a true 0, with two base DT/DE often as 3-Techniques, and then two EDGE rushers at a 7-Tech or Wide-9 (need to be an UBER athlete). For the Raiders, it’s clear they will have a competition with nose tackle between 7th rounder Brandon Cleveland, UDFA Gary Smith, and free agent Benito Jones. The winner of the nose tackle competition is going to need to live off two core factors, athleticism & a minor ability to rush the passer. Among the three, Brandon Cleveland is the best athlete, though he can get pushed around at times which can create an issue with his ability to truly hold a 0-technique role. Benito Jones & Gary Smith are adequate athletes, but struggle to present a real threat in the twist/stunt department, which Cleveland does extremely well. As above, the defensive line will work heavily with twists/stunts, something Leonard has done through his career with the Raiders defensive line. A core part of being able to pull off twists & stunts is athletic ability, and versatility on the DL. The versatility piece isn’t a concern for the Raiders, with their IDL having a ton of ability to rotate across the unit especially Adam Butler. Butler is coming off a down 2025 season, and even if he’s starting to regress, he’s still shown high end versatility with 50% of his snaps at 3-Tech, 15% at 4, and 21% coming from 0-2 technique. Additionally, Thomas Booker & Tonka Hemingway who are undoubtedly the best two pass rushers on the Raiders interior, both have versatility with Booker playing 31% at 2-Tech, 44% at 3-Tech, and 17% at 4-Tech. Meanwhile, Tonka Hemingway played over 250 snaps at 1, 2 (400), 4, and 5 Technique with another 753 snaps at 3-Tech during his time at South Carolina. Jonah Laulu is also a versatile piece on the interior, but works more towards the 2/2i technique than a 3/4 technique. Another name to note is 6th rounder JJ Pegues, who does haver versatility to play 0, 2, 3, and 4 technique with good strength vs the run, and quality athleticism. In terms of the EDGE rushers, Maxx Crosby & Malcolm Koonce both fit the traditional 7/9 Technique pass rusher, though both have an ability to rush from a 5-Tech role as well, though I don’t expect that much this year. Crosby has played 88% from 7-Tech, Koonce 66%, and new free agent signing Kwity Paye 78% though he does have some experience working as a 6/5 Technique which could be a core role for him. I’d expect Paye to still play at 7-Technique, largely as a run defender, and he should be able to tap into his athleticism to stunt and twist. 3rd Rounder Keyron Crawford is a core piece of this defense, should he develop. Crawford can drop into the flats, work exceptionally well in pass rush games, and his athleticism allows him the ability to align all over the defensive line. Additionally, UDFA Cian Slone can do similar things to Crawford, and he plays with a ton of athleticism which should allow him to work in small samples if he makes the roster. (Photo by Steve Marcus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders held a workout with 2022 Pro Bowl running back Miles Sanders on Monday, according to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler . This news came just one day before the Raiders’ veterans report to training camp (Tuesday, July 28), and four days after the rookies reported to camp (July 23). Former Pro Bowl running back Miles Sanders worked out for the Raiders today, per source. Sanders, a free agent, is fully cleared from a knee injury that required surgery and cut short his 2025 season in Dallas. pic.twitter.com/1XpN9HmUTt — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) July 27, 2026 Sanders, 29, has played for four teams in seven years. The Penn State product was originally a second-round pick by the Philadelphia Eagles in 2019, earning the Pro Bowl bid during his last season in Philadelphia by rushing for 1,269 yards (4.9 ypc) and 11 touchdowns . However, the Eagles decided to let him walk during the following offseason, and his production has declined every season since setting career highs four years ago. In 2023, Sanders signed a four-year, $25.4 million contract with the Carolina Panthers. However, he battled injuries and struggled to find his footing with the Panthers before being released with two years left on the deal. The running back had just 939 yards from scrimmage and four total touchdowns in 27 games (seven starts) with the Panthers. This past season, the former Eagle returned to the NFC East, inking a one-year contract for the veteran minimum with the Dallas Cowboys. Sanders continued to battle the injury bug, suffering a knee bruise and ankle sprain in training camp before being put on season-ending injured reserve after having chondral tissue graft surgery on his left knee, per ESPN’s Todd Archer . He played in just four games with the Cowboys, collecting just 147 yards from scrimmage and 1 touchdown. Meanwhile, the Raiders could use some depth behind Ashton Jeanty. The front office was expected to be more active in the running back market, but only used a fourth-round pick on Mike Washington Jr. from Arkansas and signed Indiana’s Roman Hemby as an undrafted rookie during the offseason. Last year’s holdovers, Dylan Laube and Chris Collier, have a combined 17 career touches from scrimmage during the regular season. In other words, the position group is pretty young. Jeanty, who is heading into his second season, is the only running back with double-digit rushing attempts. Also, the team could use a reliable pass-catcher out of the backfield, and Sanders has 183 catches for 1,274 yards and four touchdowns in his career to add more reason for the Raiders’ interest. In addition to Sanders, the Raiders also hosted the following players for workouts on Monday, per ESPN’s Ryan McFadden . WR K.J. Hamler WR Deven Thompkins WR Casey Washington TE Zack Kuntz LB Buddy Johnson LB Jamon Johnson DE Patrick Johnson After the workouts, the Raiders announced the signings of Buddy Johnson, Patrick Johnson and Thompkins. In corresponding moves, the team released wide receiver Jonathan Brady, linebacker Chris Thomas and defensive tackle Laki Tasi. Tasi, who was a former professional rugby player and part of the NFL’s IPP program, is the most significant of the bunch. His story helped him become a popular player within the fanbase last season despite not playing a down during the regular season and spending all of 2025 as a practice squad offensive lineman. Silver and Black Pride will continue to monitor the situation and report any signings prior to and during training camp. In Other Raiders’ Links: Fernando Mendoza film breakdown: S&BP’s latest Mendoza Mania column dives into the No. 1 pick’s performance on a big stage in the Big Ten Championship against Ohio State . Keyron Crawford’s timeline: “His 2026 season should be slightly inconsistent with Crawford likely behind Maxx Crosby, Malcolm Koonce, Kwity Paye for rotational snaps and he’ll likely also be pushed by UDFA Cian Slone who’s made waves in the off-season so far,” S&BP’s Tristen Kuhn wrote. “…Year two & three are likely the biggest for Crawford, 2027 can likely see one or all of those above him on the depth chart gone.” Mendoza ready to learn: “‘Being a part of the Silver and Black, we want to compete every single day and do the best that we can for the organization and best for the team so we can win games,’” Mendoza told Paul Gutierrez of the team’s website . “‘Everybody in the quarterback room is a top-tier quarterback and it’s going to be competing with each other, not competing against each other.’” Jon Gruden hypes up Klint Kubiak: “Enter Klint Kubiak, who could solve a lot of problems,” the former head coach said in a video posted on his X/Twitter account . “Not only did they get a young, up-and-coming head coach, they got a guy who can really call plays and coach quarterbacks, and run the offense.”

title: Dolphins training camp 2026: Physicality takes center stage
summary: The 2026 Miami Dolphins are looking to end the “soft” perception of the Mike McDaniel era as they enter their first training camp under head coach Jeff Hafley. While speed and pre-snap motions were a major focus of McDaniel’s offense, building around players who could take the ball the length of the field if everything […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - JUNE 09: Head coach Jeff Hafley of the Miami Dolphins looks on during OTA Offseason Workouts at Baptist Health Training Complex on June 09, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 Miami Dolphins are looking to end the “soft” perception of the Mike McDaniel era as they enter their first training camp under head coach Jeff Hafley. While speed and pre-snap motions were a major focus of McDaniel’s offense, building around players who could take the ball the length of the field if everything went right on any individual play, the 2026 version of the team will be looking to power through opposing defenses and stopping offenses. Size and strength will become a major factor for the Dolphins, if Hafley’s vision comes to fruition. The Dolphins reported for training camp on Tuesday, starting their build up for the regular season. Hafley met with the media on Tuesday, talking about the plans for camp and what he wants to see from the team and highlighting the focus on physicality the team will have this summer. Asked about what message he has for the team on day one of camp, Hafley explained, “Getting back to how we want to practice. The competitiveness, eventually the physicality, which we’ll still have to wait until pads come on, but I want it to be competitive and I want them to feel a sense of urgency in that.” Continuing, the first-year head coach turned to what he wants the fans to see of the team at training camp practices and in the three preseason games, saying, “I want them to see a physical team that that lays it on the line, that plays together, that has fun together and that can execute without making a lot of pre-snap, post-snap mistakes. A smart football team who plays as hard as they can for as long as they can and enjoys playing together, and that’s really important because those are the things that we can control.” In recent years, the NFL has moved away from multiple physical, full-speed practices in the heat of the summer during training camp. Many teams, including the Dolphins under McDaniel, strayed from live tackling during workouts, looking to keep the players away from injury by avoiding direct contact. The Hafley Dolphins will swing back to bringing the contact. “They do. They do. Are you excited about that? They do,” Hafley answered when asked if his practice plans include live tackling. The Dolphins have been seen as a soft team that crumbles as soon as they are met with physicality for the last few years. Hafley clearly wants to shed that image, and he is going to be looking to ensure the fans see it during this summer’s training camp.

In four seasons with the Raiders, Ferrell amassed 10 sacks, 15 tackles for loss, two forced fumbles and a fumble recovery. He spent the 2024 season with the Washington Commanders, before playing for the Los Angeles Chargers (1 game) and the San Francisco 49ers (8 games) in 2025. In his entire seven-year career, Ferrell has 21 sacks, 184 combined tackles, 29 tackles for loss, four forced fumbles and two fumble recoveries. summary: Today is the day that the Minnesota Vikings report for training camp in Eagan, and one of the team’s stalwarts has an extra bit of business to attend to before things really get underway. The Vikings and right tackle Brian O’Neill have agreed to a new four-year, $96 million contract extension that will keep O’Neill […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - JANUARY 4: Brian O'Neill #75 of the Minnesota Vikings speaks with players on the bench against the Green Bay Packers in the second quarter of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Today is the day that the Minnesota Vikings report for training camp in Eagan, and one of the team’s stalwarts has an extra bit of business to attend to before things really get underway. The Vikings and right tackle Brian O’Neill have agreed to a new four-year, $96 million contract extension that will keep O’Neill in purple through the 2030 season. No word yet on how the deal is structured, but it will almost certainly reduce his cap number for the 2026 season, which was set to be a team-high $23.1 million. O’Neill is currently the longest-tenured member of the Vikings’ roster (unless/until Harrison Smith makes his return), as he was drafted by the Vikings in the second round of the 2018 NFL Draft. He’s been a two-time Pro Bowl selection in his time with Minnesota and has started 120 of the 124 games he’s played in for the Vikings in his career. The Vikings now have their bookend tackles signed for the foreseeable future, as Christian Darrisaw is signed through the 2029 season and O’Neill is now signed through 2030. As we’ve said for a long time, the Vikings have their tackle situation figured out. Now they just have to solidify the interior of the offensive line. Congratulations to Brian O’Neill on his new contract extension with the purple!

title: Vikings Choose Date for Adrian Peterson’s Ring of Honor Induction
summary: Back in May, we learned that running back Adrian Peterson would be the newest inductee into the Minnesota Vikings’ Ring of Honor during the 2026 NFL season. Now, we know exactly when that enshrinement will take place. The team has announced that Peterson’s Ring of Honor induction ceremony will take place at halftime of the […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 03: Running back Adrian Peterson #28 of the Minnesota Vikings celebrates after a touchdown during the game against the Dallas Cowboys at Cowboys Stadium on November 3, 2013 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Back in May, we learned that running back Adrian Peterson would be the newest inductee into the Minnesota Vikings’ Ring of Honor during the 2026 NFL season. Now, we know exactly when that enshrinement will take place. The team has announced that Peterson’s Ring of Honor induction ceremony will take place at halftime of the team’s Monday Night Football contest against the Buffalo Bills on 9 November. You can set that one in stone, because it’s a Week 9 matchup and Monday Night Football contests can’t be flexed out until Week 12, per league rules. Peterson, who is also in his first year of eligibility for Pro Football Hall of Fame enshrinement this year and should be a no-brainer, first-ballot lock, holds pretty much every meaningful Vikings rushing record and is fifth in NFL history with 14,918 career rushing yards. It’s hard to believe that it’s been a decade since the last time he carried the ball as a Viking, but his last season with the team came in 2016, when he battled injuries and appeared in just three games. Peterson is one of two Vikings to score more than 100 touchdowns as a member of the Vikings, as he found the end zone 102 times while wearing purple (97 rushing touchdowns, five receiving touchdowns). He also remains the last non-quarterback to be named the NFL’s Most Valuable Player, having won the award for his incredible 2012 season where he nearly set the single-season NFL rushing record just one-year removed from tearing his ACL. As we mentioned, Peterson should be getting the call to Canton this coming January, but the Vikings are going to get him into the Ring of Honor first, and now we know exactly when that’s going to happen.

title: From Vikings UDFAs to Draft Picks: The Top 10 Mr. Mankato Candidates for 2026
summary: Training camp is underway and The Real Forno Show is already deep into one of the best traditions in Vikings fandom. On this episode of the Vikings 1st & SKOL production, Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano break down the Mr. Mankato award—the informal honor for the under-the-radar player who shines brightest in camp and […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - MAY 27: Elijah Williams #99 of the Minnesota Vikings participates in a drill during an OTA workout at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on May 27, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp is underway and The Real Forno Show is already deep into one of the best traditions in Vikings fandom. On this episode of the Vikings 1st & SKOL production, Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano break down the Mr. Mankato award—the informal honor for the under-the-radar player who shines brightest in camp and the preseason. Forness walks through the criteria (third-round pick or later, under 100 offensive or defensive snaps), reviews past winners from Adam Thielen and Stefon Diggs to Max Brosmer, and explains why wide receivers and cornerbacks dominate the history of the award. “The best positions to win this award are positions that can help you stand out, and the best way to stand out is to make big plays,” Forness said. “Who makes big plays? Players who are on the ball, wide receivers, cornerbacks.” He noted that only one trench player (Tashawn Bower in 2017) has ever claimed the honor. Forness then delivered his personal top 10: Key Points from the Episode: The Mr. Mankato criteria: Founded by Phil Mackey and Judd Zulgad, the award honors an under-the-radar player who shines in training camp. Eligibility requires being a third-round pick or later with fewer than 100 offensive or defensive snaps (special teams snaps excluded). Past winners include: Adam Thielen (2014), Stefon Diggs (2015), K.J. Osborn, Jalen Nailor, and Max Brosmer (2025) — Brosmer is excluded from this year’s list for the spirit of the award. Wide receivers dominate: As Tyler noted, “Your best bet’s gonna be being a wide receiver. It’s straight up.” Pass catchers get the most opportunities to make splash plays, the lifeblood of this award. #10 – Jacob Thomas (S, James Madison UDFA): An intelligent, Swiss Army knife safety with real opportunity in a thin safety room. #9 – Demond Claiborne (RB): Tyler is openly lower on Claiborne than consensus: “He’s gonna look great in shorts. When the pads come on, that’s where my concerns lie.” #8 – Zemaiah Vaughn (CB): The 6’2″ corner is reportedly bigger and stronger in 2026, but Tyler notes he’s already seen a full camp from Vaughn, raising the bar. #7 – Charles Demmings (CB, 5th round): A Senior Bowl standout from the FCS level who impressed against Power Four competition and has the hip fluidity to stick in man coverage. #6 – Gavin Bartholomew (TE): A mystery man with a clean slate — the 2025 draft pick missed all of last year’s camp, giving him an almost fresh-start advantage. #5 – Jakobe Thomas (S, 3rd round): A box safety who profiles as a run-disrupting “point and shoot” player, with second-team snaps lined up and plenty of opportunity to make noise. #4 – Tai Felton (WR, 3rd round) : The 6’2″, sub-4.4 speedster needs a strong camp. “Felton has a lot to prove right now” — new GM Nolan Teasley has zero prior connection to him. #3 – Dontae Fleming (WR): Tyler’s personal favorite: “Every time I was at practice and watching, he shined.” Second-year familiarity with the offense gives Fleming a real edge. #2 – Dillon Bell (WR, UDFA): Already generating serious buzz from Vikings beat reporters, Bell’s physicality and “keep-away speed” make him the consensus favorite — but the hype could work against him. #1 – Elijah Williams (DL): After 42 dominant preseason snaps in 2025, Williams returns with a fully developed NFL body. “I think he’s going to be a big surprise to a lot of people, but not to me.” Forness made a point of dismissing personality as a factor. “Mr. Mankato’s all about on the field. It does not matter about the personality… This is about how do you do on the field and how are you standing out?” He also explained why several popular names—Domonique Orange (“Big Citrus”), Max Bredeson, and punter Brett Thorson—did not crack the list, citing limited splash-play potential. The episode closes with a preview of the Kevin O’Connell and Nolan Teasley training-camp opening press conference on Tuesday, and the early practice schedule (first public session Saturday, first padded practice Monday). title: ‘Unbelievable’ Kayshon Boutte unfazed by rumors about his Patriots future
summary: Between the Romeo Doubs signing and the A.J. Brown trade, no position on the New England Patriots’ roster has made more headlines this offseason than wide receiver. Of course, one other player is also responsible for that: Kayshon Boutte. The fourth-year wideout, who was among the Patriots’ most productive pass catchers in 2025, has been […]
full_text: Foxboro, MA - July 29 - Wide receiver Kayshon Boutte (9) of the New England Patriots makes a catch during Training Camp at Gillette Stadium. (Photo by Matt Stone/MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images Between the Romeo Doubs signing and the A.J. Brown trade, no position on the New England Patriots’ roster has made more headlines this offseason than wide receiver. Of course, one other player is also responsible for that: Kayshon Boutte. The fourth-year wideout, who was among the Patriots’ most productive pass catchers in 2025, has been the subject of trade rumors throughout the spring. And yet, with the first four days of training camp in the books, he remains in Foxborough — and not just that: seemingly unfazed by the speculation about his future, no other member of Drake Maye’s supporting cast has had a more notable impact on the practice fields so far. Boutte has made the biggest play of the day in all three of the competitive sessions, including a 40-yard back-shoulder touchdown catch over All-Pro safety Kevin Byard on Tuesday. “That dude is unbelievable,” fellow wideout Kyle Williams said after practice. “I’m super proud of him. Obviously, he’s picking up where he left off, and this is only the beginning for him.” Maye sees Boutte’s impact thus far in camp the same way. “It’s nothing new. I mean, you guys see it. All year last year and the year before, he just keeps doing things right,” the Patriots’ starting quarterback said on Saturday. “I’m proud of him for getting in there, jumping in there. And he understands if he’s got something down the sideline and a ball down the field, he’s got a chance it’s coming his way.” A sixth-round selection in the 2023 NFL Draft, Boutte’s arrow has been pointing up since his sophomore campaign. He quickly developed a chemistry with then-rookie Maye, and continued to enjoy his QB’s trust during their second season together. As a consequence, he finished 2025 with 42 catches in 18 games for 719 yards and seven touchdowns. While not a world-beater in terms of productivity or consistency, he still had an active hand in the Patriots’ offensive fortunes: the team’s starting X-receiver, he provided a deep element none of his teammates were able to duplicate. That was a problem from the team’s perspective, however, and the reason why it went out and brought in Doubs and Brown over the offseason. And with those in the fold, as well as DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Efton Chism and the aforementioned Kyle Williams rounding out the depth chart, Boutte found himself as the potential odd man out. And yet, he continued to impress the coaching staff with his professionalism. “I have a lot of respect for Kayshon,” head coach Mike Vrabel said. “We went through this last offseason: he had a great offseason, he had a good training camp, and that played out during the season. He was a large part of our success. His communication through this offseason with Todd [Downing] and myself, he is a pro. He understands what his job is, and he has gotten off to a good start. I have a lot of respect for him for the way that he has handled all these different situations, the conversations outside of here, and the noise that does not affect his performance on the field.” Had New England gotten an attractive trade offer, the situation might have worked out differently. However, despite being willing to listen particularly around the draft, nothing concrete ever transpired. And so, the 24-year-old stays put. Based on the the first week of training camp, the Patriots offense is all the better for it.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Denzel Ward contract extension raises floor for Christian Gonzalez deal
summary: While the contract negotiations between the New England Patriots and Christian Gonzalez are ongoing, the cornerback market in the NFL was reset. The Cleveland Browns and five-time Pro Bowler Denzel Ward reached an agreement on Tuesday that would reportedly pay him $62.2 million over two years, including $52.3 million in guarantees. While full details of […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez (0) works out at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect While the contract negotiations between the New England Patriots and Christian Gonzalez are ongoing, the cornerback market in the NFL was reset. The Cleveland Browns and five-time Pro Bowler Denzel Ward reached an agreement on Tuesday that would reportedly pay him $62.2 million over two years , including $52.3 million in guarantees. While full details of the pact are not yet available, reports indicate that the 29-year-old is now indeed the highest-pair cornerback in football on the basis of annual average value. His $31.1 million AAV barely beats the previous record set by Trent McDuffie’s $31 million per-year deal signed with the Rams earlier this offseason. This is also something the Patriots and Gonzalez will have noticed. New England’s No. 1 cornerback, after all, is trying to become the top-compensated cornerback in the game himself. According to team owner Robert Kraft, the organization is willing to help him in that quest and has an offer on the table that would at least have put him above McDuffie. With Ward now signing a new deal, however, the floor has been raised ever so slightly. Ward’s $31.1 million per year is the new benchmark now, a minuscule increase in the grand scheme of things but one that nonetheless has reshaped the market. Gonzalez, after all, is not the only CB vying a new deal: Seattle and fellow 2023 first-round draft pick Devon Witherspoon are working on what will be a record-breaking pact themselves, and the belief is that the Patriots and Gonzalez are waiting for this one to drop first before committing. If so, and assuming Witherspoon also wants top-of-the-market money when he signs his own deal, we can now expect Gonzalez to make at least $32.3 million annually on a new pact. When that pact will be signed remains to be seen, but the 24-year-old fully participating in training camp can be seen as an encouraging sign. “It’s different, but at the end of the day, it’s business and I’m blessed to be able to do this as my job,” Gonzalez said following Tuesday’s practice at Gillette Stadium . “So, you know, can’t get too much into it. Get to wake up and come out here and play football for a job. So very blessed, just happy that I’m able to come out here, run around and do what I love for my living.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: How Kyle Williams hopes to stand out in Patriots’ wide receiver room
summary: Four practices into his second training camp, Kyle Williams finds himself buried on the New England Patriots’ wide receiver depth chart. With the top of the group seemingly set in stone, he has been fighting with fellow sophomore Efton Chism for the sixth spot on the depth chart. Consequently, quality reps have been hard to […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JULY 23: New England Patriots wide receiver Kyle Williams (18) runs for the ball during a drill during the New England Patriots Training Camp on July 23, 2025, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, MA. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Four practices into his second training camp, Kyle Williams finds himself buried on the New England Patriots’ wide receiver depth chart . With the top of the group seemingly set in stone, he has been fighting with fellow sophomore Efton Chism for the sixth spot on the depth chart. Consequently, quality reps have been hard to come by. Knowing the need to stand out in a crowded room, the 23-year-old therefore has a simple plan: make the best of every opportunity, however small it might be. “You don’t know what is promised and what’s not,” Williams told reporters after Tuesday’s practice . “So, every day just coming up whether it’s in the film room, meetings, on the field pre-practice, after practice, just doing extra stuff to give myself the advantage to take forth to these opportunities.” So far, those opportunities have been few and far between. On Tuesday, for example, Williams caught just one pass while working with the second team. “It’s just control the controllables,” he said. “A lot of things are out of my control and when I get a chance to be able to control those things, I try to take the most of it. But I don’t really have expectations. I just show up every day just ready to take advantage of the opportunities given to me.” During the offseason, Williams did just that — and the Patriots recognized it as well. This is why he was announced as one of the club’s offseason award winners by head coach Mike Vrabel. Unfortunately, the honor did not help him climb the depth chart. At the moment, Williams finds himself behind the likes of A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Kayshon Boutte and Mack Hollins in the pecking order. The aforementioned Efton Chism has also gotten some reps over him in recent days. For the Patriots, the depth at receiver is a positive. For Williams, it is a problem, to a degree. “Iron sharpens iron at the end of the day,” he explained. “When you have guys like A.J, Pop, Mack — from top down, these dudes can play. It just forces you to come out here and compete at a higher level and have no slack in your game.” During the offseason, Williams focused on several areas in hopes of turning into a more complete player. Assisted by Hollins, the 2025 third-round draft pick tried to work on his physicality while still maintaining his speed. The ultimate goal was to become more versatile. During his rookie season, that versatility was lacking: Williams ran routes virtually exclusively from the X-receiver spot, where he served as a backup to Boutte. Playing that role, he finished his first year in the league with just 12 receptions that he took for 223 yards and three touchdowns. In his eyes, getting those numbers up starts with getting the snap count up, which in turn starts with diversifying his skillset. “The more you can do, the more opportunities are given,” Williams said. “For me, a big thing that I was trying to emphasize this year was expanding my role. I wanted to be able to move from the slot to the outside and be able to have those opportunities to expand and show my different traits.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: 6 performances of note from the Patriots’ fourth training camp practice
summary: Coming off a walkthrough on Monday, the New England Patriots turned the tempo and intensity up a notch on Tuesday. The two-hour session behind Gillette Stadium was the most competitive so far this training camp, and quite an eventful one. To recap the action, please head over to the latest version of our Patriots training […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots linebacker Elijah Ponder (91) does a drill with tight end Hunter Henry (85) during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Coming off a walkthrough on Monday, the New England Patriots turned the tempo and intensity up a notch on Tuesday. The two-hour session behind Gillette Stadium was the most competitive so far this training camp, and quite an eventful one. To recap the action, please head over to the latest version of our Patriots training camp notebook . For who caught our eye, please keep reading. Standout of the day WR Kayshon Boutte: Boutte continues to make big plays on a daily basis. On Tuesday, his biggest moment came when he caught a deep touchdown from Drake Maye during 11-on-11s. Lining up in his typical spot as an X-receiver, the fourth-year man was able to get a step on safety Kevin Byard on a go route and showed some tremendous ball tracking and concentration skills to complete the over-the-shoulder catch for a score of 40-plus yards. It was not Boutte’s only reception on the day. He also caught a throw from Maye over the middle during 7-on-7s and added pair of catches when backup Tommy DeVito targeted him on out routes. It was an active day for a player who, through four practices, has been New England’s most impactful wide receiver. Other performances of note QB Drake Maye: The Patriots’ quarterback started a bit slowly and his connection with A.J. Brown remains a work in progress, but he overall had a good day — an encouraging development after struggling with accuracy during the last full-speed practice on Sunday. Maye got into a rhythm during 11-on-11s, finding Boutte on his long touchdowns and also connecting with Hunter Henry and Rhamondre Stevenson for long completions. WR Romeo Doubs: The Maye-Brown connection is not yet where it needs to be, and the same is true for the one between the Patriots’ starting quarterback and fellow offseason addition Romeo Doubs. He continues to be part of the top receiver trio alongside Brown and DeMario Douglas, but he was targeted only once late during the session. The tight ends: New England’s top tight end duo was heavily involved on Tuesday, with Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon on the receiving end of multiple passes. Henry hauled in two Drake Maye throws during team drills, beating Kevin Byard on a corner route and Marcus Jones on a deep out. Eli Raridon, meanwhile, started his day with a contested grab versus Dell Pettus and later added two more catches — all on passes from Tommy DeVito. Undrafted rookie Tanner Arkin, meanwhile, seemingly continues to lead the blocking tight end competition. ED Elijah Ponder: No Harold Landry, no problem? Filling the veteran’s role with the starting defense, the second-year edge was the most notable of New England’s pass rushers on Tuesday. He finished with a would-be sack and drew a hold against Caleb Lomu. Ponder’s development at a position missing two of its supposed top three players — Landry and second-round rookie Gabe Jacas — has been a definitive positive so far. LS Julian Ashby: The long snapper position is arguably the most anonymous in football, so whenever you hear a team’s snapper mentioned by name, chances are something went wrong. That was the case on Tuesday: Ashby delivered a low snap on one of Andy Borregales’ field goal attempts, forcing the second-year kicker to hook the kick to the left from 45 yards out. It was Borregales’ only miss on six attempts. The Patriots will enjoy their first off-day of the summer on Wednesday before returning for their fifth practice of training camp on Thursday. Gates are scheduled to open at 9:15 p.m. ET for that session, with practice again set to start approximately an hour later.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Christian Gonzalez hopes to keep contract talks private after Robert Kraft comments
summary: On the first day of Patriots training camp, owner Robert Kraft said the team had offered Christian Gonzalez a contract that would make him the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history. While Gonzalez appreciates Kraft’s words, he is not interested in negotiating his contract through the media. “Everybody knows what Mr. Kraft has done, a ton […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 25: New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez arrives for the first day of training camp on July 25, 2026. (Photo by John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images On the first day of Patriots training camp, owner Robert Kraft said the team had offered Christian Gonzalez a contract that would make him the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history. While Gonzalez appreciates Kraft’s words, he is not interested in negotiating his contract through the media. “Everybody knows what Mr. Kraft has done, a ton of respect for Mr. Kraft and what he’s done with this franchise,” Gonzalez said Tuesday. “And it’s just something we don’t want to handle in the media. You know, I keep that with the team and my team and go on about that.” When asked whether he was upset at Kraft’s comments or felt the owner was pressuring him, Gonzalez reiterated that he hopes to keep contract discussions between his representatives and the Patriots. Asked whether he is confident an extension will get done, Gonzalez simply replied, “I hope so.” After sitting out voluntary OTAs this spring, Gonzalez reported for mandatory minicamp but did not participate in competitive team periods. That changed at the start of training camp, where the cornerback has been a full participant through the first four practices. “I mean, it’s ball. I’m gonna come out, play some ball, and have fun,” Gonzalez said. “We had a tough ending of the year, that sits on everybody’s mind all year. Just wanted to get on the field and do what I do.” It remains to be seen whether that participation level will continue once the Patriots transition to full pad work following Wednesday’s off day. “I’ll be out here,” Gonzalez said. Before training camp opened, Gonzalez’s teammates wondered whether he would be on the field while awaiting a new contract. Knowing Gonzalez, they weren’t surprised to see him participate fully and have appreciated him doing so. That has helped Gonzalez at times when it comes to blocking out the outside noise. “It’s different, but at the end of the day, it’s business and I’m blessed to be able to do this as my job,” Gonzalez said. “So, you know, can’t get too much into it. Get to wake up and come out here and play football for a job. So very blessed, just happy that I’m able to come out here, run around and do what I love for my living.”
author: Brian Hines

title: Patriots training camp recap: Kayshon Boutte delivers another highlight
summary: Following a walkthrough on Monday, the New England Patriots ramped things back up on Tuesday; players echoed practice felt like the first real one of the summer. That included their first day wearing shells while running nearly two hours long. Here’s what went down on the practice fields behind Gillette Stadium. Attendance PUP/NFI: ED Gabe […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - June 11: New England Patriots wide receiver Kayshon Boutte makes a catch at minicamp on June 11, 2026. (Photo by Barry Chin/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images Following a walkthrough on Monday , the New England Patriots ramped things back up on Tuesday; players echoed practice felt like the first real one of the summer. That included their first day wearing shells while running nearly two hours long. Here’s what went down on the practice fields behind Gillette Stadium. Attendance PUP/NFI: ED Gabe Jacas, RB Terrell Jennings, TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler Injuries: CB Carlton Davis, CB Charles Woods, RB Rhamondre Stevenson The Patriots active roster featured perfect attendance again on Tuesday while five players remained on injured lists. Rookie Gabe Jacas did briefly make his first appearance on the field in street clothes as an observer. Early in practice, cornerback Carlton Davis departed with a member of the medical staff and did not return. Charles Woods, who then filled in for Davis, then also left the field. Late in practice, running back Rhamondre Stevenson walked off before final conditioning work with what appeared to be a heat issue. Takeaways Big play Boutte: In the Patriots two competitive practices this summer, the highlight of each day came from wide receiver Kayshon Boutte making impressive grabs down the field. With the intensity ramped back up on Tuesday, Boutte was on scene again for the highlight of the day getting behind the defense to haul in a 40-plus yard touchdown from Maye. DRAKE & KAYSHON 🎯 pic.twitter.com/K12OK9uijE — New England Patriots (@Patriots) July 28, 2026 Beyond his long score, Boutte hauled his lone other target from Maye and also a pair of passes from Tommy DeVito. While Boutte entered training camp with an uncertain future due to his contract, the 24-year old has been the best offensive player in camp through the first week. Ending strong: Opening practice with their first 7-on-7 period of the summer, Drake Maye started on the shaky side with a pair of overthrows. That continued through the early full-team work as Maye tossed four total uncatchable passes. Later in the day, the QB settled in and delivered the aforementioned touchdown bomb to Boutte and several strong downfield throws to Hunter Henry on a corner and a deep out. Maye’s last throw of the day then put the exclamation mark on his strong finish, as he stepped up in the pocket and floated a pass right in the bucket to Rhamondre Stevenson on a corner route out of the backfield. Drake and A.J.: Of Maye’s four uncatchable passes on Tuesday, three were in the direction of new wide receiver A.J. Brown. After Maye overthrow an open Brown on the first pass of the day in 7s, the duo appeared to be on the wrong page on Maye’s first two passes in 11-on-11s as their chemistry continues to be a work in progress. Throughout the day, Maye did connect with Brown three times (one coming in 7s) — all coming in the underneath area of the field. As for the rest of New England’s pass catchers, it was another quiet day for Romeo Doubs who saw just one target late in the day from Drake Maye in the flat. DeMario Douglas and Boutte were active again, while Efton Chism III caught his long target from Maye before adding two receptions from Tommy DeVito. The backup QB also connected once with Kyle Williams and Mack Hollins underneath. Ponder’s pressure: After being named an offseason award winner, second-year pass rusher Elijah Ponder got off to a strong start in the Patriots’ most physical practice of the summer. Ponder was active along the edge and was in the backfield near Maye on multiple occasions — forcing one bad throw in the process. New England could use someone to emerge from their young group of pass rushers, and Ponder, who has consistently run opposite of veteran Dre’Mont Jones, has started off strong. Other notes: Rookie tight end Eli Raridon continued to be active as a pass catcher hauling in all three targets from DeVito — including a downfield reception and a catch after settling in a zone. UDFA Tanner Arkin also got on the board with the backup QB while continuing to mix in with the first-team. With Morgan Moses (rest) limited during competitive periods, Caleb Lomu and James Hudson rotated in as the top right tackle. Running 1-on-1s in the trenches with shells on, offensive tackle Will Campbell got off to a strong start with a pair of wins. Charles Woods was first-up to replace the injured Carlton Davis in the secondary. With Woods then in-and-out of practice, veteran Kindle Vildor manned the boundary opposite of Christian Gonzalez. New England’s defense debuted some dime looks with Marcus Jones and Mike Brown on the field together. Andy Borregales went 5-of-6 on field goals between roughly 30-to-50 yards with the lone miss coming off a bad snap from Julian Ashby. The Patriots will be off on Wednesday after four straight practices before returning to action on Thursday, for what is expected to be the first day of full pads. Potential rain in the forecast may push the team inside which would close the practice to the public.
author: Brian Hines

title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for WR Kobe Prentice
summary: The New England Patriots did not even make it through one training camp practice without suffering their first season-ending injury of the summer. On Sunday, after what appeared to be a harmless slip-up on his part the previous day, second-year man Jeremiah Webb was placed on IR and therefore shut down for the season. To […]
full_text: WACO, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 29: Kobe Prentice #16 of the Baylor Bears reacts after catching a pass during the second half against the Houston Cougars at McLane Stadium on November 29, 2025 in Waco, Texas. (Photo by Sam Hodde/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots did not even make it through one training camp practice without suffering their first season-ending injury of the summer. On Sunday, after what appeared to be a harmless slip-up on his part the previous day, second-year man Jeremiah Webb was placed on IR and therefore shut down for the season. To take his spot on the roster, the team turned to a wide receiver offering a similar profile: Kobe Prentice, who was added to the club through the waiver wire . Hard facts Name: Kobe Prentice Position: Wide receiver Jersey number: 19 (w) Opening day age: 22 (3/10/2004) Measurements : 5’9 5/8”, 184 lbs, 9 1/8” hand size, 30 1/8” arm length, 73 5/8” wingspan, 4.39s 40-yard dash, 7.16s 3-cone drill, 4.50s short shuttle, 36” vertical jump, 10’3” broad jump, 12 bench press reps, 5.76 Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: Carolina Panthers (2026), New England Patriots (2026-) | College: Alabama (2022-24), Baylor (2025) Prentice was a hot commodity coming out of Calera, AL, High School. The four-star recruit was the recipient of more than 20 scholarship offers, including from the University of Maryland. He initially committed to become a Terrapin, but when Alabama entered the mix shortly thereafter he changed his mind: he decommitted after just two weeks and moved to the Crimson Tide another two weeks later. Prentice’s career in Tuscaloosa was off to a hot start, but after catching 31 passes for 337 yards and two touchdowns as a true freshman he failed to take the next step. He caught only 29 more passes over the next two seasons, and eventually entered the transfer portal to finish his college career with a one-year stint at Baylor. Prentice did not hear his name called in the 2026 NFL Draft, but quickly agreed to a rookie free agent deal with the Panthers. He lasted only three months in Carolina before getting waived and subsequently claimed by the Patriots. Scouting report Strengths: Prentice is a speedster at the wide receiver position, whose 4.39-second 40-yard dash puts him in the 96th percentile among wide receivers. His explosiveness makes him a dangerous player with the ball in his hands and allows him to separate from coverage or pursuit players. In general, he transitions quickly from receiver to runner and is able to pick up yards after the catch. He also plays with a reliable set of mittens: a natural hands catcher, he dropped only five passes throughout his entire college career for a rate of 4.2%. Weaknesses: Checking in at under 5-foot-10 and 184 pounds, Prentice is on the smaller side. Despite his stature, however, he also is not the shiftiest of players; he certainly is explosive and has great straight-line speed, but his agility is lacking both during his release and at his breaks. He also has been up and down as a blocker, a byproduct of his size, and has not showed a lot of versatility in college: between Alabama and Baylor, he primarily played in the slot and did not see any special teams snaps. 2025 review Stats : 11 games (1 start) | 279 offensive snaps | 35 targets, 26 catches (74.3%), 380 receiving yards (14.6/catch), 6 TDs, 2 drops | 0 penalties Season recap: After an encouraging start to his career at Alabama, Prentice fizzled out over his second and third seasons in the program. With only one year of eligibility remaining, he therefore decided to take matters into his own hands and entered he transfer portal while his junior season was still ongoing. Two weeks later, in mid-December, he officially moved to Baylor. His first and only season with the Bears was a mixed bag. In some respects, Prentice bounced back from a lackluster 2024 campaign: he played the most offensive snaps of his career and also set new highs in terms of receiving yards (380), touchdowns (6) and average yards after the catch (7.5). However, as was the case during his final year in Tuscaloosa, he again was used in a relatively limited capacity: he mostly played in the slot and ended up as the No. 4 wide receiver in most of the major categories, including playing time, targets, receptions and receiving yards. The only outlier was those aforementioned six touchdowns, which placed him second among his teammates. Part of that might have been injuries. He dealt with some undisclosed bumps and bruises down the stretch that seemingly had a negative impact on his production: he averaged 44.2 receiving yards and 1.0 touchdowns over the first six games of the season, with those numbers dropping to 23.0 and 0 over the second half of the season. 2026 preview Position: F-receiver | Ability: Camp body/Practice squad candidate | Contract: Signed through 2028 (2029 RFA) What will be his role? Based on his college usage and first two practices in a Patriots uniform, Prentice projects as a slot receiver providing depth behind current top option DeMario Douglas. However, he also could fill a different role in New England: his first practice saw him used as a punt returner, a role he played neither at Alabama nor Baylor. What is his growth potential? Prentice has some athletic skill that could help him find a spot in the NFL, but he likely will have to accept a specialized role. What could that role look like? Maybe he could be a rotational option on offense plus a kickoff and punt returner. Maybe he can grow beyond such a usage, but his college success suggests that there might be a cap on what he can do. Does he have positional versatility? His size and average agility limit Prentice’s usage on offense; he primarily projects as a DeMario Douglas-like package player from the slot. Special teams, however, is where he could truly leave his mark if he can prove himself on kickoffs (where the Patriot have a definitive need) and punts (where Marcus Jones is an All-Pro talent). What is his salary cap situation? Claiming Prentice off waivers meant that the Patriot absorbed the rookie contract he had received from the Panthers after the draft sans the $15,000 in guarantees they gave him. This mean that he currently is on a non-guaranteed $885,000 base salary that simultaneously functions as his cap hit. Under the Top 51 rule, however, he currently has no impact on New England’s books because that salary is not high enough to enter the group of 51 most-expensive cap figures. How safe is his roster spot? Prentice has the talent to make it on an NFL team, but he is facing an uphill climb in New England. At the moment, A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Kayshon Boutte and Mack Hollins are the clear top five at the position, with sophomores Kyle Williams and Efton Chism fighting for the spot(s) behind. Unless there are injuries or trades, including top slot Douglas, the 22-year-old making the roster seems to be an unlikely outcome. Summary: For Prentice to make the roster or at least New England’s practice squad, he will need to show that he can be a factor in the return game. The Patriots giving him reps in that area in his first practice might be a sign of things to come — and a positive one. What do you think about Kobe Prentice heading into the 2026 season? Will he find a way onto the practice squad? Could he even factor into the kickoff return mix? Please head down to the comment section to share your thoughts.

title: Contract details for Patriots draft pick Gabe Jacas
summary: It took until the first day of training camp, but the New England Patriots and second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas finally reached an agreement on his rookie contract. On Sunday, he arrived in Foxborough to put his signature under a four-year, $8.7 million deal. While since put on the non-football injury list, Jacas signing his […]
full_text: BLOOMINGTON, IN - SEPTEMBER 20: Gabe Jacas #17 of the Illinois Fighting Illini looks on during a college football game against the Indiana Hoosiers on September 20, 2025 at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Indiana. (Photo by Joe Robbins/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It took until the first day of training camp, but the New England Patriots and second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas finally reached an agreement on his rookie contract . On Sunday, he arrived in Foxborough to put his signature under a four-year, $8.7 million deal. While since put on the non-football injury list , Jacas signing his pact is a major step toward him becoming the player the Patriots drafted him to be: a core member of their edge rotation and potential cornerstone at the position for years to come. That, of course, is the best case outcome. However, the team is also protecting itself against an alternative scenario. With that said, let’s dive into his contract details as provided by Over the Cap . ED Gabe Jacas: Contract details Base value: $8,656,970 Maximum value: $8,656,970 Guarantees: $6,591,473 Base salary (2026): $885,000 Base salary (2027): $1,278,499 Base salary (2028): $1,671,998 Signing bonus: $2,755,976 2026 (age 22): Base salary: $885,000 Signing bonus: $688,994 Salary cap hit: $1,573,994 2027 (age 23): Base salary: $1,278,499 Signing bonus: $688,994 Salary cap hit: $1,967,493 2028 (age 24): Base salary: $1,671,998 Signing bonus: $688,994 Salary cap hit: $2,360,992 2029 (age 25): Base salary: $2,065,497 Signing bonus: $688,994 Salary cap hit: $2,754,491 The protections mentioned above make Jacas’ contract somewhat unusual as far as rookie deals go, particularly those handed out to second-round selections in this year’s NFL Draft. The reason for that is the uncertainty surrounding his left knee. To recap: Jacas dealt with a hamstring injury that limited him during the pre-draft process, but he also underwent what has been described as a “clean-up” procedure on his knee at one point in the offseason. That surgery and the subsequent status of his knee is why the team inserted an injury waiver into the rookie pact, as first reported by Mike Reiss of ESPN. The waiver voids after 2028, the third year of Jacas’ rookie pact. That is also when the salary guarantees in his contract end. For comparison, the players selected right before and after Jacas in the second round of this year’s draft — Eagles TE Eli Stowers and Jaguars TE Nate Boerkircher — all have guarantees extending into their fourth seasons; Stowers has a $482,466 guarantee in 2029 (23% of his base salary), Boerkircher a $248,183 guarantee (12.1%) Even with the rookie wage scale in place, Jacas’ deal looks different from those around him. Most elementary, the 55th pick in the draft has fewer guarantees in his deal than the 56th pick. The structure of the deal as well as waivers such as the one embedded into Jacas’ contract are not standard practice in the NFL. However, the knee issue apparently prompted the team to take this unusual step — one that could allow the Patriots to alter the deal should medical reasons prevent the young defender from reaching pre-defined parameters. For example, the contract language and details of the waiver might allow the Patriots to void guarantees should his left knee force him to miss regular season playing time. As far as 2026 is concerned, however, head coach Mike Vrabel sounded confident that that is not expected to happen. “Nothing is 100%. I don’t anticipate that whatsoever. I don’t,” Vrabel said ahead of Monday’s practice at Gillette Stadium . “I am excited where he is at. I am excited that he wants to be here, he wants to get going, and he does not want to be on the field with the trainer, I will tell you that. He wants to get back out there, play ball and be the player that we drafted and wanted to be here.”

title: Beyond the Game: How a chance encounter revealed the heart of the Saints community
summary: The New Orleans Saints are celebrating 60 years in New Orleans this season. Throughout those six decades, the franchise has experienced its share of unforgettable highs and challenging lows, but one constant has remained: the enduring bond between the team and the city it calls home — a connection that extends far beyond the bright […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints are celebrating 60 years in New Orleans this season. Throughout those six decades, the franchise has experienced its share of unforgettable highs and challenging lows, but one constant has remained: the enduring bond between the team and the city it calls home — a connection that extends far beyond the bright lights of the Superdome. For Metairie resident Leslie Pedigo, a recent encounter with Saints defensive tackle Christen Miller became more than just a chance meeting. It became a powerful reminder of the kindness, compassion, and lasting connection that continues to unite the Saints, their fans, and the community. Pedigo shared the story on social media, writing: I want to take a moment to tell the New Orleans Saints about one of their newest players. Today I was grocery shopping at Rouses in Metairie. My groceries were already spread across the conveyor belt when a very large gentleman walked up behind me with one bag of fresh shrimp. I told the cashier, “Go ahead and ring him up first. He only has one item.” He smiled and thanked me… then set his shrimp beside my groceries and told the cashier to ring up everything together. I immediately told the cashier, “No, don’t do that. He doesn’t have to buy my groceries.” He looked at me with the kindest smile and said, “My Momma always taught me to do good deeds, and I’d like to bless you today. Please don’t take that blessing from me.” How do you argue with that? He paid for my groceries, grabbed his shrimp, looked at me and simply said, “God bless you,” before walking out. I stood there speechless. The gentleman behind me laughed and asked, “You don’t know who that is, do you?” I said, “No, sir.” He smiled and replied, “That’s a Saints player.” So I hurried outside, stopped him, apologized for not getting his name, and introduced myself. He reached his hand out and said, “I’m Christen Miller.” I asked if he played for the Saints. He smiled and said, “Yes, ma’am.” I asked if we could take a picture together, and he graciously said yes. Christen never acted like he was somebody important. He never sought attention, never expected recognition, never made the moment about himself. He simply chose kindness when no one was watching. To the New Orleans Saints—you didn’t just draft an athlete. You drafted a young man of character. And to Momma Miller… thank you. Thank you for raising a son who understands that true strength is shown through humility, generosity, and faith. Your words clearly stayed with him, and because of that, a complete stranger went home reminded that there is still so much good in this world. Christen, thank you for your kindness. You reminded me that there are still good people in this world. And to your mom… thank you for raising a son whose character speaks louder than any statistic ever could. Truth be told, I don’t know much about football. I’d usually choose dragons and fantasy novels over Sunday games. But this season, I’ll be cheering for my new favorite player—not because of what he does on the field, but because of who he proved himself to be in a grocery store checkout line. Who Dat. Well done @fatchr7s ❤️ pic.twitter.com/BqX9vlAneI — New Orleans Saints (@Saints) July 28, 2026 Christen Miller was just drafted by the Saints in April. Born and raised in Georgia, he’s not only a rookie to the team but also new to the culture of New Orleans. Yet his random act of kindness came naturally—it wasn’t planned or scripted. Instead, it embodied the spirit of a city that values compassion and community. It’s a reflection of why the Saints are woven into the fabric of New Orleans, where giving back and looking out for others extends far beyond the football field. Moments like these are a reminder that, in New Orleans, it’s always been about more than just the game.
